Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:43:19 GMT

Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.

"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.

"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.

"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."

The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.

Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.

Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.

"You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview in 2006.

He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed".

Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas.

"We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011.

It was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers.

When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles.

In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University.

The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library.

Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:33:49 GMT

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock after running more than 36 hours into overtime with countries unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.

If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.

In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."

The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.

"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."

Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.

He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting new global energy demand, outstripping oil and gas.

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War continues, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.

This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as co-hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:33:49 GMT

Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

On artificial intelligence, Sir Tony said that "AI is like fire - it can cook your food and burn your house down".

Sir Tony added the risks of AI are "very considerable" and that tech "can be used for good or bad". "It's a new world," he said.

But he fears the UK does not have the same "dynamism" and "energy" as other countries when it comes to the fast-changing technology sector.

Burnham was in Brussels on Friday to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU - which originally began under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

The prime minister added that beyond the deal "we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

He fell short of discussing whether the UK could rejoin the EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the UK-EU deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Earlier this year, Sir Tony urged PM Andy Burnham to restart negotiations on the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU - but with caveats.

Writing in a paper from the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change published in September, the former prime minister wrote: "We should be clear that we want back into a formal relationship with the EU. But it must be a Europe on a credible path to reform."

"This is not about rerunning the debates of 2016 but taking a new approach rooted in the reality of 2026," he added.

Who was 'a consistent threat'? Newcastle v Arsenal player ratings

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:29:48 GMT

Noni Madueke and Harvey Barnes both scored in a thrilling second half at St James' Park

Arsenal and Newcastle played out an entertaining 2-2 draw at St James' Park on Saturday.

The Gunners took the lead through Eberechi Eze in the first half before Harvey Barnes equalised after the break.

The hosts went ahead when Malick Thiaw bundled in from a corner before Noni Madueke brought the Gunners level with an excellent strike, and that is how it finished.

BBC Sport's Alex Howell has rated the players - and you can have your say too.

What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean?

'The world got to see today' - who is new Spurs star Williams-Barnett?

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:21:01 GMT

This video can not be played

Teenager Williams-Barnett shines as Spurs beat Ipswich

Luca Williams-Barnett's performance in his first Premier League start was that good it had two of his Tottenham team-mates labelling him "incredible".

The 18-year-old winger delivered the opener with his first senior goal and then played a pivotal role in Dominic Solanke's second as Spurs comfortably beat Ipswich 2-0 at home.

As full debuts go, it does not get much better than that.

Yet what might be a sign of the excitement about his potential was manager Roberto de Zerbi calmly explaining that "his talent is bigger than this performance".

The Tottenham boss obviously believes this is just the beginning for the talented teenager.

Williams-Barnett became the youngest Spurs player to score in the Premier League since Gareth Bale against Fulham in September 2007.

They would be pretty impressive footsteps to follow in if he was to get close to the player Bale once was for the north London club.

But for the slightest of touches on his fizzed ball across the area from Ipswich goalkeeper Christian Walton before Solanke turned home, Williams-Barnett would have become the second-youngest player ever to both score and assist in a Premier League game, aged just 18 years and 51 days old.

Only Michael Owen, who did it at 17 years and 364 days for Liverpool in 1997, would have done it at a younger age.

"He's incredible, honestly," Solanke told Final Score. "We get to see him every day in training so we know what a player he is - the confidence he has, the ability he has.

"The world got to see it today, which is great for him. His confidence and ability is amazing. He'll help us a lot."

Luca Williams-Barnett scored on his first start in the Premier League

Williams-Barnett was born in Luton and played for his hometown club before moving to Spurs at the age of 10.

The teenager has been generating excitement with his performances for the club's underage teams for some time.

Back in the 2023-24 season, he played for Tottenham's Under-18s aged just 15 and in the following campaign he scored the Under-18 Premier League goal of the season against Leicester having become renowned for fine long-range strikes.

Williams-Barnett has been around Tottenham's first-team since the 2024-25 campaign as he was on the bench for three Europa League games and a Premier League match but his debut came last season as a substitute in a Carabao Cup game against Doncaster Rovers under previous boss Thomas Frank.

Last December, he scored five goals in a Under-19 UEFA Youth League game against Slavia Prague.

But this season looks to be his real breakthrough.

Williams-Barnett featured in the EFL Cup as a substitute in a 5-1 victory over Charlton in August before coming off the bench against Crystal Palace and Leeds in the Premier League.

Yet it was still a bold choice from De Zerbi to make Williams-Barnett the club's sixth youngest starter in Premier League history given Spurs were coming into this game on the back of a defeat by Leeds United which checked a recent upturn in form.

However, the Spurs boss was rewarded with a man-of-the-match worthy display.

His goal was one of endeavour as he brushed in front of Ipswich defender Abdoul Ouattara to reach Pedro Porro's cross and become the club's youngest scorer on their Premier League full debut.

Throughout the game, he was looking for the ball constantly and not afraid to run with it and try to make things happen.

"Obviously I am so happy for him, every day in the training session he shows his quality," Tottenham defender Destiny Udogie told BBC Match of the Day.

"Honestly he's just an incredible football player. I hope he keeps doing what he's doing."

The winger was unfortunate not to get the assist but the goal does not happen without his powerful cross.

The England youth international was not afraid to take on a shot and his four attempts were all on target while he had a passing accuracy of 77.4% among his 44 touches.

Only Solanke took on more shots in the game with four of his five on target.

"To see him come in and do that on his first Premier League start is crazy," added Solanke.

"He's a great person and is obviously still young, you know what young boys are like.

"But he's very dedicated and so brave on the ball which is great, in his position I think you need that."

This video can not be played

Roberto De Zerbi post-match interview - Tottenham Hotspur v Ipswich Town

Williams-Barnett was replaced by Savio in the 64th minute which brought a standing ovation from the crowd but, with the Brazilian then being forced off later on with an injury, there may be more opportunities in the coming weeks.

Obviously there will be more excitement about the talented teenager now which De Zerbi will have to manage and he has picked midfielder James Maddison as a good mentor for the attacker.

"He's played very well, but his talent is bigger than this performance," the Spurs boss told BBC Match of the Day.

"It was the first game and I am very happy, I am very delighted for his performance, but he is a big, big, big talent.

"The management of the younger talented players is different because you can't take risks to lose their enthusiasm and their positive mentality. But I think Tottenham's dressing room now is a good environment for him.

"I put [James] Maddison to play very close to him to speak the same language but also to help him and put him in the best conditions to play. To play with freedom, to play with his qualities because his qualities are very big.

"He has to work hard but also he has to keep the passion to keep the love of football."

Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 19:20:22 GMT

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

Ireland beat world champions South Africa in thriller

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 18:46:29 GMT

This video can not be played

Highlights: Ireland 20-17 South Africa

Nations Championship

Ireland (17) 20

Tries: Baloucoune 2, Kelleher Con: Prendergast Pen: Prendergast

South Africa (10) 17

Try: Van den Berg, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Feinberg-Mngomezulu

Ireland exacted revenge on world champions South Africa with a thrilling win in Dublin after England's victory over New Zealand dashed Andy Farrell's side's hopes of reaching next weekend's Nations Championship final.

With banned South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus hosting a watchalong stream from his team's hotel, the Springboks fell to back-to-back Test defeats for the first time since November 2022 after last week's loss to France in Paris.

A losing bonus-point, however, is enough for South Africa to top the southern hemisphere table and secure a place in the final against England or France, who face Argentina on Saturday night (20:10 GMT).

Ireland, who were shown five cards during last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, led at the break after two tries from Robert Baloucoune and a Ronan Kelleher score, with Morne van den Berg crossing for the visitors.

After Canan Moodie had a try ruled out early in the second half, Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast - who was cleared to play by a disciplinary panel earlier this week - stretched Ireland's lead with a penalty.

However, hooker Malcolm Marx's 57th-minute try hauled South Africa back into it before yellow cards for Ireland captain Dan Sheehan and Springbok replacement Marco van Staden - the latter upgraded to red - set up a nail-biting denouement in the final 10 minutes.

But amid a hair-raising atmosphere inside Aviva Stadium, Ireland held on for a much-needed win after six successive double-digit defeats by the Springboks, New Zealand and France.

Victory moves Ireland into second before France's meeting with Argentina in Paris.

Nations Championship - Ireland condemn South Africa to back-to-back defeats

Robert Baloucoune (14) scored two first-half tries for Ireland

After an explosive build-up headlined by Erasmus, who was banned for six matches on Tuesday after questioning the integrity of match officials in last week's game against France, Saturday's contest in Dublin had a lot to live up to.

But it delivered emphatically during a breathless first half as Ireland fronted up impressively to South Africa's immense physicality.

In last year's meeting in Dublin, Ireland ended a nightmarish first half with 12 players on the field as South Africa - and their mighty scrum - played the game on their terms.

Fuelled by the pain of that encounter, Ireland attacked the game with real gusto and while South Africa fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicked the first points of the game, Ireland bossed possession and territory for much of the opening half.

There were plenty of moments for the sold-out crowd to cheer, with perhaps the biggest roar reserved for the hosts winning a rare scrum penalty after 26 minutes.

Baloucoune was exceptional, too. In addition to faring well in the aerial battle, the rapid Ulster wing displayed his finishing skills to get Ireland on the board, slipping past Damian Willemse and touching down after being picked out by Stuart McCloskey.

While Baloucoune - who also crossed twice against Fiji last week - was denied a second try by a superb piece of last-ditch defending by Springbok number eight Cameron Hanekom, Joe McCarthy won a turnover to deny the visitors momentum.

From there, Ireland kicked to the corner and eventually worked the ball back to Baloucoune on the right, who dived over in the corner for his second.

But with both conversion attempts missed by Prendergast, Ireland were pegged back when South Africa won a penalty inside green territory, with Van den Berg dotting down off the back of a scrum.

Unlike last year, though, Ireland had the final say of the half and restored their lead when Kelleher scored off a well-worked line-out.

In a bizarre twist, banned South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus hosted a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel

South Africa's frustration deepened early in the second half when Moodie's fine finish in the corner was ruled out after the replacement back was pushed into touch by Mack Hansen.

Ireland pulled further clear when Prendergast atoned for his missed kicks at goal with a penalty to put the hosts 20-10 up.

But after world player of the year Marx forced his way over with more than 20 minutes remaining, Ireland were denied a fourth try when Sheehan - in his first Test start at number eight - was held up on the line.

Sheehan was then yellow-carded at the same time as Van Staden, for a croc roll and dangerous clear-out respectively, and while South Africa pushed for a late winner, Ireland held on for a statement win.

Reacting from what looked like a conference room at his team's hotel, Erasmus slammed a table in frustration at full-time before his stream ended, spelling a disappointing end to a tumultuous week for the two-time World Cup-winning coach.

Hormuz swim highlights environmental cost of war

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 16:12:31 GMT

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.

Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".

He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

The swimmer is believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in March.

He swam from Musandam Island in the strait to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 4km (2.5 miles) from where he was swimming on the first day.

On the second day, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from the burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier Tara Gas and later passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

"My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers on board," Pugh said.

"The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences - not just for crew members, but also on the surrounding marine environment."

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often receives less attention than the human cost.

"War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart, and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes," he said.

"But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped."

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 13:29:55 GMT

Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity £1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".

Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over £11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."

He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another £7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."

Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."

The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.

The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 13:17:38 GMT

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBC

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:00:03 GMT

The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

Catherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy.

In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.

She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.

The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.

This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.

She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.

Among the film crew for the documentary, as director of photography, was Will Warr, who has worked with Catherine and her family before.

His pictures have been used in a video birthday message by Catherine and a Christmas card which showed a relaxed image of the princess and Prince William and their children.

The filmmaker also made the personal video statement that marked the end of her chemotherapy in September 2024, with her message: "Out of darkness, can come light."

Kate Phillips, the BBC's chief content officer, said it was hoped the 30-minute documentary "will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges".

Catherine was treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital and funds from the distribution of this documentary, which is to be broadcast in other countries, will be paid to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

When cancer patients finish treatment at the London hospital they can symbolically ring a bell.

"I didn't ring the bell," says Catherine, speaking to her brother James Middleton.

"Maybe this is your ringing the bell," he says, about carrying out the Three Peaks Challenge and this documentary about her healing.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 04:34:00 GMT

A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.

Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

'I was exhausted': Two days in the shoes of a tradwife

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:29:00 GMT

Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.

As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.

The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.

While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.

For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife.

On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life.

"I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.

During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.

She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress.

"What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."

The tradwife phenomenon has been popularised on social media which has been a major driving force in its expansion.

Some US creators have millions of followers - Hannah Neeleman, widely seen as one of the world's leading tradwife influencers, has 10.3 million users following her Instagram account, Ballerina Farm.

However, another popular American influencer, Nara Smith, has rejected the label. Smith married young, has four children and her content centres on cooking food (or even making toothpaste) from scratch, but insists she's no tradwife.

"They kind of used me as the poster child of the tradwife movement, which was very bizarre to me," Smith said on the Call Her Daddy podcast. "Sure, do I love cooking... but that's a passion of mine, it's a hobby - it's not something that I need to be doing."

The tradwife trend has also made its way into popular culture, with author Caro Claire Burke's satirical novel Yesteryear selling more than 1.4 million copies and Hollywood actress Anne Hathaway has signed up to produce and star in a film adaptation.

Much of the tradwife lifestyle is played out on social media with glossy images of baking and planting vegetables, but Molly Edwards has been a tradwife for more than 15 years, long before TikToks existed.

She sees the role as more than "just floating around in a dress, baking sourdough".

"It's very connected to our faith," she explains in the documentary, "and what we believe God has designed women to do and to be in their homes, just under the guidance and leadership of our husbands."

Jay tells BBC News she saw how much work Molly did which had "parallels" with her upbringing in a conservative Muslim family, which included her entering an arranged marriage when she was 19. She and her husband divorced about five years later.

"I've helped raise my siblings, I know my way around a kitchen, I can cook, I tutored my siblings," Jay said. "Other than the chicken coop, it's not unfamiliar territory. But I think doing it for two days - I know this sounds ridiculous... it's just the relentless pace of her life."

While Molly manages the house, her husband Aaron is a full-time theologian who shares his views on religion and anti-feminism on social media.

When speaking to Jay, Aaron explained the reason the household work was down to his wife: "Molly's obviously omni-competent and brilliant but submission is still really hard," he says, "and when I say something that Molly disagrees with, that's when the submission really matters."

"It happens at least once a month where something will happen where Molly will have a certain idea… it might be something trivial like how we should organise the day and I might have a bigger vision where I go, 'No, that's been overridded.'"

Jay admits that during her interviews with Aaron, there was some "sparring", with the pair often not seeing eye-to-eye.

"He doesn't like feminism," Jay said, "he thinks feminism's ruined society."

"He definitely romanticises a bygone era, which I think [means] you're going down a dangerous path. [He had] the idea that women were better off in the Victorian times - according to who? What evidence do you have of that?"

While Molly says her social media does not make money, some tradwives do look to turn a profit through their posts.

West Sussex couple Megan and Joseph Landreth-Smith have three children and have an Instagram account with nearly 6,000 followers.

Megan often gets brand deals to share products on her Instagram, which she says helps with some extra income and "feels like a really natural fit" around what they are doing already - producing content while being with their children.

Just like many influencers, trolls can be a problem, but they also help to bring in some money.

With her husband Zion, Yorkshire-based life coach Laura Zachary promotes a course called the Academy of Biblical Wifery, based on their born-again Christian beliefs, to more than 32,000 Instagram followers.

"The more disagreement on a comments section, the more people that come to it and the more you get paid".

In a busy and complicated world, Jay said she appreciates why some women see the attraction in living in what seems to be a more simple way as a tradwife.

But after a few days of experiencing a tradwife's role, she was exhausted and frustrated, saying the belief that men were in charge of everything was "where I draw the line".

"I came away having a lot of respect for [Molly] and to a degree understanding the appeal," Jay said, "but I think for me the submission was the hardest part to grapple with and seeing submission in real life play out in front of me - that was an interesting experience."

The "appeal" which Jay identifies goes much broader - a report published by King's College London found 79% of women surveyed were drawn to the relaxed, calm lifestyle it portrays.

But its co-author, Prof Heejung Chung, who specialises in researching the tradwife phenomenon, said that it can be the tip of a political change.

The content might begin with "nice dresses", said Chung, but can "draw them towards more extremist, far-right, or nationalist ideologies, which ultimately seek to curtail women's autonomy and reinforce patriarchal authority".

However, her report concludes most young women and men surveyed showed "largely progressive views on gender roles".

For those who liked the content, it was down to its "lifestyle imagery", rather than "the traditional gender division of labour or power".

But this does not mean the tradwife movement poses no risk to gender equality, the report says, and its "growing popularity... should not be dismissed or trivialised".

Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:06:11 GMT

Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.

Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.

The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.

It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.

Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.

Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at £532 to a £699 Samsung.

But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at £616 (down from £749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.

Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.

There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.

Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.

Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.

The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide in November 2025.

A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.

He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.

Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.

He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?

BBC News Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:03:16 GMT

After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?

What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.

He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they go for an equally big name as a ‘Bond girl’, or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.

Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".

Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."

And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?

No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya, whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.

The duo have already shared three films together this year and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.

Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".

But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.

Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".

Speculation is also growing over Pattinson’s partner, actor and singer Suki Waterhouse. She once said she’d love to play "a bad-ass Bond girl".

But there isn’t a precedent for husband-wife couples in the films, and it may be more likely that she picks up a cameo role, if indeed she wants to.

Meanwhile, TV presenter Maya Jama has picked up new interest following her storming run on Celebrity Traitors. After she quit Love Island, rumours swirled that she could be the next Bond girl - but she’s just signed a Netflix deal, so it’s unclear whether that would still be a possibility.

Another strong contender is Florence Pugh who, like Zendaya, also stars alongside Pattinson in Dune: Part Three. Earlier this week she threw her hat in the ring to be in the new Bond film - although as a villain, rather than his leading lady.

"She ticks quite a few boxes if they're looking for someone bankable," says Rose. "I could absolutely see her as a Bond woman who turns out to be the villain, someone Bond thinks is on his side, but she's actually been playing him the whole time."

Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)

Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said.

Other names that have been floated include Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley, Marisa Abela, Emily Blunt, Lily James, Chase Infiniti, Inde Navarrette, Simone Ashley, Deva Cassel and Ambika Mod.

And it could easily be someone totally different. Producers have previously chosen a Bond girl who isn't particularly famous yet - or is on the cusp of stardom.

But then there’s the wider question of whether the whole idea of a “Bond girl” is now somewhat outdated.

Historically, the character had little agency and existed primarily as Bond's romantic interest - and the term "girl" itself is also criticised for infantilising women.

Monica Bellucci rejected the label. She told the Guardian ahead of her appearance in Spectre in 2015: "I can't say I'm a Bond girl because I'm too mature to be a Bond girl. I say Bond lady; Bond woman."

The way the films have treated Bond girls "hasn't always aged well", says Rose.

Some scenes from 1960s Bond films are "basically rape", and "wouldn't fly today", said No Time To Die director Cary Fukunaga in 2021 - referring to Thunderball and Goldfinger.

In reality, we have come a long way since then.

Over the years, producers have taken steps to usher the franchise into the modern era.

These days, the women of Bond are now much more likely to be sharp, capable equals to 007 - and what's defined as "attractive" has also evolved.

Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).

We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.

Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.

"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".

Many people say, however, there is still further to go.

Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."

"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," suggests Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”

Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.

“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and filmmaker.

"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."

More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.

“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”

None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.

"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.

But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.

“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.

Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.

But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."

There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit".

"Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 23:20:33 GMT

The livestream begins.

A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."

In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Or not, as the case may be.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."

In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."

Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.

"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.

But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.

Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".

The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.

Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.

One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".

"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.

Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.

"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.

"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.

"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."

Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.

Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.

"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling. "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."

Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."

She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."

With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera
