What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:07:55 GMT

The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."

One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.

A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.

If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.

British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.

The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.

The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.

The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.

The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme.

In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".

Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why... are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?

"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"

Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.

The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.

Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.

He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

I've only sold five copies of GTA 6, says shop owner

BBC News Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:29:33 GMT

The owner of an independent game shop says he has only sold five copies of the highly anticipated open-world action-adventure Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA 6, as it is known, is estimated to become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.

But Richard Tewksbury, who runs Super Game Shack in the Silver Arcade in Leicester, said he had seen "embarrassing" sales of the game because it was only released as a digital download and not on disc.

"People are super, super, super hungry for this game - so it's already doing crazy numbers already - but that's not translated for us," he said.

"I've only sold four copies on PS5 and one copy on Xbox," added Tewksbury.

"It's because it's all digital - no-one sadly wants to buy a code in a box. We gave it a little go, but they just knocked it dead with making it digital. For game shops, it's a write-off.

"I'm really behind the game - I think it's amazing - but for shops, it's just not great."

In June, developer Rockstar Games said physical copies would contain a code for a digital download rather than the more traditional format. The company has been contacted for comment.

Tewksbury said, while he thinks the game is "amazing", the choice to not sell physical copies with discs was "not great" for smaller stores.

The release of the blockbuster came after two delays to its initial launch date in autumn 2025.

In advance of the launch, GTA 6 generated an estimated £1.25bn ($1.65bn) in revenue based on an estimated 17.07 million units sold, sales tracker SensorTower said.

However, Tewksbury said sales at local stores had been poor because physical editions contained download codes rather than discs.

"It is possibly the biggest game hype there's ever been - 13 years people have been waiting for this," he said.

GTA 6 is one of the first major games to only be released without a traditional disc version.

However, Tewksbury said the reality for game shops was that this style of release would be the future of the industry.

Many consoles are now without physical disc drives and PlayStation announced in July that its games would no longer be released on discs from January 2028.

Sony, which owns PlayStation, said the move came "as consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital".

"This is the way it's going to be," Tewksbury said.

"It's a big effect for us because it was such a massive game - everyone wants it.

"A lot of people aren't even aware that you could actually get it as a code in a box in a shop.

"Suddenly everyone's already pre-ordered it months in advance because the download is so large and [they] aren't thinking about us."

There was frustration from many gamers when it was announced that there would be no disc copies of GTA 6.

Rob Spence, physical media collector and TikToker, said there was "outrage" over more games being released without a disc.

"There're so many great benefits to physical media," he told BBC Radio Leicester.

"For me personally, it's that ability to touch, to hold, to really admire the artwork that goes into the casing and how it's all put together.

"I always think there's nothing better than walking into a room and seeing a library or a shelf full of great pieces in a collection that can't ever be taken away from you.

"There are so many great retailers out there, like the shop in Leicester, people should go and support them.

"Nothing beats holding the game."

Spence, from Rothley in Leicestershire, said town and cities might see "another wave" of closures, if stores did not find ways of further diversifying as sales of physical games decreased.

"It's a very sad thought and unfortunately, this is just the first wave of these types of releases," he said.

"We are now going to see more of this in 2027, and then we're going to see a lot more of it in 2028."

He added the gaming community could lose its "sense of belonging" that came with the stores.

"We all remember that community feel these shops should have, whether you came in at 10am on a Saturday with your pocket money to buy a latest release - we're going to miss all that," he said.

"But we're also now going to miss the midnight releases, when again, there was that sense of community, that sense of belonging.

"That sort of party atmosphere to be one of the first to get your hands on a game - that will all go."

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

If the past year was the “mathpocalypse”, a claim that AI has helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis is its most stunning horseman yet. Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic says he has used AI to solve this problem, which has sat at the heart of mathematics for nearly 200 years. This is not just the latest in the series of famed mathematics problems to fall to AI, but could be the biggest mathematical result of the century. Accordingly, mathematicians have received the news with a combination of exhilaration, bewilderment and caution.

“If true, it would, in my opinion be the greatest achievement yet by AI, and one of the greatest proofs in the history of mathematics,” says Thomas Bloom at the University of Manchester in the UK. “The Riemann hypothesis has represented a major barrier in our current understanding of the way numbers behave – if the AI proof has correctly solved it, this would represent a huge leap in what we know.”

Rainer Dietmann at Royal Holloway University of London is similarly in awe. “If it turns out to be correct, this is not only huge, it’s the biggest result in pure mathematics ever… It’s like having found the Holy Grail,” he says.

Advertisement

Dating back to the 1800s, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers. Because they cannot be factored into any smaller whole numbers, primes are like the atoms of numbers – they are the simplest units out of which any other number can be made. However, predicting when a prime will show up in a list of numbers is notoriously difficult. In 1859, Bernhard Reimann hypothesised a formula that would stunningly reduce that difficulty, but didn’t finish a proof before he died. Mathematicians have been trying to wrangle it ever since. After years of approximate results, including an AI-generated proof released by Open AI in October, Alpöge’s work may have finally confirmed Reimann’s centuries’ old intuition.

“It has captured the imagination, presumably because it is about something that we can all understand – the prime numbers – and because it has resisted the efforts of so many for so long. And it is important to mathematicians because it is so useful for other problems: a lot of theorems begin, “assume the Riemann hypothesis…” says Chris Daw at the University of Reading in the UK.

The new proof has not been formally reviewed by other mathematicians, which would be required for publication in an academic journal, and Alpöge hasn’t released the full proof, which he described in a public statement as being over 250,000 pages long. Instead, he has released the version of the proof that has been adapted for verification in the proof-checking software Lean, which is 17 million lines long. Anthropic and Alpöge did not respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

Michael Levitin at the University of Reading says hundreds of thousands of pages of Lean output won’t be easily checked. “In proportion to the magnitude of this claim, we should be appropriately sceptical,” says Bloom. “Even after the Lean formalisation has been independently checked, it remains possible that the AI might be taking advantage of some subtle undiscovered bug in the code. I’d feel more confident once we have a combination of the Lean compiling correctly, with no bugs found, and also human experts [having] had a chance to discuss the ‘big picture’ of the proof and whether it seems plausible.”

“Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to understand the proof themselves. And that will of course take time, since we only move at biological speeds,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. It is here that this new result, with its prospect of incredible historical significance, exemplifies the trouble mathematicians have had with AI over the past year, as it has been used to check one problem after another off their most coveted list of open questions.

Put simply, AI-assisted work benefits tremendously from prior work by human mathematicians, yet its end result isn’t immediately understandable to them. Coming to terms with the new proof will almost certainly take a long time, and it brings to the fore big questions about the future of mathematics. “Pretty much every mathematician will need time to process this. If AI can do this, what can it not do – in mathematics, at least?” says Daw. Many mathematicians already feel a sense of grief and anguish over how quickly AI tools have been solving problems that would have previously consumed a human mathematician’s whole career, and Dietmann says this new proof could have a similarly negative effect.

“What looked impossible one year ago has become reality. Many other problems in mathematics, computer science and related fields will fall as well, and it will become increasingly difficult for humans even to follow and understand,” he says. “While this progress is tremendous, it will massively amplify the despair by many in the mathematical community.”

Some mathematicians are more optimistic. “This is a very exciting time for pure mathematicians, and we are needed more than ever,” says Alex Bartel at the University of Glasgow in the UK. “AI is capable of spitting out proofs at a much faster pace than we are used to, but our task remains that of properly understanding what is going on… and that work is as fulfilling as ever, but there is now a lot more of it. The announcement of a very long proof of the Riemann hypothesis only reinforces my view.”

Mere hours after Alpöge’s announcement, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, wrote in a blog post that mathematician Alessandro Masullo has also put forward a proof of a generalised version of the Riemann hypothesis. This proof was completed without the use of AI, and it is 940 pages long. It has also not yet been checked by other mathematicians nor confirmed using Lean.

This day will be remembered as a shocking one, and the aftershocks may continue. “I can only compare this achievement to the aliens with a vastly superior intelligence coming to the Earth and explaining to us all the sacred mysteries we ever dreamed of,” says Alexei Skorobogatov at Imperial College London. “Humanity managed to create an amazingly powerful yet completely alien form of intelligence. The only event in history I can compare it to is the discovery of a nuclear bomb. Hopefully, AI will be put to better use!”

Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Flying in the face of Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, quantum physics could turn the famous force repulsive instead of attractive – and we could soon test the idea in the lab.

A hallmark of gravity as we know it is that it pulls objects with mass together: gravity explains why the moon orbits Earth, and why an apple falls to the ground after detaching from the tree. While this is well established, there is still no agreement on how gravity works at scales dominated by quantum effects, and what quantum properties it may have.

Now, two research teams have independently found that quantum effects can make gravity act repulsively, pushing objects apart instead of pulling them together.

Advertisement

Could gravity produce quantum entanglement if it’s not fully quantum?

“Gravity is always attractive – this has been the cornerstone of gravity from Newton to Einstein,” says Pablo Saldanha at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil, who worked on one of the studies with Vlatko Vedral and Chiara Marletto, both at the University of Oxford. “Anti-gravity or repulsion: no one has seen that before,” says Sougato Bose at University College London, who co-authored the other study with Lev Vaidman at Tel Aviv University in Israel.

A key concept for both studies was that of a quantum superposition state. Consider a car driving down a city street. When it arrives at an intersection where one road forks into two, it can take either the left or the right branch. But a quantum car would have another option: to enter a superposition of taking the left road and also the right one, assuming a state where it is impossible to tell where the car is exactly without disturbing it.

Another quantum object, called a “probe”, moving along a path parallel to both the left and right road branches, would be gravitationally attracted to the car. In both new studies, the researchers mathematically modelled an analogous setup and used equations to show that this gravitational interaction would make the car and the probe inextricably connected through the link of quantum entanglement.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The two teams mathematically examined a scenario equivalent to the two roads – left and right – merging some time after they had split apart. At this point, a measurement taken by the probe can reveal how each of the paths shaped the superposed car’s quantum state.

Quantum mechanics is probabilistic. This means that if this experiment is repeated many times, the final state of the car won’t always be the same, but will follow some distribution of states instead, reflecting its capacity to follow a combination of the left and right branches. The researchers in both experiments found that if all but some specific states were then discarded after the measurement – a technique called post-selection, partly pioneered by Vaidman – then the probe should theoretically experience gravitational repulsion and be pushed away from the car in the experiment. “That repulsion, that going away [from the superposed object], is created at the time of the measurement,” says Bose.

Even Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which has for over a century proven to be an incredibly accurate description of gravity, doesn’t predict this kind of gravitational repulsion. “There is a measurement that will somehow conditionally give you repulsive gravitational force,” says Vedral. Confirmation that such a repulsive force occurs would demonstrate the quantum nature of gravity.

If gravity is a truly quantum entity, something as simple as measuring the strength of an object’s gravitational field should change its quantum state

Because this measurement effect is inherently quantum, just like the possibility of a superposition state is, the scenario the two teams explored doesn’t have any non-quantum analogues. But it could still be tested in experiments.

Objects that can stay in a superposition state for the duration of an experiment would have to be very small, says Bose, and yet also still massive enough for gravity to make a difference to their behaviour. Bacterium-sized objects should do the trick. He and Vaidman calculated that the probe object at this scale would experience acceleration roughly smaller than a quadrillionth of gravitational acceleration on Earth. Vedral says that he and his colleagues are already working with experimentalists who specialise in unusually large quantum objects.

Tomasz Paterek at the University of Gdańsk in Poland says that the new idea is “brilliant”. Past studies explored making the force between electrons attractive, even though it is usually repulsive, through post-selection. But this is the first time that the same process has been shown to potentially reverse gravity’s character too, he says. In Paterek’s view, lab experiments that use gravity to quantum entangle objects could be achievable in the near future – but he cautions they will be really difficult to perform.

Physical Review A DOI: 10.1103/df22-8kb6

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

New Scientist November 20, 2026

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven, and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution.

Advertisement

The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers. These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention.

He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers.

But the formula only works if all the zeros always sit on the same vertical line when plotted in a coordinate system where the horizontal axis tracks their real number constituents and the vertical axis their imaginary ones. Riemann calculated some of these zeros, which confirmed his idea, but could not prove the hypothesis more generally. It became the biggest unsolved problem in all of mathematics. “It is a legendary problem, the queen of all the Millennium Problems,” says Scott Armstrong at Sorbonne University in Paris. “For the whole field of mathematics, there could not be a bigger theorem.”

In the intervening years, mathematicians used computers to verify that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros line up on Riemann’s vertical line and much work has gone into proving that the zeros at least must lie in a strip of the coordinate systems around this line. In fact, a previous release of AI proofs by OpenAI on 6 October contained the proof of a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, placing the non-trivial zeros in the neighbourhood but not exactly on the line Riemann predicted.

In a statement released to the public, Alpöge wrote that his proof, developed with Anthropic’s Claude AI, is over 250,000 pages long, and it has not yet been fully read, digested or understood by the mathematics community. Even its translation into the language of the proof-checking software Lean is 17,000,000 lines long. That means it will take time to carefully adjudicate. “I have not had a chance to read the 17 million lines of Lean, so cannot speak to their truth,” says Alex Walker at University College London. And the announcement didn’t illuminate the details of the method, he adds.

OpenAI has released hundreds of papers claiming to make progress on the biggest open problems in mathematics – here are some with the most potential

Consequently, it is currently unclear exactly what mathematical tricks the AI leveraged, though early commentators suggest that it drew on a vast swathe of mathematics spanning several fields including number theory and arithmetic geometry. Some have suggested the AI made connections across these fields that don’t already clearly exist in the literature.

The Lean code is in the process of being adapted to efficiently run on a computer that can review it, which will provide a crucial check on the new proof. “While Lean itself has some issues, so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates have had to be retracted,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, it may take years to unravel all the details of the new proof and reap any of its mathematical insights, he says. But the ramifications will certainly be enormous and extensive.

Notably, it resolves the biggest open question of number theory by finally making primes make sense. Numerous results also build on the assumption that Riemann was right and will now stand on firmer ground. And then there are implications for functions similar to the Riemann zeta function, known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis. “An extremely large number of results have previously been proven subject to the generalised Riemann hypothesis,” says John Nicholson at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Germany. He says there are also a number of fast algorithms for computing quantities in algebraic number theory whose correctness depends on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis even has ties to theories of chaos in quantum systems in physics.

“The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers,” wrote Enrico Bombieri at Princeton University when outlining the Millenium Problem more than a quarter of a century ago. Now, thanks to a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, that distribution may have been shown to be not that dangerous after all.

US bill aiming to boost clean energy could backfire

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Among the grass, sagebrush and tumbleweeds on a cattle ranch in Rawlins, Wyoming, workers have been building roads and pads for 600 wind turbines. Meanwhile, emission lines are being strung from the site to a hub in Nevada, where the electricity generated can help power Las Vegas and Los Angeles.

It will be one of the biggest wind farms in the US, a win for the economy and the climate. But it took 18 years to get the approvals to start building. Even less complex projects now typically wait five years to connect to the grid.

These delays are the target of a 400-page permitting reform bill backed by Republicans and US President Donald Trump as well as many Democrats. It has just passed the Senate and will now be taken up by the House of Representatives.

Advertisement

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it far easier to build renewable energy projects and transmission lines. One of its authors, long-time climate champion Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, says it would be the country’s “biggest implemented climate bill”.

But BAAJA would also speed up permitting for natural gas plants and pipelines, coal mines and data centres, while weakening environmental regulations. The American Petroleum Institute has even sent a BAAJA-branded food truck to hand out free tacos on Capitol Hill. The climate movement is split. Some experts fear the bill would increase greenhouse gas emissions, and former Vice President Al Gore called it a “serious mistake”.

Both sides say BAAJA is a gamble, but supporters say it’s one worth taking. Jigar Shah, who formerly oversaw infrastructure loans at the US Department of Energy, says it would set up a race between clean energy and fossil fuels. “The world’s best energy developers right now are in the clean energy space,” he says. “Why wouldn’t I bet on the world’s best energy developers?”

Free newsletter

Climate policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.6°C of warming by 2100, and greenhouse gas emissions are not yet falling, partly because additional renewable energy supply has been outpaced by additional demand from data centres. Data centre energy demand will double by 2030, and in the US, 60 per cent of that demand will be met by natural gas, according to the International Energy Agency.

The US grid, which is fractured into three separate grid regions and seven electricity markets, needs to speed up the build-out of renewables and transmission lines from the sunny, windy areas in the central US to the population centres near the coasts. But grid operators and regulators are overwhelmed, developers disagree on who should pay for transmission lines and court battles can last years. As a result, more than 2000 gigawatts of electricity generation and storage projects are awaiting grid connection, most of them renewable.

BAAJA would allow the federal government to override states’ objections and force grid regions to plan transmission lines together. But it would also narrow the timelines and reasons for challenging projects under environmental laws like the Clean Water Act, and, in some instances, cut lower district courts out of these cases. It essentially gives up tools to stop fossil fuel projects in exchange for tools to accelerate clean energy ones.

Environmentalists like Bill McKibben have warned that accelerated pipeline construction could lock in fossil fuel demand, and weaker protections would disempower concerned residents.

“Why would we choose now to give the fossil fuel industry what it’s wanted forever?” says David Watkins at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Compromise will be required; I just think the balance here is off.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Following this month’s election sweep, Democrats will take control of Congress in January and could potentially renegotiate the bill. But Trump would probably veto it, and even when the party controlled both Congress and the White House in 2022, it failed to pass a proposed permitting reform bill.

“You have a lot of newly elected oil-and-gas-state Democrats,” cautions Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh at Columbia University in New York.

Think tanks have projected that although the bill would increase liquefied natural gas exports, it would boost the build-out of renewables more than coal and gas plants. This would eventually reduce electricity prices by 3 to 5 per cent and US annual emissions by 0 to 4 per cent, depending on the future costs of clean tech and fossil fuels, according to Rhodium Group.

But modelling by Kevin Kircher at Purdue University in Indiana found that BAAJA would raise US annual emissions by 2 per cent. While energy demand will increase in any case, he argues the bill would increase demand still further, due in part to the Jevons paradox. This is when a decline in the cost of a resource leads buyers to consume more of it. For instance, if electricity prices did go down under BAAJA, cryptocurrency mining operations might run for longer periods or install more hardware.

“Unless all of that additional new electricity demand is met by clean energy, if even 10 per cent of it is met by fossil fuels, then emissions increase overall,” says Kircher. “People are severely underestimating the amount of new fossil fuel combustion that we will also see as a result of BAAJA.”

Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

US, Russia and China look set to block ban on autonomous weapons

New Scientist November 20, 2026

The US, China and Russia are expected to undermine attempts to enact a global ban on autonomous weapons at a conference this week. Such weapons are becoming an increasingly common feature of modern conflict, but are criticised as presenting an unacceptable risk to civilians and muddying the waters of accountability in war.

The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) is a United Nations treaty binding together 128 states to regulate excessively harmful or indiscriminate weapons. The treaty’s five existing protocols ban incendiary weapons, bombs that create shrapnel that can’t be detected by X-rays and lasers designed to blind soldiers – weapons that the global community has decided are beyond the pale.

For more than 10 years, states have debated adding autonomous weapons to the list. Members meet every five years to discuss what changes may be needed to the treaty, and this week the seventh such Review Conference is being held in Geneva. But there have been few signs of progress and efforts to bind parties to promises of action look set to fail.

Advertisement

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

The use of AI is common in militaries around the world, helping to pick targets among overwhelming piles of intelligence data and automating certain functions of weapons, including steering missiles and drones.

Humans are usually in the loop at some point, but on at least one occasion to date, fully autonomous drones have been used without human oversight to kill enemy soldiers. A senior figure in the Ukrainian defence industry told New Scientist earlier this year that a test took place two years ago that lead to two deaths.

It is that sort of weapon, where human input is minimal or non-existent, that most worries campaigners like Elizabeth Minor at pressure group Stop Killer Robots. “Machines shouldn’t make life and death decisions. Tasking weapons systems or algorithms to identify targets and kill people is just a moral red line we shouldn’t be crossing,” she says.

Free newsletter

Over the past three years, work has gone on behind the scenes in the CCW to lay out the groundwork for a ban. Peru, as chair of the conference, has proposed that negotiations should start on a protocol and that work to create that ban should finish within two years.

Minor says 130 countries support a ban or restrictions on autonomous weapons, and more than 70 are ready to begin negotiations. But she warns that the US, Russia and China, as well as other nations including the UK, Japan and South Korea, are likely to block such efforts. “What we’ll obviously see as the week goes on, unfortunately, is the weakening of this text [from Peru] at the behest of larger militarised states who want to continue to see these weapons unregulated,” she says.

Discussions are likely to run late into the night on 20 November and deliberations aren’t open to the public, with an announcement expected on 21 November. The CCW operates on unanimity, meaning that just one state can stymie action.

The US has already proposed at the meeting that further work should be carried out to investigate how existing international law applies to autonomous weapons, arguing that an update to the CCW is unnecessary, and essentially kicking the can down the road on a potential ban until the next meeting in 2031.

AIs can’t stop recommending nuclear strikes in war game simulations

Aurel Sari at the University of Exeter, UK, says autonomous weapons already fall under existing law around armed conflict, meaning those who use them must avoid attacks that would cause excessive collateral damage and take all feasible precautions to spare civilians. An autonomous weapon that can’t be used in line with these rules is already unlawful. But none of these existing laws ban their use, and Sari sees hurdles in the way of greater regulation.

“Supporters of a ban want to stop weapons that select and attack targets in ways their operators cannot predict or control. Meanwhile, states that operate defensive systems that react faster than any human can, such as systems protecting warships against incoming missiles automatically, do not want to see these prohibited,” says Sari. “A ban wide enough to meet the first concern risks also capturing these defensive systems, while a ban narrow enough to win the support of the major military powers might prohibit little that anyone intends to field.”

Because of this, the leading states that are developing these systems, among them the US, Russia and China, have different strategic priorities from others, says Sari.

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

“None of the major powers wants an agreement that would hand its rivals an advantage on the battlefield. A wide-ranging ban would appeal to them only if all their rivals observed it as well. That would require states to agree on exactly what the ban covers, to close the loopholes and to establish a reliable way of checking compliance,” says Sari. “None of these seems achievable at present.”

Countries are already using these weapons, but there is still time to act, says Minor. “I wouldn’t say that we’re too late to make rules. You can do this at any point. And there is still time to have a meaningful response to this that can prevent things going down an even worse path, but that depends on the international community really acting now.”

That could mean side-stepping the CCW entirely and taking the issue to the UN General Assembly, where you only need a majority to start negotiations on a treaty. “But they need to do it now otherwise we’ll just keep seeing this dynamic of a race to the bottom for these capabilities,” says Minor.

Unexpected stone tools from Israel raise questions about cultural evolution

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Half a million years ago, prehistoric hominins in the eastern Mediterranean produced some of the earliest known stone blades, 100,000 years before the technology became established in the region. This discovery adds to growing evidence that early humans repeatedly invented new tools without necessarily adopting them, raising questions about what really drove technological evolution in prehistory.

Blades are thin fragments of stone that are at least twice as long as they are wide. In the region of the eastern Mediterranean known as the Levant, a blade technology tradition called the Amudian techno-complex became widespread around 400,000 years ago. This replaced earlier “Acheulean” tools, which included classic teardrop-shaped handaxes, as well as flakes – sharp pieces of stone that are removed from a larger rock and are cruder and more irregularly shaped than blades.

Yet after analysing hundreds of stone artefacts at the archaeological site of Jaljulia in Israel, researchers found traces of serial blade production 500,000 years ago that used a specific technique resembling that used in the Amudian system.

Advertisement

Monsoon-driven wildfires may have shaped human evolution

“We identify an earlier, small-scale manifestation of this method, which we term Amudian–like,” says team member Vlad Litov at Tel Aviv University in Israel. He say the ancient tool-makers were “culturally conservative”, and their initial flirtation with blade tools never flourished into an established practice.

“Despite reaching the techno-cognitive capability to make some blades, these hominins still adhered to their traditional Acheulean technology,” he says.

Yet the Jaljulia hominins weren’t the only ones to experiment with blade technology long before accepting it into their toolkit. At both Kathu Pan in South Africa and the Kapthurin Formation in Kenya, archaic humans began making small numbers of blades around 500,000 years ago, only to abandon the tools for hundreds of millennia.

“At Kathu Pan, we see a really remarkable [blade] technology, but then we don’t find it anymore, and the next blade production is about 70,000 years ago,” says Michael Chazan at the University of Toronto.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The identities of the various tool-makers remain unclear, and the blades at Jaljulia, Kathu Pan and the Kapthurin Formation were all created using different methods. This suggests that unconnected hominin populations simultaneously invented the technology required to produce blades, representing a case of convergent cultural evolution.

Litov suspects the blades didn’t initially catch on because the Jaljulia hominins preferred their Acheulean tools when butchering large prey like elephants. He thinks that when proboscideans began to die out in the eastern Mediterranean around 400,000 years ago, Levantine hominins were forced to change their hunting strategies, providing an incentive to switch to the smaller Amudian blades.

“We think the widespread adoption of blades was tied to a shift toward hunting smaller prey, which required more precise, meticulous butchery to maximise caloric yield, alongside delicate tasks like skinning,” says Litov.

Combining archaeological evidence with ancient DNA and data on past climates shows us how long and winding the story of human evolution is, stretching back millions of years to when the first primates arose

Yet Chazan questions how much of an advantage these early blades provided. “Why would something that seems so highly adaptive [like the Amudian-like blades] not be sustained?” he says. “I think part of the answer is that they’re not superior. There’s nothing inherently better about a blade than a flake.”

Likewise, Steven Kuhn at the University of Arizona suggests that blades may have become truly useful only once humans learned to combine them with more advanced technologies to produce tools assembled from several parts, including those with a handle or “haft”.

“My opinion is that certain forms of blade production were advantageous in contexts where many tools were hafted,” he says. “Until hafted tools became important parts of toolkits, blades were just another source of sharp edges.”

The secret maths problems hidden throughout Japan

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Mathematics is rarely done in public. I’m not talking about arithmetic – of course, simple sums are common when shopping, though perhaps less so in an increasingly cashless age – but actual mathematics involving reasoning, logic, proof and even beauty. While statues, paintings and other artworks are sprinkled throughout the public realm, I can’t recall ever encountering mathematics in the wild.

Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?

Because of this, I was delighted to recently discover the Japanese practice of sangaku. Translated variously as “framed calculations” or “mathematical tablets”, these were painted wooden artefacts hung in temples and shrines across Japan depicting mathematical problems. Thousands of them were created during the Edo period of around 1603 to 1868, but only 900 survive today.

Now, thanks to a team led by Antonia Karaisl at Waseda University in Tokyo, many of these have been digitally preserved in an online catalogue called the Sangaku Archive.

Advertisement

“Sangaku have sort of fallen off the radar of public knowledge in Japan. They are positively obscure outside the country, so I thought that documenting them in a bilingual, centralised archive might help,” says Karaisl.

Here is a relatively easy example to understand (the diagram on the left):

This problem consists of a number of circles. The yellow one has a diameter of 5 units and the three red ones all have a diameter of 4. They sit snugly inside and around a white circle that has a chunk of another circle taken out of it. At the bottom of the picture is a black line. The tablet asks how long this line is and gives an answer – 16 units – along with a method for calculating it.

Crucially, the tablet doesn’t provide a proof for why this method works (it involves some elementary geometry). That was often the point of sangaku, to offer a challenge to the viewer.

“Sangaku serve to signal knowledge without actually transmitting it. They contain enough information for you to understand the problem and that the author has solved it,” says Karaisl. This is because mathematical knowledge at the time was closely guarded by private schools, so the sangaku were a way to advertise what students might learn.

This wasn’t their only purpose, however. “People had other motives to dedicate a sangaku: commemorate a personal feat or an event, or just doing it for the joy of it – much like social media, I guess,” says Karaisl.

Looking at the sangaku, I can’t help but be reminded of video games in which you wander through a world encountering puzzles along the way. Take The Witness, for example, which takes place on an island filled with puzzles that all involve drawing lines on a grid. That description sounds boring, but the sense of discovery and communication between the player and the game developer is incredible, as you explore both a visual landscape and a conceptual one to learn a strange new logical language.

Building the Sangaku Archive was its own journey of discovery, says Karaisl. A book published in 1998 lists the known locations of the extant sangaku, but actually getting in touch with local caretakers so she could access and photograph them all was much harder work. “Email is rare – it’s mostly phones, faxes and letters,” she says. “In the hopeless cases, the best you can do is physically go to the location and hope you’ll find a human being nearby who can tell you more – and if you’re lucky, someone will know someone who knows someone whose cousin’s wife’s brother holds the key or something.”

For the 70th anniversary of New Scientist, explore our immersive timeline of the biggest moments in science since 1956, from Sputnik 1 to the proliferation of AI chatbots

Karaisl says she has visited around 400 sangaku locations, most in small, rural shrines as the less remote ones have been destroyed by war or earthquakes. In one case, she cycled to a small temple in a mountainous area, only to find herself within 50 metres, but on the wrong side of a river, she says. “Since I was late already, I had to leave the bike in the bushes, clamber down the slope and across the river to then climb up through the thicket and come breaking out of the forest like some stray ogre with sticks and leaves on my clothes and in my hair, rather than coming up the road to meet the priest and the caretaker in a civilised fashion.”

Another fascinating aspect of sangaku is that that they record a particular way of doing mathematics that is unfamiliar to Western-trained eyes. During the Edo period, Japan had an isolationist outlook to Europe, and this included mathematics – for example, the development of calculus by the Europeans Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz in the 17th century didn’t reach Japan until much later. Many results were developed by Japanese mathematicians independently, and sometimes before, their Western counterparts.

Part of this Japanese approach to mathematics was a focus on experimental calculations, rather than deduction, according to Tsukane Ogawa at Yokkaichi University, Japan. When Euclid’s Elements, perhaps the foundational text of mathematical proof, arrived in Japan via a Chinese translation in the Edo period, Japanese mathematicians seemed uninterested. Rather than starting from a series of axioms and deriving logical proofs, Japanese mathematicians preferred to perform calculations, such as finding many digits of pi, and infer logical conclusions – the exact method demonstrated by sangaku.

Karaisl and her team continue to work on the archive, and she says she hopes that it will reach a broader audience beyond the research community. Personally, I’m fascinated by the idea of a culture that saw mathematics as something worthy of putting on public display, and the remaining sangaku are absolutely beautiful to look at. I would love for someone to take inspiration from The Witness and create a game with finding and solving sangaku at its heart.

The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury

New Scientist November 20, 2026

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

Advertisement

Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.

Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.

Free newsletter

Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.

Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.

Family of Harlee-Rose Niven, 2, killed by teen stepmum Jessica Mulford, ‘devastated’ by reduced sentence

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

Jessica Mulford killed her toddler stepdaughter Harlee-Rose in April 2022. Composite photo / NZME

The grandmother of a toddler killed by her teenage stepmother says their family has been left devastated after discovering her prison sentence has been slashed.

Jessica Lee Rose Mulford’s actions split 2-year-old Harlee-Rose Niven’s pancreas, after a strangulation five months before her death.

Mulford’s prison sentence has now been reduced by almost 30%, prompting outrage from the toddler’s family.

“I’m disgusted, beyond disgusted,” grandmother Lori Niven told NZME.

“I just don’t think anybody realises how unbelievably hurtful this is for our family.”

In February 2025, Justice Neil Campbell jailed Mulford, then 20, for five years and seven months when she appeared in the High Court at Hamilton.

Mulford challenged her sentence, with the case eventually reaching the Supreme Court after an unsuccessful appeal in the Court of Appeal.

In a reserved decision released on Thursday, the Supreme Court found that Mulford’s age - 17 at the time of the earlier strangulation offence - and youth-related issues reduced her culpability.

The court quashed her original sentence, finding a starting point of four years and nine months’ imprisonment was more appropriate than the seven years set by the sentencing judge.

One Supreme Court justice indicated he would have gone even lower.

Mulford was then resentenced to four years’ imprisonment.

For Niven and her family, the decision has reopened the pain of losing Harlee-Rose.

“Two of my four daughters went to the trial and followed it all the way through.”

Niven believed Mulford should have been given a longer prison sentence, not a shorter one.

“This is why we’ve got a high crime rate, because no one gives a f***.

“There are no consequences.”

She said the pain of losing Harlee-Rose was something her family would never get over.

“People say it changes with time. Well, no, it doesn’t because it just gets rehashed constantly.”

Niven also felt Mulford had failed to take accountability for her actions.

The now 22-year-old has become eligible for parole and appeared before the Parole Board for the first time in August.

At the hearing, the family shared the same view - they felt Mulford lacked accountability, and they opposed her release.

Despite being classified as low security, Mulford has been involved in several incidents behind bars.

According to the board’s decision, she has lost a prison job for signing an invoice without authority, been involved in fights and been found in possession of unspecified “items”.

Mulford told the board her memory of Harlee-Rose’s death was “hazy”, which she attributed to trauma and drug abuse.

“Ms Mulford maintains that she does not remember the offending although her counsel emphasised this is not a denial,” the decision stated.

Overall, she was considered at medium risk of general and violent reoffending.

While Mulford did not seek parole, the board found she remained an undue risk without completing further rehabilitation, which she was keen to undertake, and declined an early release.

She is next due before the board in May.

Harlee-Rose died from her catastrophic injuries on April 9, 2022, while living in Hamilton with her father Dylan Berry and his partner, Mulford.

The earlier strangulation occurred while they were living in Tauranga on November 9, 2021.

At sentencing, Justice Campbell convicted and discharged her on the strangulation charge.

He said that, while the cause of Harlee-Rose’s death had been determined, the mechanism remained unknown.

“But it is consistent with stomping, kicking or punching” with such force that it split her pancreas in two, lacerated her liver and would have left her unconscious within minutes.

In September last year, Mulford’s counsel, Nick Dutch, failed in a Court of Appeal bid to have her prison term halved, arguing that her age, background factors and the starting point warranted a greater reduction.

The Court of Appeal judges said that, while another judge may have given a slightly greater discount for her young age and mental health at the time, they would not.

“We are not persuaded that an allowance of 15% amounts to error warranting appellate intervention in a case involving, as this one did, such extreme violence against a defenceless toddler.”

Dutch and co-counsel Rebekah Webby then took the case to the Supreme Court, challenging the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss the appeal.

In the Supreme Court, the defence submitted that the uplift for the strangulation meant Mulford was effectively serving a prison sentence for that charge.

Contact the Open Justice team

They argued that, had Mulford been charged at the time for the strangulation, she would have been dealt with in the Youth Court and would probably have been discharged without notation.

“It was inherently unfair that Ms Mulford was sentenced to a higher term of imprisonment only because the prosecution was not promptly commenced,” the decision stated.

Justice Stephen Kos, writing for the Supreme Court, acknowledged that the earlier violence increased the seriousness of the manslaughter because the fatal assault was not an isolated act.

It should have made Mulford aware of her “capacity to lose control”.

“At the same time, however, it would be appropriate to take into account that the earlier violence occurred when the offender was a child, subject to very similar agency-reducing circumstances as applied at the time of the index offending, which in turn reduces its significance in terms of culpability.”

Her youth-related factors, isolation, inexperience, impulsivity and inability to cope with stress, alongside associated mental health issues such as depression and mental distress, also reduced Mulford’s culpability.

While considering the earlier offending, the court said it would have adopted a six-year starting point for the manslaughter if she had been an adult.

However, after considering other case law and legal factors relating to her age at the time of the strangulation, the court concluded that a sentence of four years and nine months was appropriate.

They allowed a 5% discount for Mulford’s previous trauma and mental health, and a further 10% for her “good rehabilitation prospects”.

“The end sentence, therefore, is one of four years’ imprisonment.”

Belinda Feek is an Open Justice reporter based in Waikato. She has worked at NZME for 11 years and has been a journalist for 22.

Quest Mt Maunganui wins Supreme Franchisee of the Year at 2026 awards

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

Quest Mt Maunganui has been recognised as New Zealand’s top franchise.

A Mount Maunganui hotel that opened three years ago has been named one of New Zealand’s top franchisees.

Quest Mt Maunganui Apartment Hotel reports 93% average annual occupancy, and its owners Avelien and Tere Strickland say their biggest challenge at times is not having enough rooms.

The hotel was named Supreme Franchisee of the Year at the 2026 New Zealand Franchise Awards.

The awards recognise excellence across the country’s franchising sector, including individual franchisees, franchise systems and support professionals.

The Stricklands said the recognition reflected a long-term focus on staff development, retention and building a business that can thrive without relying on them every day.

Avelien said the award was about the team behind its success.

“I don’t really like the spotlight myself.

“But it’s so exciting for our team. They do such a wonderful job every day and to be able to bring that recognition back to them is really nice.”

Avelien spent 15 years working in Quest’s New Zealand corporate office in franchise support, gaining extensive knowledge of the franchise model and accommodation industry.

When the opportunity to take over the Mount Maunganui franchise arose in 2019, it provided a chance to return home while stepping into business ownership.

The couple signed the franchise agreement that December, planning to open in 2021.

Covid-19 delayed the project, and the hotel opened in June 2023.

“We felt very confident that it’s a recipe for success. The combination of the Quest Brand and the location of Mount Maunganui — how can it not be in a location like Mount Maunganui?”

Since opening, the hotel has recorded an average annual occupancy rate of 93%, with corporate travellers making up about 80% of guests.

Avelien said the 40 self-contained apartment model, which combines hotel services with facilities such as kitchens and laundry amenities, appealed to longer-stay and business guests.

She believes the biggest contributor to the hotel’s success has been its staff.

The business employs 22 people across full-time, part-time and casual roles and Avelien said it has prioritised staff development.

Employees complete Quest training programmes in customer service and leadership, while permanent staff can gain industry qualifications through a partnership with ServiceIQ.

Staff can also work towards team leadership certificates, management qualifications and hospitality diplomas.

The couple also offer staff two complimentary nights at the hotel each year and a profit-sharing scheme that distributes 10% of the business’ net profit to employees twice a year.

Avelien said the goal was for staff to leave with experience and qualifications.

“I’m realistic that people are not going to be with our business forever, because life changes and challenges change and what people want may change.

“But what I really like is the idea of when someone does eventually decide to leave us, they’re leaving better than what they arrived.”

She said staff turnover had remained low compared with industry norms, with many employees still working at the hotel three years after opening.

The Stricklands said an important part of building the business was creating an operational structure that gave their team confidence and autonomy.

“It’s given us space to be able to always be working on our business and not in our business.”

Avelien said this approach proved its value when the hotel opened, and her mother became critically ill.

The team helped keep the business running while Avelien spent time with her mother and Tere cared for their young children.

“It reinforced for us the importance of not building a business that relies on us being there every day.

“It’s given us space to work on the business rather than in it. It’s also empowered by our team.”

The Franchisee of the Year title is not the first recognition for the hotel, which was named Quest Franchise of the Year last year.

Avelien believed Tauranga’s growing appeal for business events and visitors has increased demand for high-quality accommodation, and investment would benefit the economy and community.

Franchise Association of New Zealand chief executive Katrina King said the results were encouraging given economic challenges facing businesses.

She said the awards recognised businesses that had continued to adapt, back their teams and find ways to improve, even in a challenging trading environment.

King said it was encouraging to see established franchises maintaining strong results alongside newer businesses making their mark through fresh thinking and innovation.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post.

Two sections owned by Rotorua landlord Stephen Bhana up for mortgagee sale

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

Stephen Bhana's two properties on Day Place and Exeter Place are up for mortgagee sale.

Two prime sections of residential land owned by controversial Rotorua landlord Stephen Bhana are up for mortgagee sale.

The sections are at 29 Day Place in Springfield and 22 Exeter Place in Tihiotonga. The mortgagee auction is set for December 1.

A year ago, Bhana’s family home on Devon St was also put up for mortgagee sale, but was pulled from the market shortly before the auction. Bhana and his sister, Jasu Bhana, still own the property.

The two sections owned by Stephen Bhana now up for sale are being marketed by Bayleys Rotorua and touted as rare finds in sought-after locations.

The Rotorua Daily Post asked Bhana about the mortgagee sales.

The Exeter Place section is on 809sq m of land bordering farmland and overlooking Rotorua.

While the site needs clearing, it is being marketed as potentially the perfect setting for an architectural masterpiece.

The site has a colourful background. In 2013, the Rotorua Lakes Council ruled the derelict property on the site be demolished because of serious safety and fire concerns.

The rundown property had been vacant for 25 years and locals fought for it to go after it became a hangout for squatters.

It had a fire in 2010, after which the council deemed the building dangerous and insanitary and required Bhana to make repairs.

When this work was not completed, the council took the matter to court.

Tihiotonga residents wrote to the court describing how the state of the dwelling had affected them.

A dangerous and insanitary building notice was placed on the property in November 2012, deeming the building unsafe to enter and an ongoing risk to neighbouring properties.

The following year, Judge Chris McGuire ruled the council could demolish it.

The cost of demolition was charged to the property.

The council told the Rotorua Daily Post the $79,297.35 payment was made in full.

The Day Place section is described as a full-size 758sq m section on flat land in a quiet cul-de-sac surrounded by quality homes.

It is said to be one of Rotorua’s most sought-after residential locations and borders Tihi Rd Reserve.

Bhana and his family trust, the Ranolf Trust, have attracted media attention over the years for owning dilapidated properties and having conflicts with tenants.

The Bhanas have been taken to the Tenancy Tribunal numerous times and have been the subject of Rotorua Lakes Council-enforced court action for owning properties that were “dangerous and insanitary”.

Among shoddy living conditions mentioned in tribunal orders were mould, leaks, rotting wood, no hot water pressure, broken locks, windows, appliances and power sockets, and faulty drains.

The Rotorua Daily Post reported this year that Tenancy Tribunal adjudicator John Greene said there was a “pattern of behaviour that was difficult to fathom” from Bhana and his sister, Jasu.

In one tribunal case this year, their tenant Michael Waikato used a handwriting expert to successfully challenge claims he had signed a document accepting responsibility for property damage.

The expert said the signature and initials were consistent with Stephen Bhana’s handwriting.

Waikato was awarded exemplary damages of $5800.

In another Tenancy Tribunal case, the Bhana siblings’ Ranolf Trust was ordered to pay a tenant thousands of dollars in exemplary damages and compensation for Residential Tenancies Act failings.

Greene noted in that decision that Stephen Bhana had used the same defence to the tribunal several times before, and each time it had been rejected.

“What I observed from the landlord’s behaviour (especially Mr Bhana, less so his sister) was a rambling attempt in almost forensic detail to avoid responsibility (or liability) that flew in the face of the evidence, photographic and documentary, before the tribunal.”

Greene said the tribunal could not stop people from being landlords.

“But it can punish them for repeated or serious non-compliance.”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Sand, sun and social boundaries: The unwritten rules of the Kiwi beach - Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

No discussion on beach etiquette is complete without mentioning the great Kiwi beach umbrella. Photo / Sylvie Whinray

Summer is on its way, and I have to admit, I’m getting excited.

Because summer means a return to the beach.

And I apologise to those who live inland, but a day at the beach is as Kiwi as togs, togs, togs, undies.

So I think I’m entitled to a little excitement. And perfectly justified in calling my undies togs.

And apparently, this year we’re in for an El Niño summer – which is Spanish and meteorological for an upper-upper-thigh-chafingly hot summer.

But regardless of how upper-upper-thigh-chafingly hot it does or doesn’t get, one thing is certain. Kiwis will be heading to the beach.

And while we might think a day at the beach is all about relaxing, there’s actually a sophisticated system of rules, regulations and social expectations governing almost everything we do on the sand.

These rules have never been written down, never been debated in Parliament or chiselled into stone tablets for future generations to ignore.

It’s a bit like Fight Club. Nobody talks about the rules, but somehow everyone is expected to know them.

Well, I’m about to break the first rule.

So, let’s start with the first and possibly most important rule.

Beach territory.

When you arrive at the beach, you don’t simply throw your towel down anywhere.

There’s a complicated assessment process involved.

You scan the sand, consider the direction of the wind, calculate the distance to the water and, most importantly, establish how close you can reasonably sit to another family without crossing an invisible border.

Too far away and the other family starts wondering if you’re planning to set up a nudist volleyball court.

Too close and you’ve effectively moved into their lounge without knocking or bringing a housewarming present.

The generally accepted rule is that if you can hear the intimate details of someone’s relationship problems, you’re too close.

And if you can read their book over their shoulder, you’ve crossed the demilitarised zone and wandered into North Korea.

You’re now officially in hostile territory.

Of course, this all changes when the beach starts filling up.

Suddenly, the comfortable 5m buffer becomes 3m, then 2m, until eventually you’re sharing a patch of sand with a complete stranger who’s somehow managed to position their towel directly beneath your umbrella.

And for the male readers, the same rule applies at the urinal.

If there’s an entire row free, don’t position yourself next to the only other bloke there and start a conversation.

Which brings us to another important rule.

Sand management.

Sand is an unavoidable part of going to the beach. We accept that.

It gets in your shoes, your sandwiches, your car and, if the wind is strong enough, places on your body that could require medical attention to remove it.

But there’s a difference between accepting sand and deliberately distributing it.

We’ve all experienced the person who stands up, grabs their towel and gives it an enthusiastic shake without checking which way the wind is blowing.

One moment you’re eating a perfectly good sandwich, the next every mouthful sounds like someone’s changing gears without using the clutch.

Or simply driving an old Land Rover.

And somehow, the offender always looks surprised.

Then there’s the matter of music.

Once upon a time, the soundtrack to a Kiwi beach was beautifully simple.

Waves crashing, seagulls squawking, children laughing, and the occasional parent shouting: “Don’t go out too far!”.

Now, thanks to modern technology, anyone with a Bluetooth speaker can appoint themselves the official entertainment director of an entire coastline.

And it’s remarkable how confident these people are that everyone shares their musical taste.

I imagine they’re the same people who have a subwoofer in the office and insist on punishing everyone with their Friday afternoon DJ set.

You might be enjoying a quiet afternoon listening to the ocean when suddenly someone three towels away decides what the beach really needs is a four-hour playlist of electronic dance music.

I’m not against music at the beach.

But surely the unwritten rule should be that if people 200m away can identify the song, it’s probably too loud.

Of course, no discussion about beach etiquette would be complete without mentioning the great Kiwi beach umbrella.

These things are wonderful in theory. A little portable patch of shade, protecting us from the summer sun while we relax with a good book.

And given how often we’ve been reminded about the dangers of the Kiwi sun, you’d think a beach umbrella would be one of the safest things you could take to the beach.

But in practice, the umbrella can often be more dangerous than the sun itself.

Every summer, somewhere in New Zealand, a perfectly innocent family is enjoying a picnic when a sudden gust of wind transforms a nearby beach umbrella into the umbrella equivalent of an unmanned drone.

Only without the benefit of GPS guidance.

You can always spot the owner of these weapons of mass embarrassment.

They’re sprinting across the sand like they’re competing in the Olympic 100m, shouting apologies to people who are too busy ducking for cover to respond.

Which brings us to a very important rule of beach cohabitation.

When you leave the beach, take everything with you.

Your rubbish, your chilly bin, your towels, your umbrella, and, ideally, the children you arrived with.

Because for all our little territorial disputes, flying umbrellas and disagreements over music, the Kiwi beach is still one of the great things about living in this country.

It’s one of the few places where it doesn’t matter what you do for a living, what car you drive or how much money you’ve got in the bank.

Everyone gets the same sand between their toes, the same salt in their hair, even if these days that’s mostly back hair because the follicles on top have given up the fight, and the same chance to spend a few glorious hours doing absolutely nothing.

But while most of these unwritten rules are open to interpretation, there are a few that aren’t.

Swim between the flags, never swim alone, keep a close eye on the kids, stay out of the water if you’ve been drinking, and if you’re unsure about the conditions, don’t go in.

And if you do get into trouble, remember to float on your back and signal for help.

Because at the end of the day, the most important rule of all is making sure everyone gets home safely to complain about the bloke with the Bluetooth speaker.
