Pastures Past: How introduced hares became a pest in rural New Zealand

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

European hares were introduced to New Zealand for sport in the 1850s. Photo / Pexels, Karel Drozda

Kem Ormond takes a look at the world of farming back in the day. In this week’s Pastures Past, she’s found newspaper articles on hares.

Hares may look cute, but they can damage pasture and compete with livestock for grazing; however, in New Zealand they are generally considered less destructive than rabbits.

European brown hares were first released in Canterbury in 1851, having been introduced primarily for hunting and sport.

Improving the food supply of early settlers may also have been a consideration.

During the 1860s and 1870s, acclimatisation societies imported and released hares more widely around the country.

In South Canterbury, hare numbers increased rapidly and were harvested commercially, with meat and skins exported overseas.

Hares were liberated in the Ashburton district to promote hunting, but they multiplied so successfully that by 1931 organised hare drives were being held to cull their numbers.

Below is a selection of historical stories from the New Zealand Herald (1868), the Waipukurau Press (1931) and the Waikato Independent (1941).

New Zealand Herald, July 10, 1868

There will take place, we see, a special meeting of the members of the Acclimatisation Society to-morrow, to consider the propriety or otherwise of introducing hares into New Zealand.

Doubtless there will be a full muster of country members, as the day is Saturday, who are chiefly interested in this matter.

Under ordinary circumstances we should see no objection to the introduction of this animal, which affords much sport both for shooting and hunting, and is excellent eating.

Every one of course, knows that the hare consumes much produce on a farm.

If, however, the farmer were free to destroy hares at will, they could easily be kept from becoming so numerous as to be destructive.

On the other hand, if the game laws of the country are to continue to prevent owners and occupiers of land from killing game even on their own farms without payment of a license fee, and if even then these animals are not to be killed at all during one season of the year, it would be better to forego any benefits that might be derived from their introduction into this province.

Perhaps the better plan would be for the Society to make the introduction of hares dependent on the alteration of clauses 11 and 18 of the " Game Act, 1867," or on the removal of the word “hares” from schedule 4 of the Act.

Waipukurau Press, September 28, 1931

Hares have become so plentiful in Ashburton County of late years that one of the means of suppressing them has been the organisation of hare drives, which have accounted for many thousands of the pests (states the Ashburton Guardian).

How different the position was half a century ago may be gauged from the following paragraph which appeared in the Ashburton Guardian on September 17, 1877, fifty-four years ago last Thursday: “Six hares (one male and five females) were liberated on the farm of Messrs Saunders brothers, Seafield, Ashburton, today. It is hoped no persons will molest them, but allow them to increase, and so promote the sport of hunting in Ashburton.”

Meet at Matangi

Good sport for a large field

Waikato Independent, July 7, 1941

The meet of the Waikato Hunt at Matangi on Saturday was one of the most enjoyable so far this season.

A large field of over 50 riders enjoyed several excellent runs over good country.

There were also many followers in cars.

The field met the Master, Mr Wynn Brown, at Mr and Mrs W. E. Bourke’s homestead, where tea was provided.

Hares led over good hunting country, which had been well laid out, but no kills were registered.

Two hares saved their scuts by running to ground after excellent chases.

When the hounds were called off, the field returned to Mr and Mrs Bourke’s homestead for afternoon tea.

Thanks to the host and hostess were extended by Mr Brown.

There are still a number of horses in the district to complete their qualifying jumps, and twelve of them were out on Saturday.

- Source: Papers Past

Gisborne Mayor calls for national climate resilience framework

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

Gisborne District Council has worked with central government and communities to progress flood resilience projects since Cyclone Gabrielle. Photo / NZ Herald

Local Government New Zealand is calling for a national plan on adapting to climate change that sets out the responsibilities of central and local government, communities and the private sector.

LGNZ president Rehette Stoltz said a national climate resilience framework would set clear responsibilities to help communities navigate difficult decisions about their future.

“The incoming Government has an opportunity to give communities certainty,” she said. “We need a framework that lasts beyond an election cycle and supports action now before the choices become more difficult and more expensive.”

The call followed an announcement by Westpac New Zealand that it would share its natural hazards risk report, used to inform lending decisions, with home loan applicants.

Westpac head of consumer lending and insurance Jo McGregor told the Herald limits on lending against properties deemed exceptionally risky would affect fewer than 2.5% of mortgage applications.

Stoltz said the announcement highlighted the need for the incoming Government to prioritise a climate resilience framework with clear responsibilities and long-term funding arrangements.

“Banks and insurers cannot build flood protection, adapt infrastructure, or make the difficult decisions needed to keep communities safe. Communities need to know what can be done, who will act and how the costs will be shared.”

Increasing natural hazard risks could place a greater financial burden on households and communities through insurance and lending decisions, with wider economic consequences, she said.

Central government needed to focus on reducing risks before disasters occurred, rather than relying on recovery, including through initiatives such as the Before the Deluge flood protection pipeline.

LGNZ wants a national climate resilience framework developed with councils, communities, banks and insurers to establish responsibilities and clarify who would pay for what.

Flood protection was essential but one could not assume more infrastructure would make every place safe in the long term, she said.

“We need to consider the full range of options for each community, including how we adapt buildings and infrastructure, where we allow development and supporting people to move out of harm’s way where necessary.”

Speaking as Gisborne Mayor, Stoltz acknowledged announcements about natural hazard risks could create uncertainty for home owners, buyers and sellers.

While she could not comment on how Westpac’s announcement might affect individual Gisborne properties, she said the council would continue providing relevant hazard information and supporting decisions about managing and reducing risks.

The council was progressing work on flood resilience, stormwater and drainage, catchment management and improvements to warning systems and emergency preparedness.

“Following the severe weather events of recent years, council has worked with central government, iwi, hapū, landowners and communities to investigate and progress flood resilience projects across the region.”

She welcomed continued collaboration with central government to provide national direction, reliable hazard information and sustainable funding.

“For Tairāwhiti, ongoing support for flood resilience, infrastructure improvements and practical risk reduction measures is particularly important.

“We also support greater clarity about the respective responsibilities of central and local government, communities and the private sector in responding to natural hazard risks.”

Stoltz said the council already considered flooding, coastal hazards, erosion and land stability when making land use planning and infrastructure decisions.

“The presence of a natural hazard does not automatically prevent development. Decisions depend on the nature and level of risk, the proposed activity and the relevant planning requirements.”

Any proposed changes needed to be supported by appropriate evidence and follow statutory processes, including public consultation, she said.

The council’s Plan Change 6, which seeks to enable more housing choices within Gisborne city, had also considered natural hazard risks.

“The proposed plan change is progressing through an independent hearings process, where relevant evidence, submissions and planning requirements will be considered before decisions are made.”

The focus remained on managing risks to people, property and infrastructure while enabling appropriate development, she said.

LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

Neonatal nurse Tracey Wright has saved babies’ lives for 30 years. Now she has 10 weeks to live

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

Tracey Wright, a neonatal nurse, was told she has weeks to live. She is now in Shanghai for Car T-cell therapy. Photo / Michael Craig

For 30 years, Tracey Wright has devoted her life to saving babies who might otherwise not make it.

Now the 56-year-old clinical charge nurse at Auckland City Hospital is fighting for her own survival.

Doctors have given Wright just 10 weeks to live.

She was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 2023. Chemotherapy put her cancer into remission. Then last year Wright discovered a lump on her neck. Her cancer had returned.

A stem cell transplant last November offered another chance. It failed.

Now her last hope is experimental Car T-cell treatment in Shanghai. Wright and her daughter, Tamsyn, 22, made the journey two weeks ago, and her husband, Brett, has just joined them.

Although doctors have told her there is a 40% chance of success, Wright promised her children she will do everything possible to stay alive.

“I don’t want my kids to be traumatised. Even if the treatment doesn’t work, I don’t want them to be left thinking if only mum gave it a try.”

About eight weeks ago, Wright noticed unusual peripheral vision while heading for coffee. Her vision worsened at work, and a colleague checked her bloods.

The next day, an ophthalmologist examining the neonatal ward tested her eyes and found she couldn’t count how many fingers were held up in front of her.

Scans on October 13 revealed Wright had a brain tumour. A neurologist told her, while she was alone, that she had less than three months to live.

“As a nurse, I am pragmatic. I’ve had these conversations with families of sick babies, so I know how devastating they are. But it was surreal.

“I kept asking myself, ‘Is this really happening?’ I asked the neurologist to call my husband immediately.

“I am terrified, and I have to say I’ve never cried so much in my life. Sometimes I hold my husband’s hand, and we’re normally not like that. I feel really robbed. I may never see my children get married or become a grandmother,” Wright said.

Initially, the nurse hoped the cancer could be beaten. Then a haematologist delivered the devastating news: it had spread to her central nervous system.

Chemotherapy risked damaging her kidneys and, at best, would buy her little more time.

It was her husband, Brett, an operations manager, who suggested Car T-cell therapy in Shanghai as an option.

At the moment, Wright’s vision is blurry and, she says, she can barely see. The past few weeks have been taken up with medical appointments, scans and blood tests.

A Givealittle link has been set up to raise the $800,000 needed for Car-T cell therapy, which is not publicly funded.

Wright’s family have rallied together to cover her travel to Shanghai and the initial treatment costs. But the family home in Pt Chevalier will have to be sold to help pay for her treatment.

The nurse who has dedicated her life to saving babies sees the bitter irony in the fact that there is no public funding to save hers.

Wright and her daughter flew to Shanghai two weeks ago, hoping she would begin treatment at Sino United Health the next day. But mechanical problems forced the plane to turn back about 4am.

During the flight, Wright developed a severe headache and was admitted to Auckland City Hospital for an MRI scan. She was discharged on November 10 and boarded another flight to Shanghai.

However, she believes the aborted journey may have saved her life.

“It was a blessing in disguise. If we had kept travelling, I think I would have had a brain bleed.

“When I got back, I started oral chemotherapy, which cost us $15,000. They also increased my steroids and will start radiation therapy when I arrive.

“It’s disappointing.”

But she believed the delay was a sign her late mother was “looking out for me”.

“I really do think that if I’d stayed on that plane, I don’t know if I’d still be here,” Wright says.

Wright has also considered whether assisted dying might be preferable to a prolonged decline.

“I’m scared the treatment won’t work. Part of me wishes I could have an injection, go to sleep and have it all over. I’ve told Brett that if the treatment affects my brain and I’m no longer myself, I don’t want to live that way.”

This week her husband and sister-in-law fly to Shanghai. Wright told the Herald she has just completed four days of radiation, with a fitted mesh mask on her face, to shrink the tumour.

“I had a panic attack. It was terrifying; my heart was racing, the mask is moulded to your face while you’re strapped to the bed so you can’t move.

“My breathing was all over the place, I thought, ‘Oh no they are going to zap my brain and make things worse’.”

Wright will next have injections to stimulate her bone marrow for stem cells.

Away from the hospital, Wright’s life has always revolved around her family.

Wright met Brett when they were both 18, through her brother Shawn’s softball team.

But romance didn’t blossom until eight years later.

“We did everything back to front. We bought a house, had two children, then got married in 2005.”

They have two children: Tamsyn, who has completed a finance degree and is about to start a job with clothing company Ruby, and Denver, 25, who works in IT in Melbourne.

Debbie Gyde, married to Wright’s brother Shawn, says putting others before herself has always come naturally to Wright.

Three years ago, she cared for her uncle, who died aged 61, while she was undergoing chemotherapy herself. Five months ago, she lost her mother to Lewy body dementia, after nursing her through the illness.

After years devoted to caring for others, Wright took an unexpected detour of her own.

At 48, she swapped her nursing scrubs for an Air New Zealand uniform.

“I had a midlife crisis and became a flight attendant.”

After two years, she returned to nursing.

Wright still has a few things she’d love to do: visit Italy, take a trip to South Africa with Debbie for her 60th, walk Daisy, her beloved dog, and spend more time with her family.

But when the day ends, and the house grows quiet, the reality of what lies ahead can be harder to escape.

“The nights are the hardest. I’ll be lying there, and the tears just start flowing,” she says.

Wright wants to be remembered as kind, helpful and someone who went the extra mile.

“I’ve been a good person all my life and feel life hasn’t given me a good hand for my ending. So live life and don’t put things off – create memories so the people you leave behind remember you.”

Carolyne Meng-Yee is an Auckland-based investigative journalist who won Best Documentary at the Voyager Media Awards. She was a finalist this year for Best Current Affairs. She worked for the Herald on Sunday from 2007 to 2011 and rejoined the Herald in 2016 after working as an award-winning current affairs producer at TVNZ’s 60 Minutes, 20/20 and Sunday.

US Ambassador assumes Trump’s America is the envy of the world – Letters to the Editor

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

US Ambassador Jared Novelly (left) and Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters. Photo / Jamie Ensor

‘Novice’ Novelly not the quiet American

As an American-born Kiwi who arrived here in 1960 at age 9, I am stunned by United States Ambassador Jared Novelly’s lack of understanding of our culture.

After nearly two years of Donald Trump’s tariffs, together with the rising costs of petrol due to a catastrophic war in the Middle East, most of us might have some empathy for any representative of the Trump Administration feeling their way through the eggshell sensitivities of most New Zealanders.

As in the ambassador’s own country, the No 1 concern in New Zealand is the cost of living, which was already bad enough before Trump’s return to the White House.

Had he been more considerate to the Kiwi way and characteristics, Novelly might have held back from bragging during his first interview about how “awesome” it would be for us to see a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier enter the Waitamatā Harbour.

It beggars belief that Novelly launches into local politics with the assumption that Trump’s America is the envy of the world.

Ambassadors with experience usually put time into getting to know the country they have the privilege to live in.

Ambassador Novelly is little more than an embarrassing novice.

Dave Brown, Mt Albert.

Climate change top of the list

Simon Bridges’ list of must-do themes (Nov 20) for the new government ignores the massive elephant in the room. Climate change, mostly ignored during election debates and by the coalition, is upon us. Adaptation to climate change must dominate all future policy, budgets and investment at every level of government. Bridges’ issues, important as they are, have limited relevance for communities facing floods, drought, sea level rise, soil loss and forest fires.

Ian McLean, professor of environmental science (retired), Tauranga.

Nurse staffing targets

Health New Zealand is championing how well it is doing in meeting its target for recruiting nurses, but the problem is the target itself, not whether it is being met.

In a year when we have had a crisis in emergency departments, with not enough staff to cope, the cancelling of surgeries because of a lack of staff and an ever-expanding waiting list for elective surgery, boasting about how well it is doing in meeting its recruitment target when nearly half the nurse graduates are missing out on jobs means a badly thought-out target is the problem.

It is madness to let the nurses we are training disappear overseas when we are struggling to get enough nurses to make our public health system fit for service. Let’s try and meet targets that are real, please.

Neil Anderson, Algies Bay.

E-scooter crash tragic reminder

Wellington teenager Jesse Roberts’ e-scooter crash recently (Nov 20) is tragic, but is a reminder of the dangers of this form of transport and the fact that little has been done to address that danger.

Why shouldn’t riders of e-scooters at least wear a helmet, as cyclists must? Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency strongly recommends wearing a helmet while riding an e-scooter, but it’s not compulsory.

However, all the times I have been out in my car or on my bike, I don’t think I have ever seen anybody wearing a helmet while riding an e-scooter. So much for people making wise choices.

The Givealittle fundraising campaign is a commendable example of a community coming together to help Jesse and his family with expenses during this trying time. However, ultimately ACC will have to front up with a payment. Given his injuries, as simple a thing as a helmet might have saved a lot of pain.

Bernard Walker, Mt Maunganui.

Pay equity breach

Politicians often throw around words with gay abandon. It fits with their lack of sincerity and craven efforts to ignore the wishes of the electorate. For the Government to say it was “saving” $12.8 billion by scuttling pay equity shows contempt for both the English language and the general public.

It might as well “save” electricity by switching off all the traffic lights.

What it did (as the courts have declared) was to breach women’s rights to equal pay, something we are not prepared to “Brooke”.

Once we have tidied up the 2026 electoral farce, the politicians have some serious rethinking on their hands.

Hugh Webb, Hamilton.

Upstream focus

In response to Michael Smythe’s letter (Nov 18), you are correct: we are certainly not 100% pure NZ. As long as the focus is on growth for growth’s sake, without any thought to damage to our environment, things will not change.

I have friends and family who fish our streams, and they certainly see the degradation. Streams and aquifers are our beacons. The damage is not seen from your car, the top offices of the Beehive, a posh apartment or corporate office windows.

It is seen by the people who adventure into our wild spaces, fish our streams. The science is there, and taking the time to listen to our freshwater ecologists might open some public eyes.

I live in hope that we will get some leaders with their eyes and ears wide open to this decline. The years of window dressing have covered up the problem and deceived a nation.

Wendy Oates, Hamilton East.

Waikato surgeon operates on young woman who swallowed full-sized fork

New Zealand Herald November 21, 2026

The fork showed up clearly in the woman's stomach in an X-ray photograph taken at Waikato Hospital's emergency department.

A young woman who swallowed a fork has had emergency surgery at Waikato Hospital to remove it and prevent serious damage to her stomach.

Auckland University medical surgery senior lecturer Dr Jesse Fischer said the woman, 27, came to Waikato Hospital saying she had swallowed a fork while trying to induce vomiting.

“It’s not abundantly clear why she used a fork, and that’s all the information we were given,” Fischer said.

“I understand it happened in a social situation at the time, but I don’t know why she needed to vomit or whether it was a party trick. She had no documented history of an eating disorder or psychiatric illness.”

An X-ray confirmed a full-sized dinner fork sitting in the woman’s stomach.

Fischer is a consultant surgeon at Waikato Hospital, primarily working in colorectal surgery but also in some emergency general surgery cases.

He said it wasn’t uncommon for surgeons to see people who had “swallowed various things at various times”, but in adult patients the cause was usually a psychiatric illness.

In this case, “We had a very well patient with a fork in their stomach.”

Sometimes people might drink too much or be experiencing pain from other causes that could induce nausea, and they would try a range of things to induce vomiting, he said.

However, nausea had a wide range of causes, which vomiting would not necessarily resolve.

He said small objects could typically be allowed to pass through the digestive system while the patient was closely monitored, but in this case the object was too large and carried too much risk.

“It’s fairly impressive it managed to get in there in the first place.”

Two attempts were made to pull the fork out through the patient’s mouth using an endoscope, as this would have minimised her recovery time.

After these failed, the team decided to use keyhole surgery by making small cuts in the abdomen, with the incision needing to be only 4cm wide to fit the largest width of the fork.

Once surgeons confirmed that the fork hadn’t perforated her stomach, they removed the utensil and closed the small hole.

“She then went home two days after the procedure and could return to a normal diet,” Fischer said.

“It was a very uncomplicated recovery.”

It showed how effective keyhole surgery could be in similar cases, although swallowing such a big object was fairly uncommon, he said.

The case appeared in a New Zealand Medical Journal article this month, highlighting the successful use of keyhole surgery.

Fischer said people should be aware there was always a risk when putting foreign bodies into the back of the throat, and it wasn’t advised.

Naivety, larrikins and ‘blood in the water’: Inside the chaotic triumph of Melbourne 1956

Sydney Morning Herald November 22, 2026

Barely more than a colony, a little over 50 years since federation, Melbourne was surprised when the world came for the Olympics – and even more surprised when they went stunningly well.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

If the world was sceptical in 1954 that a small colonial outpost in the southern hemisphere could host the world’s biggest sporting event, they were not alone.

There was the least doubt about whether Australia’s athletes were world class. It was the rest of Australia they worried about.

In July that year, two years before the 1956 Olympics, the Melbourne lord mayor, Robert Solly, summoned a meeting of the city’s key women’s groups. Representatives from the Country Women’s Association, the National Council of Women, the Girl Guides Association, the Young Women’s Christian Association and the Housewives Association (yes, you read that correctly) all gathered at the Town Hall.

Then-premier John Cain snr spoke, partly to urge the women to understand their role at the forthcoming Games would be to make visitors welcome, but also to assuage the fears of hordes of foreigners in the city.

It was agreed a committee would be formed to co-ordinate the women’s groups of Melbourne during the Olympics. The Olympics Civics Committee was formed. No women were on it.

The volunteer Housewives Brigade (again, not a typo) was also created to help make 6000 beds and tidy the rooms in the athletes’ village in Heidelberg.

The organisers were further worried there would be too few hotel beds for visitors for the Olympics and the city would need to encourage households to be prepared to open their doors to foreign tourists. This was a discussion partly to assuage the fears of locals, but also to ascertain which houses might be suitable for visitors. At the time, a quarter of houses in Melbourne had no refrigerator, two-thirds no hot running water in the bathroom and most had outside toilets.

(As it turned out, the distance to travel and the price of flights meant few international visitors came for the Games other than the athletes and teams.)

Organisers had invited the world, but had precious little idea of what hosting an Olympics involved. Two months from the Games, they didn’t have enough cooks – certainly not enough people who knew how to cook the food the foreign visitors needed.

The White Australia Policy was still 10 years from being scrapped. The early influx of European migrants after World War II had begun to alter the vegetables seen in shops, but it had not yet shifted the regular evening meal far from chops and three veg. Roast lamb was as exotic as it got.

It was August, barely more than two months before athletes were due to arrive, and the Olympic Organising Committee had still had not hired “Asiatic cooks” to prepare appropriate food. At the last minute, 10 cooks arrived, provided by a shipping line. It was emblematic of the Games being hastily cobbled together.

It was never certain the MCG would be the venue for the main stadium. There was discussion of the Showground, of St Kilda, and of building a 150,000-seat venue in Princes Park. Even Carlton’s No.1 ticket holder, prime minister Robert Menzies, saw the financial folly of that and agreed with Cain snr when he said it would be at the MCG or nowhere.

That still did not best please the Victorian Cricketers Association and the MCC, which were uncomfortable with ripping up the pitch where Donald Bradman had played. When they did rip it up and lay a track, it did not best please the visiting athletes. The cinder track was poor.

But they got a track built in time. They had found a way. As they did finding cooks. As they did getting the Olympic torch to Melbourne, buying local maps from Shell service stations along the way to navigate a route from Cairns.

As they did when the second-to-last torch relay runner was to enter Punt Road Oval to hand the torch to Ron Clarke – only to discover the gate padlocked (they had to shimmy through another turnstile). As they did cobbling together an equestrian event to be staged in Stockholm, Sweden, because quarantine laws would not allow the horses into Australia in time.

Historian and journalist Dr Nick Richardson, author of the excellent book 1956, observed the city’s “naïveté was its greatest asset”.

Australia was barely more than 50 years from Federation when it invited the world to visit. Sport would be the enticement but also the vehicle to hesitantly seek the world’s approval for the fledgling city and federated country.

An Olympic arts festival was opened before the Games began. The Victorian governor, Sir Dallas Brooks, addressed the opening, saying: “Australia is only a young country and we are very proud of our achievements, but we are fully conscious of our shortcomings. So we hope you will find something to enjoy and admire in the exhibitions, and we all look forward to learning something from your friendly criticisms.”

The journalist A. A. Phillips had coined the term “cultural cringe” in a Meanjin article six years earlier. Perhaps Sir Dallas considered it advice, not criticism.

“There was an attitude that they knew what we were not, but they wanted the world to come and tell us we were OK,” Richardson said. “It was that desperate search for a pat on the head.”

The grasping need for international approval partly missed a shift already occurring in Australia. Ray Lawler’s Summer of the Seventeenth Doll was showing, though the cast had to be persuaded to perform with Australian accents and not affect their voices with grand English flourish.

It was for the Games that Barry Humphries debuted Edna Everage in an “Olympic Sketch”, turning a mocking mirror on suburban Australia. The arrival of TV in Australia also presented the housewife from Moonee Ponds to a national audience, lampooning the same cringe A. A. Phillips had chronicled.

It spoke to a larrikinism that was drawn out by the Games. As the convoy of Olympic torchbearers wended through the streets of Sydney, a university student called Barry Larkin – a surname deserving of an extra, silent R and I – dressed in the same long grey trousers, white shirt and green tie of the official relay runners, appeared on the streets with friends.

He was bearing a torch made from a plum pudding tin atop a chair leg and carrying a flame lit from three pairs of army-issue underpants soaked in kerosene.

The police duly provided him and his cohort of friends an escort. At the town hall, he handed the “torch” over to lord mayor Pat Hills, who began a short speech as silver paint from the chair leg flecked onto his hands. Alerted to the hoax, the unamused mayor chastised “our friends at the university who apparently think this is funny”. (Pat, it still is.) The real torch arrived minutes later.

Those who had been in Helsinki for the Games four years earlier recalled the excoriating critique of US journalist Tom Van Dycke in Variety magazine that the midnight sun was the height of entertainment in a city with no licensed cafes or bars and only government-controlled venues selling alcohol.

Even the Victorian government feared what would be made of the six o’clock swill. The pubs of the state closed at 6pm, creating the nightly rush to drink as many beers in as short a time as possible after work and before the pub doors closed.

NSW had extended opening hours to 10pm the year before and Victorian premier Henry Bolte held a referendum in early 1956 proposing the same change in time for the Olympics. It was voted down by 60 per cent of voters. Only six of the state’s 66 electoral zones voted in favour of change. The suburbs were not for turning, or for late drinking.

Normally, Australia was afflicted by the tyranny of distance. During the Olympics it offered a merciful distance from tyranny. But it was not untouched by it.

Eighteen days before a Rolls-Royce convertible carrying the Duke of Edinburgh purred onto the MCG to dispatch his highness to loftily open the Games, Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest.

Days later, the Chinese boycotted the Games in anger at the recognition of Taiwan. The Soviets came to Melbourne but stayed on board a ship, the Gruzia, moored in Port Phillip Bay.

It was only two years after the Petrov affair, and months after the Suez crisis, which prompted some countries to boycott the Games in protest. More countries boycotted in anger at the invasion of Hungary, though ironically, not the Hungarian team.

The Hungarian team did not learn of the Soviet invasion until they reached Darwin and read of it in the local newspapers. They resolved to remain and compete, and as it turned out, took their fight to the Soviets in the pool.

Internationally, the Melbourne Games are better remembered for the “blood in the water” water polo clash between the Soviets and Hungarians than for anything Dawn Fraser or Murray Rose achieved in the pool.

One of the greatest international sporting moments of the Olympics is barely a trivia question in Australia. Bobby Joe Morrow won the 100 metres, 200m and 4x100m gold. Only one man had done that before, American great Jesse Owens. Only two men have done it since, Carl Lewis and Usain Bolt. Yet few Australians remember the name Bobby Morrow.

They definitely know the name of Betty Cuthbert, who became the first Australian to win three Olympic golds when she matched what Morrow did and won the sprint treble, something only Dutchwoman Fanny Blankers-Koen had done before, eight years earlier.

They know Fraser and her three medals. And of course Rose and his two golds. Shirley Strickland and her two, Lorraine Crapp and her three. The numbers offer no justice to the performances. These are athletes whose names still hover over Australian sport, over world sport, as greats. For not only did they excel in a sporting arena, they excelled in a sporting arena in this newly federated country, hosting the world for the first time.

The sepia images are etched in our minds: Cuthbert, mouth open, screaming in pain and delight as she crossed the line; Fraser beaming and waving from the pool; Rose looking like he stepped from the pages of a Boys’ Own Annual.

They are as vivid as that of Ron Clarke, who is as remembered for falling and being helped by John Landy as for being the man who, like Cathy Freeman in 2000, carried the torch into the stadium to start the Games. (In fact, Clarke and Landy’s famous moment came not at these Games, though stories become conflated, but six months earlier at the Mile Championship, also in Melbourne.)

At the opening ceremony, Clarke, holding aloft a torch spitting embers of burning magnesium onto his arm, stood on a small podium and reached into the cauldron where uni students charged with timing the release of gas had become nervous and impatient and opened the valves too early. They nearly blew Clarke off the step.

These were Games the world remembers fondly. Against the backdrop of Cold War geopolitics, of a Soviet ship in Port Phillip Bay and blood in the water of the Olympic pool, these were regarded as the friendly Games.

These were the Games in which a 17-year-old student, John Ian Wing, penned a letter recommending athletes at the closing ceremony march not by country but intermingled as one as a sign of fraternity. The idea of sport transcending nationalism was adopted and has since become a coda for all Olympics.

For Melbourne, the Games were a sporting and cultural triumph.

“For me, it is the inflexion point,” Richardson said. “If there had not been a Melbourne Olympics in 1956, where would we have found a pivotal moment? Where would it have come from? It pulled together these threads of identity and assertion of character.”

High rollers, loan sharks and a $242 million reno: The cash engine behind Sydney’s newest Vegas-style resort

Sydney Morning Herald November 22, 2026

Recriminations over cost blowouts on the lavish reimagining of Cabra-Vale Diggers Club has raised allegations of targeted sacking, sham variations and rough-housing between executives.

Everybody was a winner in the $242 million transformation of Cabra-Vale Diggers, unless you count the pokie players whose losses funded the project.

From the bones of an ex-servicemen’s club by a major railway line, in one of the most socially disadvantaged areas in NSW, it now boasts a 140-room hotel, 600-seat convention centre, five upmarket restaurants and a golden facade that bellows “Las Vegas”. All under a new banner: the Cabravale Club Resort.

But some people won particularly big.

The club’s chief executive, Boris Belevski, recently upgraded his Porsche to an Aston Martin, bought a holiday house in Queensland, and had the tradesmen who were building the club renovate his home kitchen, at no cost.

It made no difference to Belevski’s fortunes that the projected cost of the development had doubled as the plans expanded over four years, or that the club’s net profit plunged from $17 million in 2025 to $380,000 in the financial year ended June 30.

Last month, the board approved a combined pay rise of nearly $1 million for Belevski’s four-person leadership group.

Club president Walter Robinson told the Herald that the board had the “upmost confidence” in Belevski. “Boris has always acted with the highest level of integrity.”

Developer Rony Wardan also did well from the project. Not only did he make a healthy margin on the rapidly rising costs, the electrical subcontractor for the project also installed a small substation on his isolated rural property to connect it to the electricity grid.

The unusual arrangements are revealed in legal documents from a costs dispute between Wardan and electrician Shane Newton, after the bank intervened to rein in costs.

A Herald investigation has uncovered a web of influence connecting the little-known Wardan to councillors, MPs, lobbyists, the fugitive developer Jean Nassif, and claims that those who raised the alarm over the development were targeted with retribution.

The machinations behind the development of Cabravale Club Resort raise questions about who benefits from the building boom at gambling venues sitting on vast cash reserves, and whether a regulatory regime designed for grassroots community clubs remains fit for purpose.

Railway Parade, Canley Vale, home to the Cabra-Vale Diggers Club for more than a century, does not scream out as a future address of Sydney’s newest Las Vegas-style resort.

On one side sits Fairfield-Cabramatta PCYC, a windswept memorial park, the Diggers and a honeycomb of red, yellow and blond brick low-rise apartment blocks. The other side of the road is hemmed in by the southwest rail line.

Nearly a quarter of Canley Vale residents live below the poverty line. What the area does have in abundance is a fondness for gambling.

Fairfield, the local government area that includes Canley Vale, has the highest gambling losses per person in NSW. The Diggers is the area’s second most profitable club. For years, its 450 poker machines have been printing money. This year they cracked $100 million in revenue for the first time.

But there is another club in Fairfield which brings in even more gambling revenue: Mounties. When Boris Belevski was appointed chief executive in 2013, he wanted the Diggers to be No.1.

The then chief executive of Mounties, Greg Pickering, was rumoured to be on a million-dollar salary. It was a bugbear to which Belevski often returned.

“It was always a race to the top with [Belevski],” former Cabra-Vale Diggers director Ronnie Moore recalled. “He always wanted to beat that bloke. He even wanted a better car than him.”

Belevski quickly made Cabra-Vale his own, including making in-house staff redundant and hiring contractors for cleaning, catering and CCTV operations.

The club only had to open its doors for its gambling floor to turn a profit, but Belevski wanted more.

High rollers who defected to Mounties were offered thousands of dollars to return to the Diggers. The club kept them sweet with personal service and schemes that allowed players to use their loyalty points to buy utilities and groceries. In one case, the club paid for a high-value customer to have her car repaired.

Former employees said the club was not overly concerned about the personal circumstances of patrons gambling away their wages. Sometimes children would come into the club in tears begging for their parents to be thrown out of the gaming room, which staff had no power to do.

One former manager recalled executives (not including Belevski) laughing about a patron whose visits had been reduced to pension days after she lost two houses to gambling.

In early 2024, Belevski hired former Crown and Star marketing manager Vicki Le, who duplicated the casino’s promotions programs to the extent that casino terms such as “the cage” remained on the terms and conditions circulated to staff. The club went from offering $500 prizes on a Thursday night to continuous giveaways ranging from $1200 in cash to gold bullion.

A former duty manager recalled players lending money to one another, and frequent arguments on the gaming floor.

“There were two loan sharks there day and night, and if you wanted to borrow money to play the poker machines it was 10 per cent [interest] across the board, whether you had a loan for five minutes or five days,” the duty manager said.

“I’m not talking $10 or $20. This was people putting hundreds of thousands of dollars through the machines.”

Club president Robinson said the club took its responsible gambling and anti-money laundering obligations seriously and operated under the oversight of Liquor and Gaming NSW.

Departing NSW Independent Casino Commission chief commissioner Phil Crawford this month lashed the Minns government for its failure to implement the NSW Crime Commission’s recommendation for mandatory cashless gaming in pubs and clubs.

He argued that large poker machine venues should be brought under the regulation of a centralised gambling watchdog in line with the scrutiny placed on casinos.

For Cabra-Vale and its executives, the status quo has been lucrative.

Every year, staff would get a Christmas bonus of four weeks’ pay. And every year Belevski’s salary would also rise closer to the magic million-dollar mark.

But Belevski had far grander plans.

Other clubs were ploughing billions of dollars into gyms, aquatic centres, aged care facilities, child care centres and event spaces, as they sought ways to reinvest their colossal profits and maintain not-for-profit tax status. Some clubs hoped these new facilities might also offer a path out of their reliance on gaming.

Belevski’s vision for Cabra-Vale Diggers, however, looked beyond the local club scene to Macau, Las Vegas and the foreshores of Barangaroo, where Crown Resorts was building a hotel to anchor its casino. This model leaned into the venue as a gambling holiday destination, with upmarket restaurants, boutique shopping, a gym and a luxurious pool.

With the club’s catering contractor Ricky Char, a lanky restaurateur who owned an apartment at Barangaroo and had a weakness for fast cars and race horses, Belevski travelled to China, Vietnam and Macau, and took note of hotels that funnelled guests through their casinos.

(“Never again,” Char later complained to a staff member after one such trip. “I paid for everything, gave him a holiday, and he sat around in his room the whole time because he didn’t like the food.”)

In 2017, as Belevski’s arch rival at Mounties unveiled a majestic new entrance designed to “evoke the arrival experience of a luxury hotel”, Cabra-Vale Diggers submitted a development application for an actual resort.

Standing next to Belevski at a topping-out ceremony for the new resort six years later was Rony Wardan.

Wardan, a Parramatta developer with property interests throughout Sydney’s northwest, had completed the structural framework, but his focus when he rose to the lectern was less on the mechanics of the build than the handshakes which greased the wheel.

“While these tree-topping ceremonies are generally held to symbolise the prosperity of the building, I personally view this ceremony as a symbol of proposing relationships that brought us to where we are today,” he read from his speech notes.

Wardan well understood the value of good relationships.

His recruitment to the project two years earlier had raised eyebrows. A residential developer, he had no experience in club capital works. There is no evidence the project went to a competitive tender.

“The board never [saw] any of it,” former Cabra-Vale director Ronnie Moore said. “We were just told we were down to three contractors, no names or anything, and he was the successful one.”

Current president Walter Robinson said the process was undertaken in accordance with legislative requirements and that the Wardan Group was selected based on its “capability, alignment with the club’s vision and commitment to delivering an exceptional experience”.

The contract they agreed to was “costs plus”, meaning there was no fixed price and Wardan added a mark-up on costs, which exceeded their estimates by an average of $30 million per year. The Wardan Group’s 2025 financial report shows that it made a $17 million, or nearly 20 per cent, profit on its trading income.

Rony Wardan declined to confirm a figure, citing a confidentiality clause. He said the costs increased due to rising construction costs in Sydney and client-driven changes to the scope of the project. There was less than 4 per cent variance to the original budgets after cost escalation was factored in, he said. The costs were reviewed monthly by quantity surveyors engaged by the club and bank.

Wardan was also lined up to develop Cabra-Vale’s second venue, the Campbelltown RSL, a rundown structure on extensive land holdings near the suburb’s train station and central shopping district. The deal was for Wardan to receive part of his payment in real estate, which he would use to develop apartments at the rear of the club.

The absence of a fixed price on the Cabra-Vale Diggers redevelopment generated considerable enthusiasm among its contractors.

Legal documents later tendered in a costs dispute between Wardan Group and Shane Newton’s NB3 Electrical indicate that Wardan’s project manager Marco Mirigliani spruiked the job to subcontractors as a cash bonanza, with a second job at Campbelltown in the offing.

“Hey mate, this job will be easy because we [are] on a cost plus and Rony controls the board,” is what NB3 owner Shane Newton claims he was told by Mirigliani. Mirigliani denies saying this.

As the club’s vice president throughout that early development phase, Moore agreed with that assertion.

“Rony controlled that board through Boris,” Moore said.

Moore had a corporate background and was comfortable with balance sheets and budgets, but other directors were not. He said he and president Walter Robinson were the only directors willing to quiz the club’s management at board meetings.

“I had to [say to] some of these board members, ‘Come on, it’s not for me to move and second things all the time, please speak up’, and they wouldn’t do that,” Moore said.

(Wardan said he had limited involvement with the board and that every decision concerning cost or time was assessed by a quantity surveyor.)

During the procurement stage, Moore found that he had many questions for the club’s managers, particularly regarding the quantum and cost of variations. Some of these, such as a claim for greater excavation costs because contaminated soil had been found on the bowling greens, were submitted without evidence. “I was asking questions as to the budget, how they came to the budget, how they came to select the tenders,” Moore said. “I was basically asking questions that hit a raw nerve.”

Belevski invited Moore and Robinson to lunch at Warwick Farm Racecourse. Belevski asked why they had been asking so many questions at board meetings.

“After that I was wary of him,” Moore said.

Matters came to a head in late 2024. Moore had been compiling evidence to present to the board about a staff retreat at the Terrigal Pacific Coastal Resort two years earlier, where senior managers went back to a hotel room, and events got out of hand.

The chief operating officer Luke Whalan roughhoused a female executive on the bed and floor, before dragging her around the room by her hair. She lost blood after losing an earring, along with chunks of hair. The woman did not complain, but another manager was so distressed by the behaviour that he resigned.

Three witnesses confirmed the incident to the Herald. Whalan categorically denied it. “I take pride in conducting myself professionally and respectfully at all times,” he said. “What has been described to you is not what happened.”

For Belevski, the situation was precarious. The club had narrowly avoided being placed into administration 10 years earlier when his predecessor Bill O’Brien was found to have distributed extreme pornography, including images of bestiality and necrophilia, among staff. Belevski’s appointment was meant to represent a clean slate.

Editorial

But there had been two other sexual harassment matters involving club directors since then, and the regulator had required all staff to undergo annual training in appropriate workplace conduct.

When Moore started asking questions about Terrigal, Belevski seized the phones of some of those who had been in the room. He also confronted a manager he believed had taken photos, asking why he would do such a thing. “Why wouldn’t I?” the manager replied.

Complicating matters for Belevski was the possible disruption to his post-retirement income plan.

He had been working on a scheme for Whalan to succeed him as chief executive and allow him to remain on the payroll as a consultant. Belevski had run this idea past Moore, who told him it would be inappropriate. “I said, ‘No L-plates’,” Moore said, in reference to Whalan.

Then somebody sent Moore a photograph of the incident at Terrigal. He planned to present it to the board.

But he was too late.

A week before the board meeting, Moore was issued with a 12-point disciplinary complaint and summoned to explain why he should not be expelled from the club. The central allegation was that he had been derelict in his duty by not telling the board for two years what he knew about the events in Terrigal.

It also included claims he inappropriately sought reimbursement for events held at the club, refused to shake an ex-employee’s hand, and had sworn at committee members.

Reading through the list of alleged transgressions, Moore was incredulous. He was in the process of compiling evidence on what happened in Terrigal and denied swearing. The expenses he was alleged to have improperly incurred had been approved by the finance committee, detailed in minutes and budgeted.

But three weeks later, a security guard met Moore in the club’s carpark to escort him to the hearing, where he was grilled by the club’s legal representative in the presence of the board. He was not entitled to his own lawyer.

Then after 35 minutes of board deliberation, Moore’s 46-year Cabra-Vale Diggers Club membership was terminated.

For a man who had donated hundreds of hours to the club over the years, it was a shattering turn of events. Retreading the road to his termination, he always comes back to lunch at Warwick Farm where Belevski took exception to the questions he was asking about the redevelopment.

“From there, he was building a dossier on me,” Moore said. “I was gone because that board was not going to go against his wish, which was to expel me.”

Two weeks after Belevski’s ally, builder Rony Wardan, signed a contract with electrical contractor NB3 to begin work on the club in April 2022, there was an unusual request.

Marco Mirigliani asked NB3’s Shane Newton if he could do some “smaller side jobs”, including a kitchen renovation in Harrington Park in southwest Sydney that needed to be done immediately.

The home belonged to Belevski.

“It’s a high-priority job,” Mirigliani said, according to evidence given to the Australian Building and Construction Dispute Resolution Service.

“You can charge the new works like variations, or we can separately arrange the payment whenever suitable.”

Then there was another request from Mirigliani. This time for a property belonging to Wardan.

Newton was asked to “supervise” the connection of Wardan’s farm on a remote fire trail in high country north of Bathurst to the electrical grid, a distance of 550 metres, which required a third-party contractor to install a small substation.

In early 2025, Mirigliani went further, directing Newton to oversee the installation of CCTV cameras at Wardan’s Parramatta office.

The three locations where these works were performed represented “variations under the master arrangement, rather than separate contracts”, NB3 claimed.

In effect, Wardan and Belevski’s personal jobs were being billed to the Cabra-Vale Diggers Club, to the tune of a claimed $158,224, which Wardan and Belevski then refused to pay, arguing they had been done as part of the contract for the club. The Australian Building and Construction Dispute Resolution Service ordered Wardan Group to pay 87 per cent of the claimed amount, with interest.

Wardan said it had never been the group’s practice to intermingle personal jobs with client work and it did not occur on this project.

It was not only private jobs that the Wardan Group refused to pay NB3 for.

By mid-2024, the completion date for the redevelopment was pushed back from February to November 2025, and the deep reservoir of poker machine profits that underpinned the project at its outset was down to the dregs. The projected cost increased by $50 million in the first year after Wardan took over as head contractor, and $40 million the year after that.

The club was seeking additional financing, which was bound to result in more scrutiny.

In early May, Newton was informed that the club’s project manager had “stuffed his budgets”, the board was asking questions, and all variations were to be frozen.

This presented a major cash flow problem for NB3. The design had changed significantly since Newton signed the contract and he had already completed and paid subcontractors to deliver on the changes. If Wardan did not pay him for the variations as agreed, he would be left carrying the can.

In late 2024, the Commonwealth Bank extended the club a $100 million loan, and appointed its own quantity surveyor.

From that point, relations between all parties deteriorated.

At a meeting in July 2025, Newton proposed a new deed of settlement to account for the two-year delay, which had left him paying overheads during periods of idle labour and cost him two project managers who resigned in frustration. No agreement was reached.

Newton testified that after the meeting, Wardan turned to his son, the group’s general counsel Andrew Wardan, and asked, “Push the button?”

Andrew Wardan allegedly shrugged. His father repeated: “Push the button!” He then turned to Newton and said, “Good luck”.

Newton testified: “I specifically recall this interaction because … it sounded like something out of The Godfather. Little did I know what they had in store for me going forward.”

Several days later, Newton turned up at the site to find an eviction notice pinned to his door. He spoke to Wardan on the phone. “I still think this relationship is salvageable, but I have lost faith in you,” Wardan allegedly said. “If it is not, I will steamroll you and destroy your business.”

Two weeks later, NB3’s contract was terminated. The adjudicator valued the unpaid work at $1.8 million.

Wardan said NB3 was terminated for breaching its subcontract, and that it disputed the adjudicated amount, which it had appealed against and since settled.

Cabravale Club Resort opened its doors for business on November 15, 2025, a remarkable three hours after council issued the occupation certificate. The event was attended by influencers and celebrities, including television presenter Catriona Rowntree and singer Guy Sebastian. There were lion dancers, fireworks and a drone show, as well as hourly cash giveaways and a Toyota prize.

Speaking with Seven’s Sydney Weekender, Cabravale’s ex-Star and Crown chief commercial officer Vicki Le described the new integrated resort as the first of its kind in Australia, with shopping, dining, a swimming pool and a hair salon. She did not mention its 450 poker machines.

“You can have a staycation here without stepping foot outside of our venue at all,” she said.

But one week after its first anniversary, the building is still unfinished, with hoardings on the windows facing the street. The cost has climbed another $12 million since the final price was announced. It has now reached $242 million – double the amount projected when Wardan took over the head contract.

Adding to its financial concerns is the lack of progress at its sister club, the Campbelltown RSL, which is being developed by Wardan’s other company, the Bell Property Group. The crane hanging over the construction site has been idle for months, though Wardan said work had recently recommenced and was progressing well.

“There was a period of inactivity … while the client obtained their funding,” he said.

Originally a fixed-price contract for $67 million, the 2026 annual report described it for the first time as “fixed cost with rise and fall provisions”.

“Following cost increases identified under the rise and fall provisions, the club is currently in discussions with the Bell Property Group in relation to revised scope of the contract which may increase the total contracted amount should the revised scope be agreed,” the annual report said.

The report also revealed that the club parted ways with its longstanding auditor BDO. ASIC filings show this occurred two weeks before the financial statements were published.

Notwithstanding the construction blowouts, Cabravale still found enough savings to give its four key management executives a shared $800,000 pay rise last financial year, bringing their collective salary bill to $3.3 million – nearly double what it donated in community grants.

Boris Belevski announced at the October annual general meeting that he would retire in 2027, possibly to spend more time at Port Douglas, in Far North Queensland, where he and his wife last year bought a four-bedroom house with a swimming pool for $1.6 million.

Club president Robinson said the organisation stood by Belevski. “The club and its CEO categorically reject any suggestion of improper conduct, including claims that personal benefits were received from contractors or other third parties,” Robinson said.

Belevski’s son, Jay, also benefited from the relationships his father made on the job. The club’s architect, Altis, a large firm that specialises in hospitality projects, designed Jay Belevski’s backyard swimming pool and cabana in 2022. Jay Belevski said he paid for the work himself.

Wardan, meanwhile, has secured the early works contract for the $350 million development of Parramatta Leagues Club.

Scottish Premiership roundup: Celtic sweep St Mirren aside to strengthen grip at top

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:05:28 GMT

Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan on target

Hearts thrash Dundee 8-0; Frick makes winning start

The recalled midfielders Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan both scored as Celtic beat St Mirren 4-1. The champions brushed off the loss of midfield pair Mika Baur and Benjamin Nygren to injury to consolidate their place at the top of the Premiership.

The centre-forward Camilo Duran was also on target as Celtic killed the game late in the first half with three goals in nine minutes. Callum McGregor grabbed his first league goal of the season before Killian Phillips scored a consolation from the spot.

With Baur facing up to 10 weeks out with an ankle injury and Nygren nursing a heel problem, Martin O’Neill would have been delighted with how his midfield functioned.

Oxlade-Chamberlain made his fifth start of the season and McCowan his second. The pair had never started a game together before. O’Neill also introduced the former PSV Eindhoven midfielder Joël van den Berg for a debut in the second half and the 19-year-old showed some good touches.

Celtic started with a new-look front three of Duran flanked by Jota and Yang Hyun-jun. Duran was a constant threat and had two goals disallowed for offside in the opening quarter.

Yang was instrumental in the 33rd-minute opener, racing past Declan John and drilling a low pass which ultimately fell for Oxlade-Chamberlain to stroke into the bottom corner.

The South Korean soon passed up a brilliant chance, opting to look for Duran when played clean through by the goalkeeper Sam Johnstone. The pass was under-hit and Alex Gogic cleared.

Duran was on the end of a far better ball in the 40th minute, cushioning home a volley after a superb whipped cross by Kieran Tierney. Duran soon set up Jota, who was denied by Jacob Chapman, before finding Tierney, who provided another assist as McCowan drilled a first-time finish.

Celtic went four ahead in the 63rd minute when the ball broke for McGregor on the edge of the box. The captain quickly shifted the ball on to his right foot and swept it into the bottom corner.

Johnstone blew his chance of a clean sheet when he crashed into Calvin Ramsay as he came off his line to punch the ball. Phillips converted the resulting 70th-minute penalty and St Mirren kept pushing with Johnstone saving well from Ismeal Kabia and Samuel Ramos coming close.

Hearts returned to winning ways in spectacular style as they destroyed 10-man Dundee 8-0. They went into the game on the back of a run of three straight defeats but they ran riot, scoring four in the first half thanks to Sabah Kerjota, a Pierre Landry Kaboré double and an own goal by Ryan Finnigan.

Dundee were reduced to 10 men after the break with Owen Bevan shown a straight red card before Claudio Braga, Sabri Guendouz, Kerjota with his second and Stuart Findlay blew Dundee away with four more goals.

Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:00:06 GMT

Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge

Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.

Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.

With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.

It’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?

Sackings have become almost ritualistic. Football demands blood sacrifice. How else can the harvest be guaranteed but by the torching of the wicker man? How else can Crystal Palace stay up but by the sacking of Pierre Sage? Once, when the manager defined the club, bought the players, decided the tactics, set the mood, that perhaps made sense. When managers were messiahs, it requires only a slight tweak to the underlying theology to see a logic in sacrificing them.

But managers now, at least at the majority of Premier League clubs, are part of a wider structure. In one of his meltdowns at Spurs, Antonio Conte made the point that it made little sense for him to be answering questions about the broader future of the club when he had so little power compared with the tiers of executives. Why sack the manager rather than the head of recruitment or the sporting director or the chair?

The answer to that perhaps goes back to the emergence of the English idea of the manager, which began in the 1930s and blossomed in the post-war golden age of Matt Busby, Bill Shankly, Don Revie and Brian Clough. As Barney Ronay argues in The Manager, at least part of the reason he became a figure of such pre-eminence was that it was useful for the board to have a hapless ashen-faced figure standing out on the touchline to take the blame. A handful of geniuses aside, the manager was essentially a convenient scapegoat.

But does the sacrifice work? It was one of the shibboleths of football’s early data wonks that the new manager bounce was a myth. What was being witnessed when form improved after a sacking was nothing more than regression to the mean. Which sounds sensible: squads make games and are determined by finance. There is a wealth of evidence that the biggest single factor in determining league position is the wage bill.

And yet there is also evidence that new manager bounce does exist. A lot of early data analysis in football ignored the fact that those involved are human and respond emotionally to circumstance. More recent studies, though, suggest that, while around a quarter of clubs experience no improvement, the first five matches under a new manager show a 41% improvement in points per game, although the impact wears off after around 10 games.

after newsletter promotion

That feels intuitively true and is readily explicable. A manager under pressure can become embattled, lashing out at enemies real and imagined, their capacity to make lucid decisions impaired as confidence ebbs, creating a doom spiral. Replacing him breaks that pattern and permits a psychological reset.

In a world where everything is studied endlessly, a new manager should make a team less predictable. It’s possible, of course, that as those early analyses suggested, performances would have turned anyway as part of a regression to the mean, but it is curious how often the uptick in form coincides with the replacement of the manager.

Anthropologists are yet to determine precisely why United sacrifice managers so frequently, although there does appear to be some sense of deflecting blame. There is also a sense that it has become routine, that reasons that once probably did exist have been forgotten over time.

Sacking the manager is just what the club do a few months into the season, the ritual now as divorced from its original purpose as modern Hallowe’en customs are from their origins in the Christian commemoration of All Hallows’ Eve.

Will the arrival of Pochettino help? He is a far more ebullient and charismatic figure than Carrick, whose status as a dead man walking for most of this season perhaps meant players did not take him as seriously as they might have an incumbent who appeared to be there for the long term, or had them beginning to ponder moves away from United.

But this remains a mismatched hotchpotch of a squad assembled over six previous managers. If there is some style of play that would suit most of them it has yet to reveal itself.

It will take time for Pochettino to instil in a side that are habitually outrun the levels of conditioning that characterised his Tottenham, and perhaps even longer to get them playing in a coherent pattern. There will probably have to be five or six new signings (and at least as many departures). Probably most difficult of all, there is the entire culture of the club to overhaul, which may not be possible without a change of ownership.

Given United came back from two goals behind three times in their final two games under Carrick, these are not usual circumstances: beleaguered managers rarely inspire such defiance, and the fans never turned against him. In that sense, there will not be the immediate benefit that comes when toxicity is removed.

Some sort of bounce, though, is probable under Pochettino, if only because a negative pattern has been broken. The question is how long it can be maintained.

If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and smart tactical rejig, suggested that he is no mug after all.

It left Arsenal – who lost their goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City and Arteta with a face like thunder.

Only last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players.

Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending an awful lot of money, they have struggled to replace last season’s now departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

• Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February.

• Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline.

• Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta

That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were signed this summer. The other five new faces that arrived during a close season that saw a total of around £275m invested on newcomers were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man match day squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given that Bamba and Touré cost a combined £78.5m their total omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to leave González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tags on the bench.

Back on the pitch the jury remained out on Hornicek. The Czechia international has made some excellent saves this season but, here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved when he hesitated too long as the impressive Kai Harvertz closed in.

Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left back Lewis Hall, given a thorough workout by Noni Madueke.

Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, did his very best to slow the tempo but ultimately it proved a forlorn task. The red tide could only be stemmed for so long.

When Havertz dispossessed Hall, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated pass to Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance to unleash a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past the powerless Hornicek.

As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.

Given that on those rare moments when Newcastle’s attack looked as if it might flicker into life, Declan Rice always seemed on hand to reinforce his defence and smother any sort of danger, the omens were not bright for Jaissle. Arsenal’s pressing was so good that Newcastle were left seemingly incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.

Yet however far fetched that vision seemed it was something Harvey Barnes would prove fully capable of buying into. The winger is Newcastle’s best finisher and underlined that fact again early in the second half. Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch slicing the ball in Osula’s direction. Once the Dane played it into the path of Barnes it took a single, steadying, touch and an assured finish to leave the hitherto redundant Raya picking his shot out of the net.

Jaissle’s introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – who, incidentally, were all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy at the interval was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.

The home side had begun closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and, along the way had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead in the wake of a Hall corner headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.

Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty looking left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring the withdrawl of Guimarães.

Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counter-attacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying a couple of defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.
