Get Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equality

after newsletter promotion

The international court of justice (ICJ) found that the 2016-2017 military campaign by Myanmar targeting its Rohingya minority amounted to genocide in a landmark ruling. “Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to ‘prevent births’,” the Guardian reports. “Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.”

Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in the occupied West Bank when she shot in the head after Israeli settler militants fired towards Palestinian houses.

Forty-five percent of women in west and Central Africa have no power of consent, according to a new report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). In east and southern Africa and in Arab states, 33% of women are also unable to say no to their partner.

A new report by Save the Children found the highest number of children living in conflict zones since records began in 1990. Africa is home to 44% of the global total, a nearly 20% increase from 2024. The report found the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.

“Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry,” writes Stuart Heritage who bravely endured the entire documentary. “There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up.”

The Jerusalem Post reported that it obtained a transcript of Biden’s last conversation with accused war criminal Benhamin Netanyahu. “I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said. “I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.” Want to spell out exactly what Netanyahu did, Joe? He has the blood of tens of thousands of dead Palestinian kids on his hands. Dropping 2,000lb bombs on tent camps full of starving people isn’t exactly how I’d define “courage”.

So says the Wall Street Journal, which reports: “We’re in the midst of a no-smile epidemic” amongst school-age children. While I’d take all this with a pinch of imported German rock salt, there are some fun nuggets here about how social media trends are impacting school photos. “[M]ale students are tilting their head backwards,” one staff photographer told the WSJ. “They tell me they are ‘aura farming.’ I had to look it up.” I had to look it up too.

‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 13:00:01 GMT

‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout

The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.

Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.

This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else.

Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble.

The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland.

Many of these are under construction; some are little more than announcements. CoreWeave is building them by taking on staggering quantities of debt. The company now owes $47bn (£36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn of this figure due next year. It bled $709m last quarter, on revenues of $3.6bn.

CoreWeave already looked dangerously exposed this autumn, when creditors put its risk of default – being unable to pay its debts – at over 60% at some point over the next five years.

Its earnings, released earlier in November, provided a brief respite from some of their fears – its margins and revenues “knocked it out of the park”, said Jordan Chaflin, head of technology at CreditSights, a financial research firm.

That was before scandal hit Nvidia, the most valuable business in AI and the company that makes CoreWeave’s entire business model possible. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. He’s now out. This will have consequences, and no one knows what they are yet.

Huang ran his business on close relationships and, as Nvidia grew, these relationships became the scaffolding of the AI economy. Few companies will be more affected by his removal than CoreWeave.

Its vulnerabilities – and they are many – are a blueprint for the wobbly structure of the AI bubble itself, on which the fortunes of the world’s stock market and the global economy now depend.

CoreWeave is what is called a “neocloud”. Its basic business model is this: the world’s biggest AI companies, like OpenAI, want billions of people to start using their products but don’t want to sink a fortune into building the large datacentres it takes to run them. Nvidia, its primary backer, wants to sell lots of computer chips to the world’s biggest AI companies.

So Nvidia provided the finance for CoreWeave and its peers to buy its chips, stuff them into datacentres, and rent that computational power to the world’s biggest AI companies.

Nvidia owns approximately 11% of CoreWeave. There are other arrangements, too, including a $6.3bn deal in which Nvidia agreed to buy “compute” that CoreWeave cannot sell – a sort of guarantee.

That’s not the only side of the equation Nvidia is propping up. It also has invested in CoreWeave’s clients – companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and nearly a dozen others that rent these chips. A dollar that Nvidia invests in one of these can end up as income on CoreWeave’s balance sheet, and then revenue for Nvidia as CoreWeave purchases chips.

Circular arrangements like this are the scaffolding of the AI economy. CoreWeave – and companies like it – are the vehicle through which Nvidia can make its balance sheet look spectacular, and OpenAI and Anthropic can provide ever-more-powerful models to their customers without paying workmen to break earth in Texas.

Think of it as a sandwich where neither slice of bread – Nvidia or a frontier AI company using its chips – wants to finance or build, say, $1tn worth of sheds stuffed with semiconductors, so the peanut butter in the middle takes on the risk.

Analysts expect CoreWeave to be a capital-intensive – meaning big-spending – business. Someone has to be. Most appear to have accepted its considerable risk.

“Their business model is essentially … you’re doing this massive buildout of infrastructure,” said Chaflin. “It is really quite painful from a free cashflow perspective, during the buildout.”

That infrastructure “needs to get funded with debt” Chaflin said. He emphasises that CoreWeave is not the only company doing this: it is the business model of “hyperscalers” and “neoclouds” – the companies building AI datacentres to support a future, still-theoretical AI economy.

In a US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing this summer, CoreWeave listed 18 different varieties of debt it is now paying back, amounting to roughly $35bn. In its most recent earnings, which do not break down this debt, that number is up by nearly $12bn, to $47bn.

It expects its interest payments to crest over $1bn next quarter. More than $10bn of its debt comes due next year.

What is this debt? Is it sustainable? And what happens if CoreWeave can’t pay it?

CoreWeave has been a test case in creating a new kind of debt, which has allowed it to finance its operations. This is GPU-backed debt – where a GPU is a specialised computer chip.

CoreWeave borrows money against its main asset, which are those computer chips made by Nvidia.

Since this has looked like a shaky proposition to most lenders – AI is a new, frothy technology – it couples those computer chips with customer contracts. In other words, CoreWeave has borrowed money by showing banks and private credit agencies that it has the goods, and it has people paying money to use them.

This has allowed it to borrow nearly $25bn.

When CoreWeave first started doing this, many people thought GPU-backed debt was a bad idea – not least because GPUs, unlike real estate, say, lose their value over time. In October 2025, the news website the Verge called the company “an Eldritch horror” with “no obvious path towards profitability”.

But then other companies – Crusoe, Nscale, Lambda – also started to take out loans backed by GPUs. Slowly, markets started to buy into the idea. In 2024, when CoreWeave took out its first GPU-backed loan, it had to pay a high interest rate of 15%. This has decreased to 9% on some subsequent loans.

This March, CoreWeave even managed to class $8.5bn of this debt as “investment grade” – suggesting it is trustworthy – and sell it to institutional investors, including insurance companies and pension funds.

after newsletter promotion

Short-sellers, who bet on a fall in a company’s share price, are nervous about this idea. A major point of unease is the timeline for how fast the chips will lose their value, or depreciate.

CoreWeave has suggested this could happen over six years. There are market watchers who believe the real timeline could be far shorter. This could mean that at some point its loans might be backed by collateral that has plummeted in value.

No one knows if this will actually be a problem. Chaflin is optimistic. “We’re in an extremely tight environment for AI infrastructure,” he said, and there is demand for secondhand chips.

CoreWeave also has long-term contracts, he said, meaning that its customers are committed to pay for most of the lifespan of the chips they are renting.

This will work as long as those customers – such as OpenAI – stay solvent. For some of them, that might come down to: will Nvidia still finance them?

The answer is again, no one knows.

The GPU-backed debt is not CoreWeave’s only debt. Beginning last summer, the company also started issuing a different kind of debt called senior notes.

While the GPU-backed debt is backed by CoreWeave’s expensive computer chips, these senior notes are unsecured. This means there is no specific asset tied to them that a creditor could repossess if the loan becomes unpayable.

Should CoreWeave go belly-up, the owners of the senior notes are in theory entitled to be repaid first. How that repayment will be made is unclear. The company has few assets outside GPUs. It does not even own many of its datacentres outright. Instead it leases the buildings from other companies.

A spokesperson for CoreWeave said: “Customers are signing multiyear commitments for earlier-generation GPUs extending beyond their depreciable lives, with pricing above their original contracts. And we are financing our growth with an increasingly diverse and flexible funding strategy, lowering our weighted average cost of debt, and in most cases eliminating any reliance on renewals to repay that debt.”

CoreWeave had little choice but to take out these loans, and to issue this debt. It needs them to finance its expansion. The capital intensity of this – the sheer, huge sums it needs to keep going – are all part of its business model.

Will that business model work?

No one knows if CoreWeave has a long-term future. For analysts and short-sellers closely watching CoreWeave’s – and others’ – financials, the answer lies somewhere in the thousand moving pieces that compose its commitments and its dependencies.

Will it have the cash to repay its vast debts? If it doesn’t, who might step in to save it? If it defaults, who might it take down with it?

CoreWeave is bleeding hundreds of millions of dollars each quarter paying the interest on its debt. There is a real possibility that its revenues will not be as strong this year. CoreWeave makes money by renting chips out to paying customers. It says it has more than $100bn of contracts in the pipeline, a reassuring number.

But, unlike most of its competitors, CoreWeave accepts large sums upfront for its multiyear contracts. In other words, its annual revenues largely reflect years of future income for services that it has yet to carry out.

“Roughly two-thirds of the cash its business ‘generated’ was customers paying in advance, not profit from service already delivered,” said Brian Hopkins, at the research firm Forrester.

This suggests CoreWeave’s existing customers are unlikely to be enough to keep its income – $3.4bn last quarter – steady. It will have to keep finding new customers because it has already booked much of the value of its current contracts.

But there are also question marks over the solvency of its customers. Leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are heavily loss-making. They have so far managed to keep paying for “compute” – chips in CoreWeave’s datacentres – by borrowing money, and from companies like Nvidia.

Will they keep raising this money? Possibly not. Recent reporting has indicated that Nvidia, in a post-Jensen Huang world, might pull back from its role as the “central bank of AI”.

A spokesperson for CoreWeave said: “Demand for CoreWeave’s AI cloud platform is not an assumption, it’s backed by $132.5bn in contractual commitments from the world’s leading AI labs and enterprises. We grew to 1.7GW of active capacity in the last quarter and are benefiting from a very strong pricing environment.”

Finally there is the question of if political headwinds could delay or freeze datacentre projects. This is an unknown – and its interest payments rely on the answer.

“CoreWeave pays interest whether or not a datacentre comes online on time but it only earns revenue once the capacity is delivered. Local restrictions or permitting fights stretch that gap, and the company is already guiding to more than $1bn of interest expense a quarter,” said Hopkins.

What happens if it misses a payment, or if it defaults? For the pension and insurance firms that hold its debt, that is a critical question.

“The only asset on the balance sheet that isn’t pledged to someone is Michael Intrator’s kidneys,” said Amir Zabeti, the managing director of Mancala Capital, which is currently shorting CoreWeave. (Michael Intrator is the chief executive of CoreWeave.)

CoreWeave’s debt payments over the next three years are already equivalent to two years of income, said Hopkins. And the company still needs more money to build datacentres to service its customers. It is about to another round of debt.

“That leaves very little room if anything slips,” said Hopkins.

Reform UK considers pact with Restore Britain to overcome stalling performance in polls

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:22:54 GMT

Thursday’s byelection in Castle Bromwich will be latest test for Nigel Farage’s party as rival eats into support

Voters go to the polls in the village of Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands on Thursday in a little-noticed election that is the latest test for Reform at a time when it is particularly vulnerable.

Yet, while it is the Conservatives who are edging ahead in recent polls, the decisive difference could well be the performance of Restore Britain – the hard-right party set up by Rupert Lowe after the MP fell out with Nigel Farage.

Reform has lost no less than five elections since September, on one occasion by as little as two votes, after Restore attracted voters who might otherwise have voted for Farage’s party.

The possibility of offering an electoral pact to Restore is now under discussion among some figures at Reform’s Millbank HQ, the Guardian understands. There is also fervent internal opposition from some who balk at the ethno-nationalism that has found a home in Restore.

“Just take a look at some of the people who have attached themselves to Restore, as well as what some of their people have said about Jews and Muslims in their comments,” said one.

At the same time, and even after an aborted attempt to bury the hatchet between Lowe and Farage, others in Reform are leaving the door open to a reconciliation with Restore at a time when the party needs to find a way to overcome its stalling support.

“There’s an argument that we should be going after Restore and we’ll benefit from that, but there is also one where we work with them … and, to be honest, I don’t know the answer yet,” said one.

One senior Reform source said the idea of a “non-aggression pact” with Restore was in the air and there was a “deal to be done” but was more sceptical about a deeper tie up or merger.

At the same time, other senior Reform figures who are close to Farage are pushing for him to go much further towards a detente with Rupert Lowe, with efforts under way to push them back together.

Among Reform insiders, there is an acknowledgment that Farage is at least as exercised and frustrated about Restore eating into the party’s vote as he is about the investigations into his own financial affairs. One Reform politician said they envisaged Lowe ultimately being readmitted, but that the price would be the exit of Zia Yusuf, who had accused Lowe of assaulting him amid the furore that led to the MP’s suspension from the party.

However, that was before Yusuf this week appeared to praise Lowe in a conversation with the Spectator’s editor, Michael Gove. “Rupert is a force of nature,” said Yusuf, who went on to describe him as a “formidable person” in comments that drew a strikingly warm response from Lowe himself, who tweeted that he appreciated Yusuf’s acknowledgment of Restore’s progress.

“I suspect on policy and trust in politics, Yusuf and I have more in common than the former Tory ministers in Reform’s leadership,” he added.

Last week, there was a public display of Reform working with Restore when the former Tory MPs Andrew Rosindell and Suella Braverman signed an early day motion by Lowe opposing a Liberal Democrat bid to pave the way for census questions to include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as Black English or Asian English.

Even within Restore, and away from the public rhetoric, there is curiosity about the openness of Reform to some form of pact as the speculation about an early general election persists.

“Our offer remains on the table and we are open to negotiating that offer,” said a Restore source, who cited events in the summer when it looked like a reconciliation between Farage and Lowe was in the offing.

“It is Farage and others who have outright rejected it, but the ball is in their court.”

On that occasion, what seemed like tentative moves towards peace broke down amid a fresh row between the two leaders, with Lowe accusing Farage of lying after the latter had said he had reached out but had not heard back.

What remains clear now though is that Restore’s consistent nudging of 5% in serious national polls has taken some in its own ranks and even in Reform – whose leader predicted that its rival “would be lucky to get 1% anywhere” – by surprise. A Restore source said of Reform: “It feels like they’re having a bit of an identity crisis and falling below 20% has clearly given them pause for thought.”

More stark has been the proliferation of Restore branches across the UK – sometimes numbering just a handful of people but in others much larger – and the steady dripfeed of defections from Reform.

Last week, those who joined Lowe at a lavish central London dinner for members of Restore’s “Cromwell Club” for those donating £2,500 a year included Holly Vallance, the estranged wife of Reform’s honorary treasurer Nick Candy, who had frequently been cited as a potential candidate for Farage’s party.

Also there was Charlton Edwards, who was Reform’s treasurer until recently and a figure at the very heart of the courting of donors by Farage’s party.

Aside from the beef between Farage and Lowe – arguably the biggest alpha males on the right – the biggest stumbling block to a pact is the antisemitism within Restore, said one source in Reform, which has made a concerted effort to court the British Jewish community.

“Restore emerged because Rupert was out for revenge and it’s hard to ignore. But there are also things that have been said by people around Restore about Jews, Muslims, that we find deeply uncomfortable,” they said, citing the explicit antisemitism directed towards Restore’s Molly Kingsley online when Lowe unveiled her as his party’s “accountability” spokesperson.

Figures such as Charlie Downes, a Restore election candidate who is often seen by Lowe’s side, have said that only white Christians can truly be British. Another Restore member who was pictured alongside Lowe at last week’s Cromwell Club dinner, the former GB News presenter Calvin Robinson, has been condemned in recent days for comments in which he talked of the need to “drive out the Jews” from the US.

However, extreme language can also be found in Reform. Last week, the Welsh Senedd member Joe Martin became the first frontline Reform politician to use the term “remigration” – one that originated on the far right and is frequently used by Restore.

Others in Reform, meanwhile, are impressed by the social media strategy of Restore, which has on occasion been backed by Elon Musk.

Chaudhary outshines Brook as Australia pip England in gripping T20 opener

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:04:14 GMT

At the end of a bruising week for Australian cricket came a few hours of respite and a night that ended with cheers echoing around the MCG. Set 188 to win, a home side light on star names beat England by three wickets and with one ball to spare.

The off-field developments kept coming before the start of play. Cricket Australia publicly threw its support behind Pat Cummins as Test captain, while its broadcast partner Fox Cricket decided it was in everyone’s interest to stand down Usman Khawaja and David Warner from commentary duties.

ABC had no such qualms about Darren Lehmann continuing behind the microphone, however. And before the start of the match – the first of five to round off England’s white-ball tour – the former Australia head coach once again denied any prior knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the ball in South Africa eight years ago.

But when Jack Edwards drilled the penultimate delivery of the match from Sam Curran for four to seal the deal, events in 2018 – and who has been economical with the truth since – were far from the minds of the 39,000-strong crowd. Twenty20 is intended to be lighthearted fun. Sticking it to the old enemy is even better.

The star of the evening was the little-known Nikhil Chaudhary, an India-born all-rounder who was visiting Australia on a travel visa in early 2020 when the Covid-19 pandemic struck. Chaudhary stayed on, worked his way up through club cricket and became a match-winner in just his fourth outing for his adopted country.

The Durham opener Ben McKinney has earned his maiden senior England call-up after being added to the squad for the Test tour of South Africa that gets under way in Johannesburg next month. The 6ft 7in left-hander was originally part of the Lions squad that will land in South Africa at the end of November but will instead move up to the senior touring party because of Jacob Bethell's withdrawal to undergo further knee surgery.

An academy footballer at Sunderland before switching his full focus to cricket at 16, McKinney broke the 1,000-run mark in Division Two last season and has been a regular in the Lions setup over the past two years. The 23-year-old has seven first-class centuries and has captained England Under-19s.

McKinney is expected to start the South Africa tour as top-order cover, with his county teammate Emilio Gay one of the incumbent openers alongside the more established Ben Duckett. Bethell underwent a second operation on his troublesome knee on Thursday and is likely to miss the entire winter.

McKinney was one of two call-ups published by England on Saturday, with the Hampshire seamer Scott Currie set to join the T20 squad in Australia and be part of the squad for the fifth match in Canberra on 2 December.

Harry Brook and Jordan Cox are due to leave for South Africa after the fourth match in Sydney, with Will Jacks stepping up to captain the side in Brook's absence. Ali Martin

Chaudhary’s two wickets – with just 21 in the runs column – were key to derailing England’s effort with the bat which, despite being a record total on this ground, was still light at 187 for nine. The wrist-spinner shutting down Harry Brook’s 28-ball 65 via a fine edge was arguably the moment this game turned.

The 30-year-old was not done there, however, going one better than England’s captain with a 38-ball 66 from No 4 that broke the back of the chase. Edwards, 25 not out from 11 deliveries, was the finisher after two wickets earlier on.

England overcame a 1-0 deficit during the recent one-dayers and will not be beating themselves up too much. Of greater concern will be the injury to the vice-captain, Will Jacks, who was struck on his bowling hand by a rasping drive from Ben Dwarshuis and walked off with blood pouring out of the wound.

Jacks is due to captain England in the fifth match of this series when Brook flies to join the Test squad in South Africa. Speaking after the defeat, and bemoaning yet another slow start, Brook conceded it did not look too promising.

Brook also accepted that England ultimately let this match slip with the bat, with their innings one that started chaotically, promised plenty at the halfway stage, but ended up fizzling out as Australia’s spinners applied the squeeze.

After Phil Salt fell to the first ball of the match and his fellow Welshman Aneurin Donald departed soon after, Brook put on a display of remarkable ball-striking alongside Tom Banton (39 from 22). Their third-wicket stand was worth 97 runs from 41 balls and drew plenty of gasps from the locals.

That said, Australia should have shut him down far sooner, granting lives on two and three and putting down six catches in the innings overall. Brook is not a player to hand a life, let alone two. And his 20-ball half-century, having been seven off nine, included surely one of the flattest, longest square sixes on this ground.

Adam Zampa was among those manhandled initially but, after an electric catch from the debutant Lachlan Shaw on the rope removed Banton, the leg-spinner then returned to pin Jacks lbw for one. Sitting 123 for five at the start of the 12th over, England were suddenly mindful of burning more resources and finished short.

Liam Dawson struck in the first over of the reply by bowling Jake Fraser-McGurk as the opener danced down the pitch. At the other end Henry Crocombe saw his first ball on debut swivel-pulled for six by Mitch Marsh. The Australia captain’s 32-ball 37 was slightly laboured and was ended by an athletic take by Dawson.

Impetus instead came from another newcomer in Sam Harper and a frisky 15-ball 32 from No 3 that saw Jamie Overton taken for 21 off his first over. Chaudhary then made good use of the crease to take the game away, striking six fours, sending two over the rope, and enjoying some running verbal battles along the way.

I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:00:58 GMT

Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human.

Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform.

We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course. We may double down in stubbornness, insisting on our rightness. We express ourselves, connect with others, reproduce, indulge, purge; we strive toward a goal, transform in an encounter, make vows, renege them, encounter the void, try to fill it, fail, drown out the dread, and go about the humdrum tasks of everyday life as honestly as we can.

From a young age, we are nurtured and protected by our caregivers. We experience beauty and sit with mysteries. We do not exist merely for utility.

Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark.

Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside.

Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.

Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings.

Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine.

And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production.

Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity, confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live.

If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world.

So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity?

Well, I have a radical suggestion for all of us, but especially the tech billionaires searching for answers in Christianity.

Go to church.

Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones.

If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul.

In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible.

When you leave church, carry those teachings back to your offices and boardrooms. Ask how the decisions you make affect the poor, the workers whose livelihoods are being transformed, and the neighbors who will never share in your wealth.

The mystery of the Christian faith is inseparable from its demands upon how we live. You cannot claim to embrace its wisdom while setting aside the obligations it places upon you.

Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors.

The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.

The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:00:57 GMT

When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement?

What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.”

Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

While Köpnick and his team took shifts gently spraying the animal’s exposed back with seawater, dozens of reporters gathered at a vantage point on a grassy hill. Behind them, beyond a rudimentary police barrier, a crowd of increasingly emotional people began to swell. Köpnick remembers these “whale friends” wearily: “They were always having a go at us, saying we weren’t doing enough to save the whale. It was stressful.”

A stream of footage produced by the visitors fed a frenzied online audience: the whale had been dubbed “Timmy” by comedian Hape Kerkeling in the guise of his comic character, grimy tabloid journalist Horst Schlämmer. Others had also given the whale the more abstract name “Hope”, but people eventually took to using both, to complete the animal’s anthropomorphosis with a full name: Timmy Hope.

Meanwhile, furious social media exchanges became wild conspiracy theories. The general thrust of this tsunami of content was that the authorities – and by extension Köpnick – did not have the animal’s best interests at heart. Some had decided he was spraying the whale with not water but acid, to dissolve its flesh so the state’s Ocean Museum Germany could acquire its skeleton.

It became apparent that the whale had become a screen on to which people were projecting their political grievances: one YouTuber suggested its skeleton would be sold “to give even more money to Ukraine”. (Poel is in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a state where the Nord Stream pipeline was once a huge economic asset, and resentment about the German government’s support for Ukraine is particularly strong.)

Köpnick was at the frontline of this pressure, and was getting a little annoyed about it. The hairiest moment came one weekend after Easter, when a crowd burst through the police barriers and 100 protesters came running down the hill towards him. There were only two police officers on duty. “They said, ‘We can’t do anything for you now. Everyone has to save themselves,’” he says, half-amused at the memory.

At that point, Köpnick decided he’d had enough. He picked out two “pack leaders”, led them to his computer monitor and patiently explained what he was doing, that the hose with which he was watering the animal was not, in fact, a chain being used to tie it down, and that he was definitely not dousing the whale with acid.

For a man who had been the island’s fire chief since the days of communist East Germany, and usually had little more to do than rescue the odd holidaymaker who took a boat too far out into the Baltic, it was getting a bit much.

Big marine animals trapped in places they’re not supposed to be always make for a good spectacle. Their plight often stirs people to odd behaviour. Bukang-i, the shark that lost its way in a canal in Busan, South Korea, in October, attracted so many onlookers that would-be vigilantes in hi-vis vests appointed themselves its guardians. Willy, a northern bottlenose whale that mistakenly swam up the Thames for three days in January 2006, also attracted thousands of spectators eager to watch the doomed rescue attempt. Damon Albarn was moved to write a mournful song about it.

But the ordeal of Timmy the humpback triggered a uniquely intense derangement in Germany. Even the lurid jokes about the animal – as prevalent as expressions of anger and grief – seemed to inflate, not puncture, the hysteria, and it was hard to avoid seeing him as a vessel for the country’s fevered political climate. Like Timmy, people felt helpless and abandoned, and the government looked just as impotent – or, worse, seemed to be actively hindering rescue attempts. It wasn’t ideal that the drama unfolded in an election year in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, one of two eastern German states where the populist far-right Alternative für Deutschland was poised to make historic gains.

As an eccentric team of philanthropists, far-right TikTokers, vets and animal rights campaigners rallied to save the whale, people saw their efforts as an act of defiance against an uncaring government. Meanwhile, the reflexive distrust of experts who insisted that the rescue was pointless echoed a recent, much bigger crisis – the pandemic.

Kai Arzheimer, a political scientist at the University of Mainz, describes a feeling of deja vu: “What reminded me of Covid was that there was a relatively broad spectrum of protesters, with a more leftwing, esoteric area on the one side and rightwing populist people on the other, who found common ground in the story of Timmy the whale.”

In the shallow waters on the Baltic coast, the authorities were struggling to get to grips with this extremely unusual situation. Whales of this size almost never beach themselves here, and when they do they are usually already dead or close to it. To have a helpless live animal, nearly 12 metres in length, lie in the bay for weeks on end was practically unprecedented.

On top of that, it looked very much as if Timmy was suffering. The Baltic is a long way from the humpback’s natural habitat in the Atlantic, and the salt content here is so low that if cetaceans spend too long in it, they develop freshwater skin disease, which causes pustules and ulcers that burst and crack, exposing the whale to fungus and bacteria. Horrific as it looks, the disease is not necessarily life-threatening: whales regenerate skin all their lives and look for things to exfoliate with, which is one reason they often get caught in fishing nets.

By the time Timmy had reached Poel, she had already beached herself several times. (It was not until the whole saga was over that everyone realised they had been misgendering her.) She was first sighted in the bay of Wismar, a large mainland town opposite Poel, dragging 20 metres of nets behind her, some wrapped round her head and body. Animal welfare organisation Sea Shepherd Germany, along with Greenpeace, eventually cut her free, an operation that Sea Shepherd campaign leader Flo Stadler says had to be carried out with great care. “The animal reacted with a lot of stress to human contact,” he says. “We could only try it a few times before the animal showed, by noises and by flapping its fins, that it wanted to be left alone.”

Sea Shepherd could not track the whale for long, and could not prevent Timmy from stranding herself near Timmendorfer beach, a resort 50km west of Wismar that provided the inspiration for her nickname. Here, off this sandy beach, the whale was stuck and impossible to ignore.

Enter Robert Marc Lehmann, a YouTuber, wildlife photographer, animal rights campaigner and veteran of several whale rescues, who gathered his team and filming equipment and – if his documentary is to be believed – used sheer force of personality to take charge of the operation to free Timmy. His credentials were, at least initially, enough to convince local mayor Sven Partheil-Böhnke to allow him to get involved.

Stadler seethes a little at the mention of Lehmann, and it is easy to see why. The YouTuber’s alpha-male energy, his declaration that he “might be the person in Germany with the most expertise for a situation like this” and the fact that he was obviously shooting a film as well as trying to save a whale clearly annoyed some of the scientists on the scene. In one tetchy exchange from the documentary, Stephanie Groß, of the Institute for Terrestrial and Aquatic Wildlife Research (ITAW), asks him, “What are you doing here?” Lehmann turns away in disgust.

But despite his abrasive presence, there’s no denying Lehmann took on a key role in the rescue operation. Standing at the whale’s head in a diving suit, he guided excavators as they dug an escape channel centimetres from her face. He also appears to have come up with the idea of gently prodding her further into this channel using the rounded side of the excavator’s shovel. In the film’s climactic night-time scene, Lehmann screams and stamps his feet at the whale to urge her to freedom.

After three days of effort, Timmy swam clear on the night of 26 March. But the relief was short-lived: the next day, she was spotted making her way not north towards Denmark and the North Sea but back east – to where she had just been. There were desperate attempts to use police and coastguard boats to guide her into open waters – partly led by Lehmann, who ranted against ITAW for refusing to let him take full command – but they failed, and on 28 March Timmy was back in the bay of Wismar, swimming around, hopelessly lost. Relations between Lehmann and ITAW broke down completely in a storm of recriminations. Lehmann took no further part in the rescue attempt – though he continued to comment on it on his YouTube channel.

Looking at a map of the islands crowded along this part of the German coast, it’s easy to see how the animal might have got stuck in the labyrinth of shallow channels. Humpbacks, unlike other whales, mainly use eyesight rather than echolocation to guide them, and there’s no sight of open water here. Timmy stranded herself several times over the next two days in the bay of Wismar, before heading north. But Poel is shaped like a horseshoe with the opening facing south; she swam straight into this dead end.

The bay, known as the Kirchsee, is barely more than 200cm at any point – not nearly deep enough for a 12-tonne whale to manoeuvre. Sea Shepherd was still keeping watch, as was Burkard Baschek, director of the Ocean Museum Germany in the nearby city of Stralsund, who coordinated efforts to coax the whale out of Wismar bay. A physicist and expert in ocean dynamics, Baschek is a lean, tall man who adheres strictly to scientific and academic principles, which had the drawback of making him come across as a little severe in interviews.

This was a new challenge for him, too: normally the museum is responsible for collecting and studying dead sea animals washed up on shore. No one was sure what to do with a living animal that, while weak, was showing no signs of dying anytime soon. Still, Baschek was convinced the multiple strandings showed she was sick, even if he couldn’t say exactly what was wrong with her.

The state of Timmy’s health at this point is the subject of much controversy. Those who attempted to rescue her insist she was fit and struggling to survive. So did the protesters, some of whom had travelled from across Germany to stand at the police barrier, and were weeping with grief and angrily declaring Timmy was a “fighter”. Others, including Stadler, maintain she was probably deliberately stranding herself in order to find a quiet place to die without drowning. Baschek reserves judgment: “There are indications that humpbacks do strand themselves when they are weak, but whether it was deliberate or it just got stuck can’t be answered.”

In any case, Baschek says he saw surprising signs of life in Timmy while she was swimming near Wismar in the last few days of March. “Somehow the rest had given it a chance to pool its strength,” he says. “We saw it lift its head out of the water and look at us. There was definitely a will to fight in it then.” But a day later, when Timmy was stuck in Poel, her energy was apparently gone. “It was significantly weaker,” Baschek says.

By this time, Till Backhaus, environment minister of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, had decided to take charge, setting up an office on the scene and appearing at press conferences and on the news almost every day, seemingly willing to talk to any media outlet or YouTuber. (That enthusiasm seems to have worn off: his office could not find time for an interview for this article.)

Having assumed his office in 1998, 67-year-old Backhaus is the longest-serving minister in any of Germany’s 17 state or federal governments, and in 1990 became one of the co-founders of the centre-left Social Democratic Party in East Germany. But even he had never experienced anything like the hysteria of the Timmy crisis. His first response was to do what most politicians would: order an expert assessment. This report, written in the space of a week by Baschek, Groß and another sea mammal expert from ITAW, came to a simple conclusion: the whale was weak and probably sick. The water was too shallow and not salty enough. And, given her skin lesions, any attempt to help would risk further harm. In a press conference, Baschek said further rescue attempts would amount to animal cruelty.

Baschek stands by that report. “If we could have just transported it to the North Sea with a click of our fingers, its prospects would still have been extremely bad,” he says. Sea Shepherd and Greenpeace agreed, and called on the public to leave the animal to die in peace.

There was little chance of that. For many, the prospect of watching this huge animal slowly perish was too much to bear. The torrent of reels on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram did not let up. Much of the content was meant to be funny: a rock band attracted attention with a song called Blow Up the Whale. An online questionnaire helped users decide whether they were “Team Rescue”, “Team Leave” or “Team Kill”. But there were also expressions of grief and videos claiming the decision to leave the whale alone was proof of the corruption of the political establishment.

Katharina Nocun, a political scientist who specialises in conspiracy theories, says the affair was just another story for politically radical groups to exploit. “The same groups and individuals posted things about the farmers’ protests and Covid. A lot of the people who posted about Timmy had a pro-Russian attitude to the war in Ukraine, for example. The issues themselves are to an extent irrelevant; what’s important is that the perceived enemies are the same: politicians, the media, scientists.”

Backhaus, Baschek and anyone associated with the Ocean Museum or ITAW were condemned as murderers and death threats were hurled around, including at Stadler and the Sea Shepherd team. “It was a very loud, enraged mob of people who were suddenly supposedly interested in ocean and animal protection, but who basically just saw the animal as a pet,” Stadler says, still brimming with contempt. “People couldn’t deal with the prospect of watching an animal die.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

In the days after 1 April, it became clear the state was not going to do any more than provide palliative care for the whale – in the shape of Köpnick and his sprinklers. The public refusal to accept this coalesced into a privately funded, hastily organised, semi-improvised rescue attempt the likes of which had never been tried before with a marine animal of this size. It also succeeded – or not, depending on who you ask.

What made it even more extraordinary was the cast of characters involved, starting with the two millionaires who funded it: Karin Walter-Mommert, a racehorse breeder, and Walter Gunz, co-founder of one of Germany’s biggest electronic goods retailers.

It’s not clear what criteria this pair used to assemble their team, but it included a Peruvian author named Sergio Bambarén, who had written a bestselling novel about a dolphin’s quest for freedom and was nicknamed the “whale whisperer” because of his self-professed ability to communicate with Timmy. There was also a TikToker and former Hells Angel; a woman who ran a local limousine rental service; and a 22-year-old student who was appointed “technical director” after telling local reporters he believed the whale “deserved” to be rescued, then making suggestions about how it might be done.

Several vets offered their services. One flew in from Hawaii to spend several days, heavily jetlagged, giving advice before flying back under a cloud of acrimony. At least two members of the group had a history of support for Germany’s far right, and the press had a ball listing their many eccentricities and connecting them to the political fringes. Köpnick calls them a “dubious troop”.

But the initiative also recruited experts, among them Jeff Foster from the Whale Sanctuary Project in the US and Pedro Baranda, chief marine mammal biologist and strandings coordinator for a Norwegian marine animal rescue organisation named Havdyrhjelpen. “It was a team that was so disorganised,” says Baranda, an avuncular Mexican with 36 years’ experience of rescuing whales and dolphins. “They had no knowledge, no compass, and were following the intructions of a ‘whale whisperer’.” Bambarén admits he is not a qualified marine biologist, but says his practical track record with whales gave him the requisite expertise.

Baranda neverthelss felt a rescue was worth a try. He agreed the whale was weak and disoriented, but was convinced she was healthy enough to survive. “This was a big challenge,” he says, “but it was an opportunity for learning – whatever the outcome.”

Other members of the initiative had their own motivations. Kirsten Tönnies, a vet with a small practice close to Frankfurt, had written a book that vehemently documented government mistreatment of animals – and what she regards as the complicity of the veterinary establishment. She is suspicious of how scientists handle animals – and of the commission’s report: “It was a joke. I got the feeling they didn’t look at the animal directly and just summarised what was already being said. What supposedly deadly illness did they find? It was still alive five weeks after they wrote that report!”

Then, on 15 April, the unexpected happened: a week after the report he commissioned was released, Backhaus changed his mind and announced the private rescue would be allowed to happen after all. It would be “tolerated” rather than “given permission”, so that any legal liability would remain with the initiative. The protesters rejoiced. In one video, a gushing crowd can be seen surrounding the minister on the shores of Poel, hugging the man they had been vilifying as a murderer.

People have different opinions about what caused Backhaus’s change of heart. Köpnick and Stadler think it was just another case of a politician giving in to the temptations of populism under massive media pressure. Baranda thinks Backhaus had a genuine moment of empathy. “As soon as he touched the whale, as soon as he understood it had the opportunity to survive … I have never seen a person change their expression in such a … magical way,” Baranda recalls. “His face lit up.”

For the next few weeks, the initiative rubbed the whale with zinc cream, covered her with wet sheets and experimented with pontoons and inflatables. Bambarén sang to the whale underwater, and says he saw her relax and form a bond of trust with him. Tönnies’ job was to write daily reports for the ministry and the financers. Köpnick watched proceedings with a drone, at the ministry’s request, but kept his distance. Timmy swam free at one point, but got herself stranded again. Another channel was excavated, then, finally, the whale was miraculously coaxed on to a barge – a kind of floating dock that opens at the back and can be filled with water, normally for transporting ships – that had been sunk as low as possible. News reports showed a state of near euphoria among the volunteers. It was 28 April, nearly two months since the whale had first been sighted, and a month since the government had effectively left her for dead. Unfortunately, it soon emerged that the barge was not wide enough for her to turn around in, which would prove a problem later.

Four vessels then set off for the North Sea, each with different captains. Most of the rescue team rode on the Fortuna B, which was towing the barge containing Timmy. Team members took it in turns to get in the water with her and gently rub her skin. “My impression was whenever someone was in with Timmy, the animal liked it, because it wasn’t alone,” Tönnies says.

She noticed Timmy did receive some injuries on the barge, but remains convinced that, while all animal transport is difficult and stressful, she suffered less than an average cow being transported to slaughter – one of the many cruelties she campaigns against. Foster, one of the whale experts drafted into the private initiative, wrote later that he noticed “several lacerations on the anterior portion of the head, likely caused by contact with exposed bolts along the barge walls”, as well as “additional abrasions on the head region and near the blowhole, likely due to contact with the straps holding the sandbags in the front of the barge”.

But the mood on the mission was souring, and the nerves of some of the crews were evidently fraying. A statement later released by lawyers representing the company that operated three of the ships complains of an “unclear command structure”, “contradictory instructions” and interference with their work.

The accounts of the private initiative and the shipping company are contradictory on several points, but on 1 May, with the ships north of Denmark but not yet in the North Sea, it was decided the whale would be released. The barge was towed forward with the back open in the hope that she would be washed out by the pull of the water. When that didn’t happen, the release was postponed until the following morning, when several people saw the whale being pulled out of the barge by ropes or hoses attached to its tail.

Foster was the only expert allowed on the barge for the release, and while he is now refusing to speak to the media, pending a possible legal action, he did leave a disturbing account on the Whale Sanctuary Project website: “The whale was forcibly dragged over sandbags within the barge with the pectoral fins fully extended, appearing to try to maintain stability while also causing visible distress.” Baranda, watching through binoculars from the Fortuna B, saw the crew “lasso” Timmy’s tail and drag her backwards out of the barge. “I’ve never seen something so barbaric in my life,” Bambarén says.

When they came back, Tönnies says, “Jeffrey Foster was standing alone, like a person in shock. He looked yellowish-green; he was trembling, pale.”

Baschek is not keen to talk about the specifics of the release. “The events spoke for themselves, other people should judge. We made our view clear beforehand: that a rescue made no sense and would amount to animal cruelty, because the risks were immense.”

Despite this, many, including Backhaus, insisted the mission was a success. The whale had been released alive – though she did not stay that way for long. According to the environment ministry’s analysis of tracker data, Timmy is thought to have died on 6 or 7 May, four or five days after her release, and a week before her corpse was found on the Danish island of Anholt, having travelled 215km. For whatever reason, it seems Timmy was heading not into the Atlantic but back into the Baltic.

Baranda maintains the whale was healthy when she was released. Both he and Foster said the tracker data shows she dived to a depth of 150 metres more than once, suggesting she was still strong and hunting for food.

The Danish authorities were in no hurry to examine the whale: she was dragged ashore a few days after being sighted on 14 May, and the autopsy carried out on 4 June, there on Anholt beach. By now the cadaver was yellow and bloated with gas from decomposition, and holidaymakers had taken selfies on top of the animal, triggering more outrage on social media. Some of Timmy’s bones were transported to the Natural History Museum in Copenhagen. In early June, a company called Daka Denmark confirmed to German media that it had acquired the rest of the cadaver and turned it into biodiesel and biomass for cement production.

The rescue operation is thought to have cost around €2m, but Walter-Mommert and Gunz have fallen out over the bill, the former accusing the latter of failing to pay all of his share. Walter-Mommert is being sued for €1.35m by a businessman who says he provided staff, equipment and organisational support for the rescue, but has not been paid. She wants him to clarify the circumstances of Timmy’s release first. In a statement made after the whale was set free, she wrote, “We hereby expressly distance ourselves from the events and the manner in which they led to the release of the whale.” The case has yet to make it to a court hearing.

Meanwhile, state prosecutors are sifting through hundreds of charges being pressed by members of the public over events related to Timmy. Some are directed against Backhaus, some at the private initiative, some at Ocean Museum staff. According to a spokesperson for the prosecutor, the charges are all related to Germany’s animal and environment protection laws, and accuse Backhaus of “failure to render assistance”.

The saga remains a media phenomenon. Timmy T-shirts and baseball caps are still on sale, as are Timmy-themed liquors made by a small distillery on Poel. The satirical play Timmy: Hope Dies Last is being performed at a theatre in Hamburg. It has been read as both a send-up of the media circus and a comment on how an anthropomorphised animal became a quasi-religious vessel for the hopes and dreams of an unsettled society.

Tönnies created more conspiracy fodder by briefly claiming DNA tests she commissioned showed the dead whale found on Anholt was not Timmy, though she admits she is not an expert in interpreting genetic tests. She maintains the initiative showed rescuing beached whales could be done – if only someone were willing to invest money into building a special rescue barge.

“Let’s not forget that the main reason we went there was to save a whale,” says Bambarén, who refuses to blame anyone. “This whale brought out the best and the worst of what we human beings are. It came to teach us humans about empathy, about kindness, about love, about forgiveness, and at the beginning we understood it, and unfortunately at the end, we failed.”

Looking back months later, Köpnick surveys the now empty bay of Poel. Turning away, he reflects, “If this had been in GDR times, the fishermen would have just gone out there and cut it to pieces and been done with it.”

‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 11:00:57 GMT

A heatwave in the Bering Sea that killed 10bn snow crabs has led to a new hybrid emerging that has no fishing quotas

Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong.

The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species.

These hybrids carry a strange mix of characteristics: a squashed M-shape in the mouth, a cross between the flat mouth of snow crabs and the distinctive M-shape of tanner crabs, and a mix of red and green eyes, one from each of its parents.

“I was struck by how hybridy they are,” says Erin Fedewa, a biologist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Alaska Fisheries Science Center.

In the region where the ranges of snow crab overlap with tanner crabs, researchers would occasionally find hybrids, though they were a rarity. But in 2025, they recorded more than 13 times more hybrids than the historical average.

After the 2025 anomaly, the scientists waited with interest for this summer’s survey. “A lot of times it takes several years of our survey data to really understand what’s going on,” says Fedewa.

But she adds: “The very first station we sampled, I was seeing all of these large male hybrids. It was sort of like an affirmation for me.”

The 2026 survey showed that the hybrid increase is continuing, and commercially sized hybrid adult males now outnumber snow crabs.

The phenomenon was triggered by an extreme heatwave in 2018 and 2019, when the Bering Sea became nearly ice-free by early spring. The heatwave led to mass starvation and a collapse in the snow crab population, causing the death of about 10 billion crabs.

Early signs of the devastation were apparent in 2019 and became shockingly obvious in 2021 (the 2020 data is missing due to the survey being cancelled during Covid): proof of one of the largest marine mass mortality events ever recorded.

In a study looking at the relationships between the abundance of different crab species and the heatwave, Fedewa and her colleagues found that the absence of snow crabs – which compete for the same resources and might also feed on younger crabs – allowed the hybrids to flourish.

Realising the magnitude of the hybrid surge, Fedewa’s first thought was: “This is going to be such a headache for fisheries management.”

The Alaska Fisheries Science Center has been conducting yearly surveys since the 1980s to assess the populations of commercially important species, such as walleye pollack, Pacific cod, snow and tanner crabs. The survey results are used to build population models that inform fishery managers in setting the quotas. After the snow crab collapse, the fishery was closed between 2022 and 2024, resulting in hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.

In the years after the collapse, snow crabs initially displayed signs of bouncing back. But the most recent survey showed progress had stalled and there was even a decrease in some size categories. Whether this has anything to do with the hybrid boom is not known.

Hybrids now make up more than half of the commercial-sized catch – but they are not officially considered a species and therefore have no set fishing quotas.

“Legally, hybrids do not exist,” says Ben Daly, regional supervisor at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, who oversees the research and management of Bering Sea crabs, among others. “You’re either a snow crab or you’re a tanner crab. A tanner crab has two red eyes and an M-shaped mouth; everything else is a snow crab.”

So the hybrids can be legally sold as snow crabs, but they also use up the quota, which is still being kept to conservative levels after the collapse. Hoping to capitalise on the plentiful hybrids and make up for the losses of the past years, fisheries are pushing for separate quotas for the hybrids.

“That desire has validity to it,” says Daly. “The problem is twofold. Number one, we don’t know a whole lot about the ecology of hybrid crabs. Number two, snow crabs are still in a very depressed state. And so the risk is, if we set a limit based on snow and hybrids, but the fleet goes out and only targets snow crabs, all of a sudden we’re overharvesting snow crabs.”

The North Pacific Fishery Management Council, which is responsible for setting the quota, is keeping the question open for now, with a meeting in January that will bring together scientists, fishery managers and stakeholders to discuss what it might look like to be able to harvest hybrids.

In the meantime, Fedewa and her colleagues have brought some hybrids back to their lab from their last expedition to try to find out more about their ecology. Nobody is even sure if the hybrids are able to reproduce with each other.

Linking a marine heatwave to such an extreme boom in hybrids appears to be unique in scientific literature, but perhaps that just reflects the difficulty of conducting these studies. Hybrids of closely related species might look very similar and therefore go unnoticed.

“I would be surprised if this isn’t actually a common phenomenon,” says Thomas Wernberg, a marine ecologist at the University of Western Australia and the Institute of Marine Research in Norway, who studies the effects of heatwaves on marine ecosystems.

“The impacts of marine heatwaves and extreme events are pervasive. There’s really no point of the biological hierarchy that is free from these impacts,” he adds.

Amid warnings that the world is on the brink of breaching the 1.5C (2.7F) warming limit, marine heatwaves are expected to become more of a norm than an anomaly, and the effects could be far-reaching, on species and human societies.

“I think this is a perfect example of how inflexible fisheries management is in the US,” says Fedewa. “As these events or these novel outcomes become more frequent in the future, our fishery management system needs to adapt to become more flexible.”

‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said.

In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”.

Much has changed in the criminal justice system over the last 50 years, but the prevalence of rape continues to have a pernicious impact. According to Rape Crisis England and Wales one in four women over the age of 16 have been raped, with two in five rapes carried out by a partner, and six in seven perpetrated by someone the women knew. In 2024, 71,227 rapes were recorded by police, but only 2.7% of the cases led to an alleged rapist being charged that year.

The campaigning organisation Women Against Rape this week marks its 50th anniversary. It has fought for decades against a system that has often been weighted against victims, and is depositing its extensive archive at the Bishopsgate Institute to mark this milestone.

According to Ruth Hall, now in her 70s and one of the founders, WAR was set up by a small group of people she described as “ordinary women”.

The group drew up a statement of aims, photocopied on to green sheets of paper, recognising the power imbalance that came from men usually having greater financial means than women. They called for rape within marriage to be recognised as a crime and for women’s sexual histories not to routinely be part of rape trials, along with practical steps to protect women out at night such as better street lighting.

Hall says one of the early chants of the group was: “Yes means yes and no means no, however we dress and wherever we go.”

“Women were furious,” says the longtime WAR campaigner Lisa Longstaff, describing its early days. “Grassroots women got together because we were so absolutely outraged about how rape was treated.”

Campaigning for rape in marriage to be criminalised was not a quick win, but that made the victory particularly important to WAR. Fifty years ago, rape in marriage was legal and being raped by a man you knew, or in a position of authority, was routinely dismissed. Rape in marriage was finally criminalised in 1991 after years of campaigning.

On 16 July 1977 a “summons to a public trial” was organised by campaigners in Trafalgar Square, London. Women filled the square as rape and violence against women were put on mock trial by female activists, who staged the prosecution flanked by the square’s famous lions.

“It was a time when everything was being questioned,” says Hall. “It was very exciting. We organised the Trafalgar Square protest in just a few weeks, having our planning meetings in a disused bank with water pouring down the walls. In those days we only had leaflets and the phone to get the message out to women about the protest.”

The same year, in protest against the three appeal court judges who allowed Holdsworth to walk free, a group of women got into the Athenaeum, the judges’ club in Pall Mall, and dropped a banner from the first-floor balcony.

In 1995, WAR brought the first private prosecution for rape in England and Wales after a man attacked two sex workers. He was convicted on the same evidence the Crown Prosecution Service had dismissed as “insufficient”.

Establishing that refugee women seeking asylum from rape, domestic violence and other torture are entitled to protection has been another key part of the group’s campaigning work.

“We set a precedent in 1997 that due to the impact of trauma, a woman had been ‘unable, not unwilling’ to report rape,” says Longstaff.

“We are still up against institutional misogyny but things are really changing. We have always said men in positions of power and authority should not be above the law, including celebrities. Finally, some of them are being treated as the criminals they are.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

Richard Hammond: ‘I’m much taller than you think. I’m just standing further away’

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 10:00:56 GMT

The TV presenter on his costly divorce, his ‘stupid’ hair, and why his driving licence is on life support

Born in Solihull, West Midlands, Richard Hammond, 56, attended Harrogate College of Art and Technology and began his broadcasting career in local radio. He went on to become a presenter for the Men & Motors TV channel and, from 2002 to 2015, he was part of the BBC’s Top Gear team with Jeremy Clarkson and James May. In 2016, the trio started to host The Grand Tour for Amazon Prime. Since 2021, Hammond has presented the restoration programme, Richard Hammond’s Workshop, which is in its sixth season and available on Quest. He is divorced with two daughters and lives in Monmouthshire, Wales.

When were you happiest? Whenever I’m either walking on a mountain fell, or on a motorcycle.

What is your earliest memory? Sitting on a pedal car that my grandfather made. It was blue and had a white bonnet. I was in my own little world.

Which living person do you most admire, and why? All the nurses who looked after my father at St Michael’s Hospice, the year before last when he was dying. I don’t know how they do it.

What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? I can be a little impulsive!

What is the trait you most deplore in others? Rudeness.

Aside from property, what’s the most expensive thing you’ve bought? You won’t be surprised to hear it’s a car. It was the Porsche 911 Turbo S Cabriolet, which cost an eye-watering and embarrassingly large amount of money. Have I still got it? No – I got divorced last year.

Describe yourself in three words Lucky little Brummie.

What do you most dislike about your appearance? Stupid hair.

What do you owe your parents? My work ethic and sense of fairness.

What does love feel like? Small and yet vast, comforting but exciting; above all, safe.

Which words or phrases do you most overuse? So I gather.

What has been your biggest disappointment? Legal fees!

When did you last cry, and why? Watching my mum perform with her singing group in Ross-on-Wye – it was brilliant. I loved it.

When was the last time you changed your mind about something significant? I took up golf having been rude about it my entire working life. I love a total volte-face.

What is the closest you’ve come to death? How long have you got? There was a brain injury in 2006. And when I went off that Swiss mountain [in 2017] I only needed one thing to happen differently and I would have died. I was in a Rimac car and it flipped end-over-end and burst into flames. I injured my left leg.

What has been your closest brush with the law? Recently, it was fairly well publicised – my licence is pretty much on life support. The number on my dashboard was slightly larger than the number on the big round sign by the side of the road – twice.

What is the most important lesson life has taught you? The harder you work, the luckier you get.

What happens when we die? I think that those last moments stretch to become eternal, so I’m not scared to die.

Tell us a secret I’m much taller than you think. I’m just standing further away.
