‘National scandal’: residents in England rally against surge in mega-warehouse developments

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 10:00:54 GMT

Campaigners call out ‘greed’ of developers after 95% of ‘megashed’ planning applications approved in last 10 years

When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen.

He had just moved into the property in Bingham, Nottinghamshire, with his wife and toddler in June.

Now, he said he was being told: “‘By the way, there’s going to be 21.5-metre-high warehouses right next to you, and there’s going to be eight of them, and you’re going to have 400 HGVs and it’s going to be a 24-hour operation’.”

He added: “I’ll be honest with you, I cried. I was so upset.”

That planning application would add to the more than 8,500 warehouses or large distribution units that have been approved across England in the past decade, fuelled by the growth of online shopping.

Analysis of official figures by the Guardian showed that almost all (95%) of the 9,009 planning applications for “megasheds” were given the go-ahead in the 10 years up to June 2026.

Of the 4,300 approved in the last five years, nearly half (1,922) were in the east, south-east and north-west of England, and 17 were in national parks, despite them having stricter rules on major developments. Six industrial developments were approved in the South Downs national park since 2021, alongside five in the North York Moors and one in the Lake District.

England’s “golden logistics triangle” – historically the Midlands area, which is within a four-hour drive of 90% of industrial developments – has expanded significantly, with the data showing that many planned developments are in newly-held Reform councils or constituencies.

Robert Jenrick, Reform MP for Newark, which Bingham falls under, met with the developer and the local council to discuss residents’ fears about the developments.

Davis closely followed events in Astley, a village in Wigan, where a public inquiry was held over towering mega-warehouses licensed to operate 24/7 being built metres from people’s homes. The powerful fightback of Astley villagers against what they described as “torture” from increased noise, light, and traffic made them figureheads in a nationwide battle against superstructures.

Davis considers them “the canary in the coal mine”.

“They’ve been so inspirational,” he added. “Seeing their videos, I was like, ‘Well, if they can do it, I think we can and I think we should.’”

Astley’s villagers had help from the Community Planning Alliance, an umbrella organisation for around 700 community groups nationwide.

Other local groups have highlighted instances where planning proposals were subtly changed or where councils cited un-evidenced demand for warehouse space. There were also suggestions that the government was not helping, after the National Planning Policy Framework, which was published in August, made it more difficult for the public to challenge planning decisions.

“The planning system is 100% biased against communities,” said Marj Powner, who runs the CPA. “We have so little power, it’s unbelievable.”

She said developers had six months to appeal a planning rejection, whereas communities had “zero, no right of appeal, none whatsoever” if an application was approved, leaving a judicial review as their only option.

“The community have six weeks to find and instruct a legal team and put together the grounds that they may have for their judicial review, and it will cost them around £60,000, which that community has to raise from donations,” she added.

Ten minutes away from Astley, residents near a 70 hectare (173 acre) site in Gibfield began their own campaign against a development that they said would tower over their homes and take away their only green space.

The development was initially backed by the Reform-led Wigan council and is managed by the Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, which is privately run by the billionaire John Whittaker. Although the developer outlined warehouses 12.5m tall, the elevated ground level put the true height closer to 15.5m, relative to their homes, residents said.

“I think there’s just this view that we’re all kind of middle-class nimbies. We’re not. We’re normal working-class people,” said Amanda Coleman, who lives in a house immediately adjacent to the site. “It’s heartbreaking.” The site is one of a number of green belt areas controversially designated as “grey belt”. While intended for previously developed land when it was introduced in 2024, a CPRE report found that 88% of grey belt approvals upon appeal were on land that had never been built on.

Protecting nature was at the heart of many of the battles different groups were embroiled in across the UK.

In Northamptonshire, campaigners spent six years fighting two mega-warehouses on a 60 hectare (150 acre) site that is adjacent to the Upper Nene Valley Gravel Pits, a legally-protected nature reserve for golden plover and lapwing birds.

Sharon Cole, who is part of a local group, Save Titchmarsh and Upper Nene Countryside and Habitats (Staunch), appealed against the planning decision on the grounds it was in breach of international law.

She said vital habitats across the UK were being destroyed through “greed” and that developers were “ looking for all the loopholes that they can find, so they can develop [land]”.

Staunch has also campaigned for the creation of an all-party parliamentary group to scrutinise the planning process.

“When I started, I truly believed that the legal system and the planning system would come good, because we knew our facts were right, and it hasn’t happened,” Cole said.

She added: “The truth’s got to come out, because this is a national scandal across the country, what is happening within the planning system. It’s going to be the ruin of our country if something doesn’t change soon.”

A North Northamptonshire council spokesperson said the council recognised “that there are a range of strongly held views” on the warehouse proposals, but could not comment on potential legal proceedings.

She added: “In determining planning applications, the council is required to assess each proposal on its individual merits and in accordance with the statutory development plan, national planning policy and all other material planning considerations, including environmental impacts and the potential effects on designated nature conservation sites.

“Where proposals have the potential to affect nationally or internationally important habitats, the council is required to consider and comply with the relevant environmental legislation before reaching a decision.”

Wigan council said its cabinet has now formally objected to the Gibfield Park proposals, and that its chief executive has written to the Greater Manchester combined authority, requesting Gibfield be removed from the plan.

A spokesperson for Peel Land said: “Official drawings, based on detailed technical information and accurate survey data have been shared with the community as part of the consultation process. This includes cross-section drawings, which accurately show the proposed scale, height and location of the buildings for this current application.

“We’re aware there has been AI-generated images created from the official consultation documents and subsequently circulated via social media. These images are misleading and do not accurately represent the scale, height or location of the proposed employment buildings. In particular, they show buildings that are significantly taller, wider and much closer to the road and neighbouring homes than proposed. We’re currently reviewing our options with regard to our proposals for Gibfield.”

China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:47:57 GMT

Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

Cop31 live – latest updates

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

after newsletter promotion

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:00:53 GMT

Turn off your phone, get cosy and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. From Don DeLillo’s Underworld to The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton, these epic reads are worth taking your time over

Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” wrote F Scott Fitzgerald in The Great Gatsby, and after the beach reads of summer, now feels like the time to settle down to more ambitious projects. Not slim works like Gatsby, but the bigger beasts you have been circling for some time. A book to wrap yourself up in as autumn becomes winter.

The year I spent reading The Lord of the Rings when I was eight made me want to be a writer. The novel’s scope and the sheer amount of time I lugged it around with me combined, so that whatever I was doing, part of me was always thinking about it. This is what long books, in particular, can do.

Years after I left Middle-earth, the three weeks occupied by my first reading of 2666 (the longest book I’ve read multiple times) became an ongoing logistical challenge: how could I dispense with parenting, my office job and sleep as quickly as possible, so that I could immerse myself again in that torrent of words?

Hopefully some of the choices below will exert a similar pull on you. I’ve set the minimum page count at 600 – long enough that you’ll probably spend at least a week with them, quite possibly several. Books originally or usually published as separate volumes don’t qualify, so no Lord of the Rings, In Search of Lost Time, Septology or The Man Without Qualities. And, in the way of such lists, your own personal favourite is probably, scandalously, absent. But here are 20 novels that will define your life for a chunk of time, and might just change it for ever.

2666 by Roberto Bolaño (2004) Knowing he was dying, Bolaño planned to publish the five-part novel 2666 in separate volumes, which he thought would be more financially rewarding for his family. His executors went against his wishes, the monumental 900-page book becoming a sensation first in Spanish then in Natasha Wimmer’s English translation. The novel brings the fictional Mexican border city of Santa Teresa, and its horrific wave of femicides, to large-scale and unforgettable life: it is a monstrous, irresistible vortex in which cops, serial killers, academics and a mysterious German novelist all find ends of one kind or another.

Middlemarch by George Eliot (1871-2) Voted No 1 in the Guardian’s 100 best novels of all time poll earlier this year, Middlemarch is one of those “everything” books that, to quote Adam Mars-Jones on Ulysses, “swallowed me whole” when I read it. Eliot began a novel about a provincial doctor, abandoned it to write something quick about a character called Dorothea Brooke, and ended up combining the two into an utterly singular and unforgettable work. Perhaps its true brilliance lies in its being both a deeply enjoyable account of the varied fortunes of its large cast of characters, and a profound philosophical exploration of the nature of reality.

Dhalgren by Samuel R Delany (1975) The story of a young man – “Kid” – becoming a poet and having a breakdown in a semi-ruined American city called Bellona, the million-selling Dhalgren is one of the stranger and more opaque science-fiction novels – and definitely the most modernist – to have found a mass audience. A circular text, it moves between plot and plotlessness, variant versions of itself, and repetitious bursts of seemingly pointless sex and violence. One to surrender to rather than conquer, the book’s draw is its extraordinary all-enveloping weirdness.

Villette by Charlotte Brontë (1853) Written after the deaths of her siblings Emily, Anne and Patrick, Villette is the weirdest, bleakest, most puzzling of Charlotte Brontë’s novels, and my favourite by some distance. Lucy Snowe finds not only work as a schoolteacher in Villette (a fictionalised Brussels, where Brontë had taught in her 20s), but also ghosts, mental derangement and unrequited love. It features one of the great ambiguous endings in literature, what Brontë referred to as “a little puzzle”, supplied when her father objected to her original ending in which she summarily dispatched Lucy’s lover in a shipwreck.

Darkmans by Nicola Barker (2007) An epic set in the “geographical plughole” that is Ashford, Kent, Darkmans encompasses the Channel tunnel, drug dealing, salad phobias, samurai swords, the spectre of history, and the much less metaphorical spectre of John Scogin, Edward IV’s court jester. Barker’s antic novel, which was shortlisted for the Booker prize, runs to more than 800 pages of twitchy invention, relentless as – but much funnier than – a burst water main.

It by Stephen King (1986) By my count, King has written 17 novels that would qualify for this list, three of them longer than 1,000 pages. It isn’t just one of his longest novels, but arguably his best. Terrifying from the off, when Georgie Denbrough chases after his paper boat in an autumn storm and encounters Pennywise the clown, it also memorably evokes childhood friendship and, in the town of Derry, plunges into the dark side of American history: crime, racial and sexual bigotry, economic downturn and industrial pollution.

The Magic Mountain by Thomas Mann (1924) Mann began this novel in 1913, intending a comic counterpart to his tragic novella Death in Venice. He completed it more than a decade later, by which time his political outlook had entirely changed, the first world war had reshaped Europe, and the book had become a philosophical meditation on time, European civilisation and the conflict between liberal humanism and rightwing reaction. Set in a tuberculosis sanatorium, it’s also one of the great books about the terror and seduction of illness.

A Brief History of Seven Killings by Marlon James (2014) “The problem with a book,” notes one of the 75 characters in A Brief History of Seven Killings, “is that you never know what it’s planning to do to you until you’re too far into it.” What James’s Booker-prize-winning novel is planning to do is completely take over your life until you’re done with it, or it’s done with you. The attempted assassination of Bob Marley is the focal point, but the book’s braided streams of consciousness carry us from Kingston’s ghettoes to CIA plots to America’s crack epidemic.

Lies and Sorcery by Elsa Morante (1948) When Natalia Ginzburg, then an editor at the Italian publishing house Einaudi, received the manuscript of this debut novel, she read it in a day. For decades available in English only in a bowdlerised edition, 200 pages shy of its original length, the book was restored in a new translation by Jenny McPhee in 2023. This was thanks largely to repeated praise from Elena Ferrante, who said that this portrait of the artist as a young woman showed her “what literature can be”.

Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell by Susanna Clarke (2004) The world of Clarke’s richly imagined debut is a familiar one: the Regency England we encounter in Jane Austen novels. But in this version of it, magic, which is real but long fallen into disuse, is making a comeback. The conflict between the two magicians of the title – one conservative, the other willing to engage with powerful and treacherous forces – is involving, but the real pleasure of this book lies in the texture of its world; some of the most enchanting and playful moments lie in its footnotes.

The Luminaries by Eleanor Catton (2013) Aged 28, Catton became the youngest writer ever to win the Booker prize, and The Luminaries – all 832 pages of it – the longest book to be so honoured. A tale of theft, murder, ghosts and desire in a New Zealand goldrush town, the book is an ever-shifting puzzle, an ingenious astrological mechanism that constantly repositions its characters and events in relation to one another. As Robert Macfarlane, chair of the Booker judges, said: it’s “as intricately structured as an orrery”.

Underworld by Don DeLillo (1997) In the decade from 1982, DeLillo went on an incredible run: The Names, White Noise, Libra, Mao II. Six years of near-silence followed, broken by this 800-page epic about lives lived in the shadow of nuclear annihilation during the second half of the 20th century. Incredibly, by utilising the same elements that had made his work so distinctive – a fragmented narrative, the depiction of daily life saturated by mass media, and an atmosphere of what he refers to in an earlier novel as “accumulating dread” – he produced a sweeping, social epic of the kind few thought he had either the particular skills or the desire to write.

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai (2025) It gives you an idea of the scale of Desai’s novel that the lovers at its heart should meet only on page 233, just over a third of the way through the book. The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny took 20 years to write, and at one point, Desai claims, ran to 5,000 pages. Which makes the published version (688), which bounces between 1990s India and the American diaspora, and between social and magical realism, an exercise in restraint.

The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky (1879-80)Vast in scope and ambition, Dostoevsky’s final novel (he died three months after its publication) unfolds over just a few days. Dmitri, Ivan and Alyosha’s occupations divide along dutiful, professional and religious lines (soldier, journalist, monk), but all of them – plus their bastard half-brother, the servant Smerdyakov – are scarred by the monstrousness of their conniving father. It’s grim, funny, savage, and possesses irresistible momentum. Other than Shakespeare, said Virginia Woolf, “there is no more exciting reading”.

A Table for Fortune by William T Vollmann (2026) Hearing about Vollmann’s new novel, which is 3,096 pages long and costs £150, was actually the inspiration for this piece. The first two sections span the cold war, 9/11 and the “war on terror” from the point of view of a CIA analyst. The second half follows his homeless, mentally unwell son across the US. Vollmann’s longtime publisher quailed at the length of the manuscript and returned it with edits. The next time they saw it, it was 400 pages longer. He now has a new publisher. Is it worth it? I’ll tell you in about a year.

Lonesome Dove by Larry McMurtry (1985) For mysterious reasons, numerous people have recommended this 1985 novel to me in recent years. Mysterious, that is, until I began this utterly addictive story of two friends, retired Texas Rangers, attempting the first cattle drive from the Rio Grande all the way to Montana. The journey encompasses locusts, bandits, torrential rain, kidnappings and stampedes. Punctuating these episodic adventures are haunting images of American crimes: the starving remnants of Native American tribes, pyramids of buffalo bones, and the environmental destruction wrought by the cattle industry.

A Glastonbury Romance by John Cowper Powys (1932)In very simplified terms, Powys’s chaotically structured but singular 1,200-page novel is about a conflict between two residents of the Somerset town of Glastonbury. The industrialist Philip Crow wants to exploit the land and electrify the county (even the caves of Wookey Hole), while ex-Methodist minister John Geard’s ambition is to restore Glastonbury’s status as a pilgrimage site. Powys inhabits not just the consciousnesses of his living characters but also corpses and at one point a tree. Margaret Drabble compared his achievement to Tolkein’s. Although his country is “less visited”, she wrote, “it is as compelling, and it has more air”.

Ducks, Newburyport by Lucy Ellmann (2019) It didn’t win the Booker, but at 1,030 pages it remains the longest novel ever shortlisted for the prize. The book consists of a single sentence unfurling from the mind of an Ohio homemaker, interrupted occasionally by an account of a mountain lioness raising her cubs. The book’s momentum is maintained by repeated use of the phrase “the fact that”, hurtling from the domestic (washing dishes) to the political (Syria, Trump) to the relatable (“the fact that I have not read all the books I want to read, not even half”).

War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy (1869) For a long time War and Peace represented to me the stereotypical challenging long novel: to be endured more than enjoyed. When I finally read it I was surprised not only by how incredibly fun it is, but also by its many, many short chapters: 365 of them, which makes it easy to read in snatches. Yes, those snatches will go on for months, but you’ll live for them. Another surprising observation, for which Yiyun Li gets the credit: the drawing room encounters are like military campaigns and battles, while the parts about war are full of pettiness and scheming.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling by Marguerite Young (1965) There is undoubtedly an intellectually macho aspect to reading long novels with forbidding reputations. Working eight-hour days, American novelist Marguerite Young took 18 years to write Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, and on its publication in 1965 one reviewer complained that “her principle of composition is never to use one word if fifteen thousand will do instead”. I’m not going to say this one is easy, but with sustained attention Young’s visionary prose exerts a powerfully hypnotic effect. Even so it will probably remain, as the New York Times noted in her obituary, “one of the most widely unread books ever acclaimed”. How’s that for a challenge?

The Rouse by China Miéville (2026) The winner of this year’s Goldsmiths prize, Miéville’s 1,200-page novel was two decades in the making. Over that time, he has said, “it became the defining work of my life”. It braids an evocatively described English childhood of the 1970s and 80s with the story of an occult cold war military programme to weaponise the dead, the testing ground for which lies in Britain’s dwindling colonial territories. The Rouse is a weird, glitchy, gloomy and frightening book, purposefully baffling at times, but thrilling, too.

Telegraph departures signal concerns over direction under Axel Springer’s ownership

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 08:00:53 GMT

Insiders say they only see cuts, with no discernible long-term strategy, since title’s purchase by German media firm

A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times.

Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week.

Speculation swirled about the future of both its editor, Chris Evans, and his loyal deputy, Rob Winnett. It was accompanied by days of long, hushed meetings between senior figures at the title, now under the ownership of the German media company Axel Springer.

The intrigue was heightened by Evans’s apparent early return from a trip to the US. Suggestions did the rounds that both editor and deputy could be leaving – a rumour dampened by Evans’s continued presence in the newsroom.

In the event, it emerged that only Winnett was departing. Winnett, who led the Telegraph’s coverage of the MPs’ expenses scandal, is heading to the title’s bitter rightwing rival, the Daily Mail. He has been installed as its chief content editor, instantly elevating him as a likely successor to the Mail’s editor, Ted Verity.

However, at the Telegraph, Winnett’s departure is being seen in the light of widespread concerns about the title’s direction under its new owners.

Axel Springer and its all-powerful chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, swept in to buy the titles for an eye-watering £575m earlier this year, with promises of investment and expansion. However, five months into Axel Springer’s tenure, insiders say they are only seeing cuts – and no discernible long-term strategy.

“I don’t think they have a particular plan – they clearly want money saved,” said one staffer. “They’ve clearly given Evans a target of savings to make. In terms of a plan, it’s all very vague.”

Winnett’s departure, one insider said, was “a huge loss”. Winnett had been part of a team who headed to Florida to scope a base for an expanded US operation. So far, solid plans have not emerged.

It follows a recent town hall meeting between journalists and the Telegraph’s new chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol, at which reporters asked a series of questions that they felt went unanswered, and cuts in which large numbers of employees were told they were being made redundant, including senior figures in the newsroom.

Hulshoff Pol said the strategy was to reinvent the reader experience, build new revenue streams and grow internationally.

Reporters asked for more details about the wider plans behind the cuts and what the company meant in its repeated insistence that the Telegraph would become a “global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”. Staff remain unclear what the use of AI will entail.

There is also confusion about who is making the cuts. Evans is credited with keeping the Telegraph operation going during three years in which it was without an owner and unable to take major, strategic decisions. He now also appears to have been tasked with making cuts for Axel Springer. Some believe Evans is being used by the company to carry out “the bulk of the current bloodletting”.

A source said the company was having to take “difficult proposals that we believe are necessary for the future of the business”.

Some staff had initially detected a change in the Telegraph’s politics in the months after Axel Springer’s purchase. They presumed the loosening of ties with Reform’s Nigel Farage and the departures of some of its most rightwing writers, such as Allison Pearson and Sherelle Jacobs, were part of a shift towards a global centre-right audience.

However, many now believe the changes so far have been more about costs than politics.

after newsletter promotion

Elsewhere, there has been no such turn to the centre. The Telegraph’s new US podcast, The Right Track with Poppy Coburn, most recently featured the rightwing media host Steve Bannon, an ally of Donald Trump.

It has left Telegraph staff scratching their heads about the takeover. Many had expected Axel Springer to arrive with money to spend. Insiders said executives seemed to be focused on boosting advertising.

The cuts are being made despite the Telegraph making underlying profits. “This is a business that generates healthy margins, healthy profits,” said Alex DeGroote, a media analyst. “So at face value, the restructuring – all these redundancies – is not because of financial pressures.

“Even allowing for the fact that the advertising market this year has probably been a bit soft, both print and digital, the scale of the restructuring would suggest that this is quite a deep strategic rethink. Basically, I’m afraid it points to AI.”

It has all focused attention on the intentions of Döpfner, a billionaire who has made numerous attempts to buy media assets in an attempt to establish himself as a modern media mogul. He made an unsuccessful bid for the Financial Times in 2015 and subsequently bought Business Insider and Politico, and has expressed interest in the Wall Street Journal. It had been assumed he would use the Telegraph as a vehicle to compete against right-leaning media in the US.

There have recently been reports that Döpfner has been interested in acquiring a stake in TikTok’s European operations. He is said to have discussed the idea with the US ambassador to France, Charles Kushner – the father of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner – in January.

It has made Telegraph staff wonder where they stand in his plans.

“It’s all very well getting rid of the people that come in with stories and write them and produce them and present them to you on a plate, but what are you then going to do?” said one journalist at the town hall meeting. “You don’t get a room full of journalists together and not have answers.”

Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 08:00:52 GMT

Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup

If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu. You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto, the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal?

Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run.

In terms of the sheer number of people excited about it, it’s a cultural moment that might rank alongside something like a football World Cup. And so it has spawned something being called the GTA flu: millions of people around the world pulled sickies in order to devote the day of release to cracking incalculable numbers of beers and playing until their eyes go funny. This isn’t the first time GTA flu has swept the world: it happened back in 2013 for GTA V’s release, too. There is, alas, still no cure.

I asked around, and plenty of my friends and acquaintances admitted to being among the GTA bunkers, although most had booked the day off rather than feigning a cough to get their gaming hours in. One friend reported that every single man on her team had requested leave on Thursday, and I heard about another person who went a step further and timed quitting his job in order for his unemployment to coincide with this momentous week. On Thursday, I went to visit a friend, a man who had booked annual leave weeks in advance for the release of GTA VI, to see what the fuss was about.

When I arrived, he was at a quayside bar called the Rusty Anchor, losing a game of pool to a man in wraparound shades. We spent an hour or so driving around so he could give me a sense of the world he was just starting to discover – gorgeously rendered sunsets over the sea, rundown liquor stores and truck stops fringed with Florida-esque plantlife creeping through the concrete. The map for this game is huge – twice as big as it was in the last instalment and nearly as big as the real city of Miami – and getting to know all its corners will involve many, many hours of adventuring for its players.

Something else caught my eye in the news reports about GTA mania, though. I came across a post on a website describing an event being planned by players of GTA V, the 2013 instalment. Gamers would gather inside the online, collaborative version of the game and take a final, ceremonial drive through the game’s city, Los Santos. No reckless driving, no running down pedestrians, just a stately procession to say farewell to the world they had loved, before embarking on GTA VI. They were calling this “the last ride”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

I was never a GTA person. Not for any moral handwringing reasons (and look, yes, this is a game where you can and do kill people), but just because I was always more drawn to colourful platform games in my youth, or glorious time-sinks such as The Sims. But I am very much an open-world video game person. The rolling grasslands of Red Dead Redemption 2, the twinkling forests of The Legend of Zelda games, the bamboo groves of Ghost of Tsushima: all of these are places I have spent a lot of my life. Several times in any given week I think longingly about Zelda’s Kingdom of Hyrule in particular, knowing that I can just boot up the game and go there, but now that I’ve finished the main story, and practically all of the side adventures, it feels like a place I can’t quite go back to.

I miss it there. Anywhere you spend a lot of time accrues meaning, and modern video games create vast, richly detailed places to become attached to. That last ride through Los Santos makes sense to me. What my friend who I played some GTA with on Thursday was excited about mostly wasn’t firing a gun, or driving a really sick whip. It was getting to know the world.

It might seem sort of silly for people to get excited enough about a video game to risk pissing off their employers by pretending to be sick. I wouldn’t say that I approve, necessarily, of people bunking off school and work. Certainly not in a national newspaper. But I do understand. For millions of players, this week is their first introduction to a world where they will spend hours upon hours, exploring, marvelling, discovering. And, yes, sometimes shooting drug dealers.

Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist

You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 07:00:53 GMT

For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

You Can See Everything acts as if this isn’t the case. It operates in a realm of smart and artful naivety. In order to interrogate whether or not Elizabeth Holmes, founder of magical medical tech company Theranos, is – as she claims – the tragic victim of a miscarriage of justice, Nathan Fielder moves into the annexe of her home for a few weeks before she starts her 11-year prison term for fraud.

“You can see everything,” she promises him brightly, juggling babies and her godawful boyfriend. Fab access! A gift to the documentarian! So Fielder duly blinkers up and blinds himself to anything concrete. He does not discuss the court case. He does not examine the reams of actual evidence that resulted in her conviction. Beyond a long chat about the semantics of the word “can”, he does not ask Holmes what the hell she was playing at.

Instead, his technique is an extended vibes check. He looks into Holmes’s eyes, noses nearly rubbing. He asks her if she was lying. He does this a couple more times, just in case.

This is undoubtedly compelling (for a while, at least). The fine line between profundity and banality means a lot of the movie, with its pore-boring closeups, is pretty gripping.

But it’s also perverse and dangerous. You Can See Everything rejects the idea of a generally agreed consensus over what has happened – even as an aim, and even at a time when that concept is under considerable threat.

In its clever, meta way, Fielder’s film therefore presents the most pernicious attack on objective truth I’ve seen – precisely because it’s so liberal and slippery.

It is a massive slap in the face for the judicial system. As well as for Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung, the primary Theranos whistleblowers, and all the journalists who meticulously investigated the case over many years, including John Carreyrou and Amy Chozick, whose New York Times reporting is not covered by the film, except to dispute one barely-relevant element of it.

It is also an insult to the victims of the Theranos scandal. Not just the millionaires who lost money but the many, many people who suffered because they were fed false medical results by Holmes’s dodgy box.

That background means the film’s soapiness can stick in the throat. The more we’re encouraged to wonder whether Fielder might fancy Holmes a bit, and maybe it might actually be mutual, the more the real-world consequences of her actions seem to hover unhelpfully over footage of them flirting.

A fascinating and bleak fraud case is digested into a thin vehicle for dopey ponderings. Things like: are you for real? Am I for real? Can you ever really tell if anyone’s for real?

And that, I think, is one of the reasons the film has been so successful. Just like the rest of us, Fielder is uninterested in facts – he’s all about the feels. We all seem to believe that the really essential truth now is an emotional one.

You Can See Everything taps the zeitgeist like few movies before it. For me, that’s what makes it so frightening.

I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 07:00:51 GMT

The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

One in eight young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are classed as not in education, employment or training (Neet). Until I finally secured an office job this September I was one of them, going down to the jobcentre every week hoping there’d finally be a good work opportunity.

Here is what life was like: for a long year after graduating in 2025, things that I had taken for granted while working student jobs at university – routine, colleagues, a purpose in life – felt far away. Yet there remained hope. Hope that one employer would say yes, and you could finally stop spending weekdays at your local library, with its view of a graveyard.

Perhaps some people can rationalise long-term unemployment after university as an opportunity to take a sabbatical from life or become a lady of leisure. But try being a lady of universal credit (UC). The glamour of doing nothing all day – with no money – isn’t so glamorous after all. You have all the free time in the world, but you can barely afford to do anything – the £338 a month is just enough to cover the occasional coffee as a treat.

Or maybe you won’t get any UCpayment at all. I was sanctioned by the job centre for three months for not applying for a restaurant vacancy that I hadn’t been told was mandatory. That was despite having applied to hundreds of jobs – from a surf camp in Spain to a year-round Christmas shop in Edinburgh. Throughout this time, with no money, I was still expected to attend weekly meetings at the job centre in my home town.

UC is a far cry from life at university. While I was on it, the Department for Work and Pensions asked for all my bank statements. Every supermarket basket, train ticket, coffee shop trip all under their watchful eye. It made me feel guilty for every purchase I made. I was interrogated during a particularly brutal phone call about my transactions; even an innocent payment from my grandfather was treated as suspicious.

Now, you may think that finally finding a job has brought about a sense of relief. Yet getting the job is just the first hurdle. Like many young jobseekers, I was offered a fixed-term contract. Sure, I have a job for 12 months, but what next? A friend of mine was unemployed for six months after his fixed-term contract ended. Eleven other people were hired by my employer at the same time as me – what will we all do once this period ends? You feel, in a sense, trapped, bouncing between benefits and fixed-term contracts.

Having looked at the Milburn review, there are many aspects that I think look very promising. For a start, the aim of doubling apprenticeships over the next decade is laudably ambitious. For too long a degree has been privileged as the best route towards prosperity, and it is encouraging to see an embrace of alternative pathways. Incentives for employers to hire young people, including cuts to national insurance and a previously announced Youth Jobs Grant of £3,000 for hiring those who have been Neet for six months, could make all the difference too. I was also pleased to see that employers will be encouraged to hire those who are disabled or have been in care through an additional £2,000 payment.

As someone who knows how it feels to be on UC all too well, I think the introduction of a new “youth allowance” could be a good opportunity to reform how young people are treated by the welfare system. But if it is just as dehumanising as UC – with its sanctions and intrusiveness – what difference is this making for young people? Is it the same thing with a different name?

One of my biggest concerns with the report is that its help is focused on those under the age of 25. That is, of course, the working definition of a Neet. But it suggests that there is no plan for those who age out of Neet-hoodand are still facing the same issues in the job market. The graduate employment crisis is not new, and there are many people who have been Neet and are now approaching 30. They still need all the help they can get, otherwise they will truly become a lost generation.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Jobs and opportunity guarantees will only reassure young people once we see what kind of work is being offered, and that these steps are genuine ones towards long-term security. Will the placements mostly be work experience, with only limited opportunities for full contracts? If we’re offered fixed-term contracts, like I was, what is the plan to ensure we aren’t eventually cut loose by employers and then back to square one?

The Milburn review does give me hope. We’ll just have to wait and see if the government learns the right lessons from it, meets the moment and finally does right by the younger generation.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:53 GMT

The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control

Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease. That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying.

There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths. The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died.

The crisis in DR Congo is following a familiar pattern, beginning with the delay in recognising the appearance of the disease, partly because it is in an area scarred by conflict, which in turn accelerates its spread and heightens suspicion, even violence, towards those trying to intervene.

In west Africa 13 years ago, nobody knew how to handle a disease they had never seen before. Touching the body of a victim, even after death, risks infection, so burial without proper protection endangers all those present. But the arrival of anonymous burial teams, swathed in protective gear that made them look like space aliens or evil spirits, and taking away the dead to be buried no one knew where – often in unmarked graves in the early stages – was equally disastrous.

Instead of seeking treatment for victims, families kept them at home and buried them secretly when they died, making it impossible to contain the spread of the disease. It was clear that age-old burial customs had to change, but people weren’t listening to directives from remote officialdom. It took members of their own communities, whom they knew and trusted, to change minds.

Those people were local faith leaders – priests, imams and traditional healers. As the then country director in Sierra Leone and Liberia for Cafod, the Catholic charity, I observed priests finding verses in the Bible and imams doing the same in the Qur’an to persuade people to change their habits in the face of this devastating disease. They succeeded where others had failed to gain a hearing, and played a crucial role in getting the outbreak under control.

Living in Sierra Leone at the time with my wife and two daughters, we all suffered the wider effects of Ebola. Part of my work was to go into the field to manage burial teams, train volunteers, and provide equipment for protection and decontamination. I feared for my own life. When I got home, I would have to tell the girls not to come near me until I had bathed and changed all my clothing. At one point I feared I had caught the disease. It was four days of terror, during which I had to tell my family to keep away from me.

I know what those tackling the outbreak in eastern DR Congo are facing. There have been attacks on clinics and burial teams, and those suffering this violence often find that they are feared and shunned by their own relatives and neighbours.

But the main reason for the virulence of this surge in Ebola is the drastic cut in aid between the last decade and this one.

Not only is the response to the outbreak falling behind, the funding gap is widening. Medical institutions and charities are racing to build, staff and equip treatment and isolation centres, but the UN warns that it could take up to 12 months to bring this latest surge in Ebola to an end – if the money is there.

The lesson of west Africa, however, is that faith-based organisations have a role to play. Tackling Ebola is not just a medical problem.

Kayode Akintola is Africa head for Cafod, based in Lagos

Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:51 GMT

After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’

The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter.

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity.

But this time, the man was not, in fact, planning to rape her. WT Stead was a crusading tabloid newspaper editor with an eye for titillation, intent on proving his contention that young girls were being widely sold by their parents for sexual exploitation on the streets of London.

The lurid, four-part exposé published in the Pall Mall Gazette – titled with characteristic Victorian bombast, the “Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon” – caused an absolute sensation. Mobs rioted outside the newspaper’s offices trying to get hold of copies. A reported 250,000 people marched on Hyde Park demanding the age of consent, then set at 13 for girls, be raised to 16. By the end of 1885, parliament had been strong-armed into passing legislation – colloquially known as Stead’s act – setting an age boundary which, for heterosexual sex, has remained in place in most of the UK since.

More than 140 years later, pioneering journalism and sexual scandal have put the age of consent back on the agenda. The conviction and jailing of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault, and the allegations of sexual misconduct and grooming against David Walliams, which he has denied, have drawn attention not only to abuse of power in the media, but to relationships in which very young people are having sex with much older adults.

The accusations against both entertainers – which came to light after lengthy newspaper and TV investigations, including by the Guardian – included revelations that Brand and Walliams had sexual relationships while in their 30s with girls of 16. It led to calls from campaigners and survivors to introduce a “staggered” age of consent, by which sex with 16- and 17-year-olds becomes illegal for adults more than four years older than them.

“I think we all agree that adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18,” said Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30.

Layla Stone, a child protection social worker who leads the Close the Consent Gap campaign group, said those aged 16 and 18 were seen as children in “every single framework of the law”. “We don’t believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults,” she said.

Latter’s argument has forced a reckoning with a question that is, depending on how you look at it, a matter of legal and moral certainty, or of endless cultural variety: is there a right answer to the question of when children come of age?

Many 16- and 17-year-olds might bristle at being described as children, after all – and in some respects, that is understandable. They can join the armed forces in the UK, and in Scotland and Northern Ireland can marry with parental permission; in almost all US states they can drive a car; in Malta and Austria, they can vote in local and national elections; and they can get a tattoo without parental consent in the Netherlands. But in the US, neither they, nor anyone else under 21, can buy a can of beer.

The law on sexual consent is as good an example as any of this quandary, according to Laura Lammasniemi, an assistant professor of law at the University of Warwick, whose work has focused on the history of consent boundaries. “Often we think of age of consent as being related to physical maturity, but there’s clearly a very strong religious and political aspect to it as well,” she said.

In England and Wales, for instance, the 1885 law on consent at 16 applied only to unmarried girls; female children could marry at 12 until 1929, and inside marriage, their sexual acquiescence was taken for granted. That disparity, like other inconsistencies, was largely moralistic, said Lammasniemi. “If the sexual behaviour was somehow considered to be potentially harmful, you needed a higher age to consent to it than you did for something like marriage, which was considered to be generally a social good.”

A similar moralism meant the legal age of sex between gay men, even after it was partly decriminalised for those over 21 in 1967, wasn’t equalised until 2000 (lesbian sex, at whatever age, didn’t appear in English law until 2003). Northern Ireland, which had a more religious and conservative culture, raised the bar from 16 to 17 in 1950 until it was equalised with the rest of the UK in 2008.

Such disparities are replicated internationally, where the boundaries on sexual consent have varied to a surprising degree. Though additional clauses covering close-in-age relationships or authority figures often complicate the headline numbers, in Italy, Germany, Brazil and much of Central America, sex is permissible at 14. In France and Sweden it is 15, while in Ireland, Cyprus, South Australia and Texas, it is 17. Fourteen US states, including California and Florida, set the minimum age of consent at 18. Argentina permits sex in some circumstances from 13.

But if sex is very often “the first form of adulthood that you get to try out”, according to Rachel Thomson, a professor of childhood and youth studies at the University of Sussex, neither the age at which it becomes legal nor the age at which teenagers start actually doing it are very helpful in defining the transition to adulthood. She highlighted data showing that, while the age of first intercourse plummeted over the late 20th century, the gap until they had their first live-in relationship or first child – both traditional markers of becoming “grownups” – has dramatically widened since.

While young people have often been blamed for indulging in an extended adolescence, in which they have lived at home longer, settled into stable careers later and delayed forming their own committed relationships and families, such decisions are often beyond their individual control.

“There has been a real transformation of the scaffolding outside of the family that makes it possible to become autonomous and independent in the world,” said Thomson. The adult transition experienced by many in older generations – “the idea of leaving school at 16, being able to walk straight into a job, being able to set up home, to start a family in your 20s” – was largely obsolete, she noted. Some young people, particularly from disadvantaged backgrounds, may have found themselves catapulted into early adulthood. But life for many others has involved “yo-yo transitions, going backwards and forwards from home to independence, home to independence”.

“Adulting”, Thomson pointed out, has become a verb to younger generations: something tried out in the short term but difficult to complete. “Culturally and historically, [we are in] a new situation where young people are often swimming round around in circles rather than swimming forwards,” she said.

The extended process of growing up has at least tallied with the neuroscience of late adolescence, which has shown that the brain undergoes continuous development into the late 20s, leading some experts to argue that adolescence should be redefined to span the ages 10-24.

“There is no single age at which the human brain can be universally classified as ‘adult’, as neurodevelopment is a continuous process without sharp transition points, marked by substantial individual variation,” Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a professor of psychology and cognitive neuroscience at the University of Cambridge, wrote in a recent paper on the developing adolescent brain.

The minimum age of criminal responsibility ranges from seven in some African and South Asian countries, to 18 in Brazil and Peru. England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and most Australian states, set that threshold at 10, and for federal crimes in the US it is 11.

In most of the world, 18 marks the most significant goalpost, after which children are treated as adults for most legal purposes and, usually, can vote. But even this milestone could be more arbitrary than it appears.

The age of universal suffrage, for instance, was not set at 18 anywhere until 1969, when the UK became the first democracy in the world to reduce the voting age from 21, a move rapidly copied by other nations. The decision by Harold Wilson’s Labour government, some academics have argued, was motivated not by a sense of 18 as the definitive age of adult responsibility, but by electoral concerns over their failure to attract younger members.

“This idea that we have this magic boundary at 18, that has never really existed,” said Christine Huebner, a lecturer in quantative social sciences at the University of Sheffield, whose work has focused on the transition from childhood to full citizenship and the impact of lowering the voting age to 16.

“And if you think about it, the rights that young people acquire are really staggered at different ages – and probably for good reason. You might argue, for instance, that making a life-changing decision about who to marry or whether or not to get a mortgage is more important than the decision of which party to vote for in a certain election,” she said.

For one recent piece of work, Huebner followed a group of young adults between the ages of 15 and 21 and asked them periodically how adult they felt at different stages, and why. “There were funny little things they mentioned. Donating blood [permissible in the UK at 17] was a big thing that made them really feel, ‘I’m contributing to society’. Or starting their first job. Driving, graduating from university.

“There are multiple little signifiers of what it means to contribute to society and they come up at different times and different circumstances.”

Carey Oppenheim, an expert in social policy relating to childhood and inequality, agreed that the pathways to becoming an adult have become “more complex, longer and more precarious – and they remain very unequal”. It left public policy and services increasingly out of step with how society has changed for young people, she said.

Oppenheim recently led a research project for the Nuffield Foundation designed to ask young people what it means to be a grownup in the context of a rapidly changing society. While the traditional markers of adulthood – getting a job, leaving home, settling into a relationship – are delayed for most, the support available to young people, such as specialist mental health services, suddenly stop at a certain, arbitrary point.

“The cliff edge at the age of 18, or wherever that cliff edge is, is not a very good way to organise support for young people as they navigate their transitions into adulthood,” said Oppenheim. As a result, her report recommended that early adulthood should be recognised as a distinct and extended phase of life, rather than something that does not exist one day and is suddenly attained the next.

“In terms of [the debate about] young people’s lives and how they achieve some of the markers of what adulthood is about, this feels like a really important time,” she said.

Why is Shabana Mahmood tackling ‘two-tier policing’ if she doesn’t believe it exists?

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:49 GMT

Is it the home secretary’s job to act tough addressing a rightwing myth or to face it down? She seems to have chosen the path of least resistance

Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr.

But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic.

There have been extremely good reasons for the decision many forces across Britain made to let uniformed police officers march openly at Pride events in recent years, rather than simply stewarding. It seemed a quick, tangible way of signalling that times have changed, that hate crimes will be taken seriously and that gay officers are welcome to serve or join. But in a case brought against Northumbria police last year by a lesbian arguing that gender critical activists had been made to feel unwelcome at Pride, a judge ruled that Pride had become so politically contested that marching breached impartiality rules, warning other forces to take note. This week, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, made clear that she supported that ban. Some forces had drifted “out of the realm of policing and into the world of politics” in trying to engage the public, she told police commissioners, suggesting in future they stick to “tea and biscuits” with residents’ associations rather than hanging out with activists.

That sideswipe came as Mahmood made a speech announcing plans to tackle so-called two-tier policing – the false and inflammatory idea that the police routinely and deliberately go soft on ethnic minority offenders. These plans have been undeniably complicated by the fact that, as Mahmood herself acknowledged, there’s no evidence that the problem actually exists outside Nigel Farage’s imagination. Her solution was to scrap a police statement on anti-racism principles that Reform UK made hay with in the wake of the tragic murder of Henry Nowak, the teenager unforgivably handcuffed by police as he was dying of stab wounds because they mistook him for the assailant rather than the victim.

The statement argues that equality “does not mean treating everyone the same”, an established principle in anti-discrimination law (forcing a pregnant woman to lift the same heavy boxes as everyone else working in your warehouse is technically equal treatment, but that doesn’t make it fair). Though there’s no evidence that it directly affected the officers’ decisions the night of Nowak’s murder, and Mahmood acknowledged she could see what it was trying to achieve, she insisted that the public find it “patently absurd”, and she wasn’t about to argue with them. So there will be a new impartiality code, including rules on avoiding politicised symbols – another Reform gripe is LGBTQ+-friendly rainbow markings on police cars – and on engaging with the public, which is where Pride marches come in.

Police should, she argued, beware “misguided attempts at course corrections” made while scrabbling to keep up with culture wars. Though if the police seem confused, they’ve arguably only been reflecting successive governments, who have done their share of handbrake turns over LGBTQ+ rights.

What Mahmood was trying to do this week was one of the hardest tasks in politics, which is to side with the public on an issue where the public is hopelessly divided. Plenty of Britons now believe two-tier policing exists, according toYouGov research this summer; unfortunately, they disagree on who is in which tier. Over half think black people are singled out for differential treatment, but they’re more likely to say this treatment is extra strict than extra lenient. A third think the police come down harder on people with far-right views, but one in five think they’re harder on people with far-left views. And though 25% think white people get a uniquely raw deal, exactly the same number think they have it easier, with a marked tendency for people to think their own group is especially hard done by. (Though YouGov didn’t poll LGBTQ+ people specifically, Stonewall research suggests one in four of those who had experienced a hate crime and not reported it said it was because they didn’t trust the police.) It’s hard to draw any firm conclusions except that distrust of the police is remarkably widespread; but evidently that’s not the story either Reform or Labour wants to tell.

If Mahmood looks increasingly out of step with a cabinet that has shifted at least rhetorically to the left under Andy Burnham, that’s in part just the nature of being a Labour home secretary. Since Labour never gets the benefit of the doubt over law and order, its home secretaries end up forced into taking the hardest possible line on law and order so that nobody can say they’re soft on it. But there is another difference between Mahmood and her new boss emerging, and it’s about the willingness to make an argument.

If the public fervently believe something that you think is nonsense, is your job to agree with them or to bust the myth? On Brexit, Burnham chose the latter, pointing out politely but firmly that it hasn’t worked out. But Mahmood seems to be choosing the former, cracking down on a “perception” of injustice she freely admits is a chimera. The trouble with boxing shadows is that sooner or later, the wrong person risks getting punched in the face.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 05:00:48 GMT

As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas

When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France, Poland, Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism.

Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states. Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east, Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south.

Of the EU’s 27 countries, 21 are run from the centre or right. But there is a new danger, and it is not just that another extreme rightwing populist party, Spain’s Vox, may be on the point of entering government. It is also the capitulation of the centre-right parties to far-right policies, as the firewall separating the right from the extreme right starts to fall across the continent.

Vox has proposed mass deportations of migrants under the banner of “remigration”. Spain’s Popular party (PP) has – as documented by an investigation published by LaSexta – been prepared to join with Vox in regional coalitions to remove gender-equality initiatives and minority-language protections, and to challenge abortion and LGBTQ+ protections. And although they disagree about its definition, the PP and Vox have both explicitly endorsed the principle of prioridad nacional – national preference in social security and health benefits.

Just as worrying is the rise of a global coalition of anti-internationalists. Reports of an early, unpublished version of Donald Trump’s national security strategy last year envisaged direct support being offered from the US to Europe’s extreme populist nationalist parties. The White House denied those reports, but in August, Reuters also claimed the Trump administration planned to provide at least $25m (£19m) in funding for conservative civil-society initiatives in Europe, including $4m for rightwing media.

Not content with stating via the national strategy document that Europe was threatened with “civilisational erasure”, Trump dispatched his vice-president, JD Vance, to consort with the extreme-right AfD party in Germany in preference to meeting the chancellor. Meanwhile, having convened in Hungary and the UK this year, the US-led Conservative Political Action Conference – which brings together conservative activists, commentators and officials – plans an even bigger “expansion into western Europe” with an Italian summit in 2027.

How to push back? One way is to exploit the truth: that what the far right offers isn’t necessarily in sync with what ordinary people want. Polling for the Rockefeller Foundation, of which I am a trustee, reveals the picture is much more nuanced if we ask Europeans what they are really feeling.

Spain’s statutory minimum wage has increased by two-thirds and the proportion of workers on fixed-term contracts has fallen by more than 40% under the government of Pedro Sánchez. With more than half of Spain’s electricity now coming from renewables, energy price rises have hit less hard than elsewhere in Europe, and consumer confidence has been much higher.

But Spain’s official polling agency, the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), found that only a third give a positive assessment of the economy, while earlier this month, concerns over housing and rents led to the country’s first general strike in 14 years along with mass demonstrations on the streets of its major cities. Indeed, across Europe, half of those polled say they don’t trust their government, while two-thirds say they are nostalgic for the past, believing their countries have lost touch with the values that built them.

But these are surface manifestations of dissatisfaction. What really worries people in their daily lives? People fear economic decline – which can mean the sense that their country is doing badly (65% say theirs has got worse in the past year), as well as personal financial disappointment over the gap between their expectations and their current experience. Nearly 50% say they are worse off than they expected to be five years ago, with 59% worrying more about money every year. They also worry that nobody is there to stand up for them or speak up on their behalf. Half of respondents say that, in a crisis, people in their community would look out only for themselves. More telling, perhaps, is that half feel the government helps other groups more than theirs.

What is striking is that, for many, this sense of civic decline, which is a more cultural phenomenon, matters as much as economic decline. But while it may mean they lend their votes to populist nationalist parties that claim to speak for their concerns, most are not populist nationalists at heart. Only 15% of those voting for the radical right take a consistently zero-sum view of the world – seeing the gains of one social group as necessarily coming at the expense of another. In Spain, only 12% of Vox voters are consistently zero-sum. And a total of 61% of respondents across the European countries polled are prepared to say they want their country to cooperate internationally, even when it means compromising on national interests. Even more, 80%, reject intolerant attitudes, believing that good solutions come from hearing many different viewpoints.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

What does this mean when it comes to actual votes? Across Europe, no more than 25% anywhere say they would vote for the radical right, and fewer – about 20% – see another ethnic group’s gain as their own loss. As few as 10% hold to the us-v-them mindset on trade, migration and technology that characterises the rhetoric and ideology of the populist movements. And despite the enormous publicity the issue receives, and legitimate concerns about illegal migration, fewer than 25% put managing migration among the top issues for countries to work on together.

Anti-incumbent voting is now commonplace. Millions are open to voting for change when they are dissatisfied, and may choose to protest with a vote for the extreme right. Sánchez is defending a strong record at home and abroad. Despite the day-to-day polls, Spain has one of the smallest us-v-them blocs and the lowest radical-right vote of the countries we polled, with votes destined for the extreme right standing at 14%, well short of the PP and Sánchez’s Socialists. The general public in Spain and in Europe are unhappy with their economic plight and fear the loss of civic cohesion, but they have not, in the main, become converts to far-right ideology. The drift is not inevitable. By knowing how people really feel, we can reach them.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010
