The Army Plans to Blow Up Tons of Toxic Explosives in Iowa. It Rejected a Safer Option.

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Army had hired a firm to turn the explosives into harmless waste, but then dropped it in favor of a controlled blast that could launch lead dust across Iowa.

By Hiroko Tabuchi and John Ismay

Reporting from New York and Washington.

In March, when the Army discovered nearly five tons of rapidly deteriorating explosives at an Iowa base, it faced two main choices: hire a company to safely dissolve the chemicals, or blow them up.

The Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions. But it canceled the deal two months later, citing safety concerns, opting to blow up nearly five tons of the material instead.

The detonation is scheduled for Monday. Residents, environmentalists and elected leaders are in an uproar because the material contains lead, and the blast could potentially contaminate hundreds of square miles with toxic dust.

The Army did not respond to questions about its canceled deal with MuniRem and why it chose to blow up the dangerous material. The details about the MuniRem contract have not previously been reported.

It is unclear why the Army did not remove and dispose of the drums of lead azide before they reached the point of deterioration that forced the decision to detonate them.

There is no safe level of exposure to lead, which is a neurotoxin. It is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. It can interfere with fetal brain development, cause cognitive and behavioral harm and increase the risk of premature births or miscarriage.

Earlier this week, the Army stated in documents clearing the way for Monday’s planned detonation that chemical alternatives “offered environmental protections by avoiding a blast plume.” The documents didn’t name the alternative method, but said it could process as much as 10 drums per day, requiring up to 22 days to get through the stockpile in Iowa.

The documents also said that the alternative had been “eliminated from detailed study” because it required personnel to handle the explosives and would drastically increase the probability of an accidental detonation, creating an “unacceptable risk to human safety.”

In a letter Friday to the Iowa governor, Kim Reynolds, the Environmental Protection Agency said that those concerns had been raised by the Army, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

The agencies said that any movement of the barrels, or even removing the lids, could cause a spontaneous detonation, posing “a significant risk to personnel and the surrounding population,” E. P. A. regional administrator Jim Macy wrote. None of the agencies immediately responded to requests for comment.

That came after the acting secretary of the Army, Adam Telle, said in a statement on Thursday that there was urgency to destroy the lead azide because temperatures were expected to drop below freezing, which could “risk further destabilization” of the material.

An environmental group is challenging the detonation permit granted to the Army by the Environmental Protection Agency. The Justice Department argued on Friday that the Army has the authority to blow up the cache, regardless of an E. P. A. permit. A federal court has yet to rule on the complaint.

While detonation of unneeded or unstable ordnance in the open air has for decades been a standard disposal method, in more recent years businesses have developed chemical processes that can break apart explosives at the molecular level. The resulting byproducts are typically nonhazardous and can be buried in landfills.

But such chemical sprays are relatively new and unfamiliar to many in the military who have spent their careers blowing up unneeded or unstable munitions on demolition ranges.

MuniRem presented its chemical technology in March to an expert panel assembled by the Army to find a solution to the lead azide crisis at the Iowa ammunition facility.

Lead azide is sensitive to heat, shock and friction, meaning it can easily detonate if mishandled. And when it degrades, these risks increase.

MuniRem’s technology uses a sulfur-based solution that breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, rather than detonating or burning them.

According to materials presented to the expert panel by MuniRem, and reviewed by The New York Times, the company presented case studies in which its solution was applied to unstable lead azide, including the disposal of 412 pounds of aged lead azide that had been poorly stored inside an ammunition bunker.

In an interview, Valentine Nzengung, MuniRem’s chief executive and a professor in environmental geochemistry at the University of Georgia, said that MuniRem had proposed spraying the bunker interiors and barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions. That would make it possible to determine how to safely open the barrels and neutralize the lead azide inside, he said.

“Our position on this is very straightforward,” he said. “We believe that any disposal decision should protect public health.”

Following the presentation, MuniRem was hired in late March to dispose of the volatile explosive. But two months later, the Army terminated the contract.

Dr. Nzengung said the Army gave no reason for the cancellation aside from the fact that then-Secretary of the Army, Dan Driscoll, had made the final determination to order the controlled detonation instead. That involves placing explosive charges around the material in both bunkers and blowing them up simultaneously, destroying the lead azide in the process.

According to emails reviewed by The Times, an Army contracting officer told the company that the decision not to use MuniRem’s chemical neutralization method “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s proposed technical approach.

Mr. Nzengung of MuniRem said the company has filed public records requests seeking more information on why its technology was dismissed, and has not received a response.

Mr. Driscoll resigned as Army secretary on Aug. 31, after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Mr. Hegseth’s removal of qualified Army officers from promotion lists without explanation.

In a statement provided to The Times, a spokesman for Mr. Driscoll said when he was in office and became aware of the lead azide problem at the Iowa plant, he commissioned a study with several federal agencies that oversee explosive safety matters and agreed with their findings that controlled detonation offered the safest possible solution, though Mr. Driscoll believed that more work needed to be done to notify state and local authorities ahead of time to coordinate a public response.

Alternatives to open-air detonation have been gaining acceptance. In 2019, the National Academies of Sciences reviewed MuniRem’s process, along with thermal and chemical alternatives to open burning or detonation, and found that it “can be conducted indoors with little danger to the user or community.”

The Academies also listed shortcomings of the chemical process, namely that it could be slow. Still, the method “has been demonstrated and validated on several field scale projects,” it noted. Workers could wear personal protective gear “to ensure no contact with the reactive chemicals when spraying the MuniRem solution,” it said.

A January 2025 E. P. A. guide to detonation alternatives also lists chemical neutralization, including MuniRem, as a valid treatment technology for lead azide.

Andrew J. Whelton, a professor of environmental chemistry and engineering at Purdue University, said any risk of fatality was a valid concern and should drive decision-making. Still, “if there was a non-detonation option that could have been chosen and the deliberate detonation could be avoided, then this is a major decision,” he said. “Open burning, open detonation is a practice that is used as a last resort.”

The Iowa base plays a critical role in the nation’s defense as the main facility for loading explosives into artillery and mortar shells used by the Pentagon. According to an internal Army history report, the site was built from 1940 to 1941 as part of the massive mobilization for arms during World War II and sits on 19,000 acres.

Deakin Donley, a retired Navy explosive ordnance disposal technician said the rapidly-approaching temperature shift meant there would likely not be a reasonable way to stabilize such a large stockpile. “Proceeding with detonation is the only viable option now, unfortunately,” he said.

This incident would be “a lesson learned for industry and stockpile management,” he added. “Ensuring routine inspections and maintenance would have likely prevented this, and it will be an example cited for decades to come.”

I'm the editor on this article. The reporters, Hiroko and John, learned that a tech company, MuniRem, had signed a deal with the Army to clean up these dangerous explosives in Iowa -- but then the Army dropped that plan, and instead decided to blow them up. This is a complicated situation: The Army says that delaying its planned explosion could put people further at risk. But the blast could release a toxic cloud of lead dust stretching for miles. We're particularly interested in hearing from readers in the potentially affected area. Tell us how you’re preparing for a potential detonation, how the situation is affecting you, and what you think is the right way to handle this crisis.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

Top Drug Kingpin Is Captured by Mexican Army as Gunfire Erupts

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro and was one of the F. B. I.’s 10 most wanted, was a victory for the Mexican government.

By Paulina Villegas

Reporting from Mexico City

A Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the F. B. I.’s 10 most-wanted fugitives was captured in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican government said on Saturday, in an operation that unleashed chaos as cartel henchmen and military forces clashed.

The arrest on Friday night of the drug trafficker, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro, was a major victory in Mexico’s campaign against its largest criminal organizations. Mr. Meza Flores was among the most powerful traffickers in Sinaloa, where a war between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel has killed thousands and plunged the state into relentless violence.

No civilians were harmed during the confrontation, the Mexican authorities said, although four Mexican soldiers and seven people suspected of being cartel members were killed.

Mexico’s defense ministry said in a statement on Saturday that the operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores had been carried out in coordination with U. S. agencies.

“This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders,” the Drug Enforcement Administration said in a statement. It commended the Mexican authorities who conducted the operation, calling the capture a “significant blow” to the cartel.

“The exchange of strategic intelligence between the United States and Mexico contributed to make this operation possible,” the U. S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, said on social media. Homeland Security Investigations called the operation “a MAJOR blow to one of Mexico’s most powerful cartel networks.”

Two more cartel operatives were arrested along with Mr. Meza Flores: his cousin, who served as his second-in-command, as well as his brother-in-law, who was his financial operator, the Mexican military said in a statement on Saturday. The three men were transferred to Mexico City.

President Trump said earlier on Friday at the White House that he told President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico at a summit this week in China that cartels were running her country. Ms. Sheinbaum has publicly rejected that characterization.

Mr. Meza Flores was the leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, originally part of the powerful Sinaloa Cartel, before starting his own group, which is known as the Meza-Flores criminal organization, in Sinaloa.

The U. S. authorities describe the group as a heavily armed and violent organization that controls drug production and distribution in parts of Mexico. They accuse it of trafficking large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States.

Mr. Meza Flores shares a similar nickname but is not related to Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the imprisoned Mexican drug kingpin known as El Chapo who helped run the Sinaloa Cartel before his arrest in 2014. The two men actually became rivals in Mexico’s drug trade, and fought a bloody turf war in the late 2000s.

Mr. Meza Flores has never been as prominent as his namesake. But even though he operated mostly below the radar, he has a reputation as a major — and violent — player in the Mexican drug trade. He was the “dominant crime boss” in northern Sinaloa, according to Adrián López, the publisher of a leading newspaper in the state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars for decades.

The operation to capture Mr. Meza Flores threw the city of Guasave into turmoil on Friday night as federal forces were attacked, according to a post on X by the state’s public security agency, which urged residents to shelter in place and avoid a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state.

Trucks burned across major roads and gunfire rang out in several neighborhoods, local news outlets reported. In footage shared by Mexican TV networks, helicopters flew overhead, one appearing to fire toward the ground.

A professional baseball game was suspended as gunfire rang out. Videos posted on social media showed fans streaming into the stadium’s corridors for shelter and players running off the field. In another recording shared by a Mexican TV network, a reporter covering the clashes ducked between two cars as shooting broke out. As the firefight ensued, some people took refuge in supermarkets, businesses, cinemas and churches.

By Saturday morning, the aftermath of the violence was evident across Guasave: incinerated cars slumped along the roads; military troops guarded the nearby Los Mochis international airport, where several flights were canceled; and convenience stores and gas stations stood charred.

Federal prosecutors in Washington, who filed indictments against Mr. Meza Flores in 2012 and 2019, updated the charges only two months ago, suggesting that the U. S. authorities were continuing their pursuit of him. At that time, the prosecutors asked a judge overseeing the case to cancel an arrest warrant issued in Mr. Meza Flores’s name in 2019 because the authorities planned to seek his arrest on the updated third indictment.

That indictment built on the ones before it but added a few new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Mr. Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel. One month after Mr. Trump returned to the White House, the State Department designated the cartel as a foreign terrorism organization. The agency had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to Mr. Meza Flores’s arrest or conviction.

The new indictment also accused Mr. Meza Flores of abducting a member of the Mexican National Guard in Oaxaca in October 2022 and killing him. It charged him further with smuggling about 6,000 kilograms, or more than six tons, of methamphetamine across the border near Eagle Pass, Texas, in February 2024.

Mr. Meza Flores’s group, previously a bitter rival of the Sinaloa Cartel, recently allied with a faction of the cartel called Los Mayos, according to Mr. López. Los Mayos has been fighting another faction called Los Chapitos for control of the cartel since 2024, after one of its founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was taken into U. S. custody.

Mr. Trump has vowed to “dismantle” the cartels and frequently raised the prospect of sending U. S. military forces into Mexico. “We can’t let the cartels run Mexico,” he said at a news conference on Friday, after confirming that he had told Ms. Sheinbaum that he thought that it was the case that drug organizations were too powerful in Mexico. “They’re our neighbor.”

Ms. Sheinbaum has repeatedly ruled out U. S. military intervention on Mexican soil, even as her government has deepened security cooperation with Washington.

Under pressure from Mr. Trump, Ms. Sheinbaum’s government has intensified its nationwide crackdown on criminal groups. The Mexican authorities have arrested tens of thousands of people, seized hundreds of tons of drugs and destroyed thousands of clandestine labs and other sites used to make drugs. Mexico has also transferred dozens of drug trafficking suspects into U. S. custody.

Alan Feuer, Emiliano Rodríguez Mega and Lynsey Chutel contributed reporting.

Paulina Villegas is a reporter for The Times based in Mexico City, where she covers criminal organizations, the drug trade and other issues affecting the region.

Trump Moves to Restrict Congressional Oversight of Contractors

The New York Times November 21, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The president’s executive order is the latest effort to blunt Democratic plans to investigate the administration’s actions.

By Erica L. Green and Michael Gold

Reporting from Washington

President Trump has directed federal contractors to seek permission from the White House before complying with congressional requests for information, the latest effort by the administration to blunt Democratic investigative plans next year.

In an executive order issued on Friday, Mr. Trump ordered contractors and subcontractors to coordinate responses to congressional queries with the White House, and to withhold information that the administration deems confidential or protected under “executive privilege.” Firms that fail to comply could have their contracts suspended or terminated, according to the order.

“The ability of the Congress to seek executive branch information is limited,” the order states. “It cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies, employees or federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core executive functions.”

The move comes as Democrats, who will take control of the House and Senate next year, plan to cast a wide net in investigating everything from the administration’s policiesto any conflicts of interest it has had. This week, Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent a dozen notices to members of Mr. Trump’s family, Vice President JD Vance and other current and former administration officials asking them to preserve documents on a host of issues.

Democrats have made clear that they intend to investigate no-bid contracts, and how alleged pay-to-play schemes might have influenced contracting decisions

Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat expected to lead the Judiciary Committee, called the order “blatantly unlawful.”

And Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who is poised to be the chairwoman of the Homeland Security Committee, said in her own statement that “every federal contractor should know that this executive order does not override their obligation to comply with congressional requests for information or subpoenas.”

She added: “Congress will get the information that it needs, and, if necessary, we will use every authority available to us to get it.”

The White House is mounting a combative response, seeking on several fronts to shield top officials, donors and members of Mr. Trump’s family.

Will Scharf, the White House counsel, sent a letter to Democrats on congressional committees saying that the White House would not respond to oversight requests until they took control of Congress in January. The White House has also maintained that congressional investigations “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” though it declined to say how. Legal experts have called the assessment dubious.

Mr. Trump, who has made retribution against his political enemies a priority of his second term, wrote in a social media post earlier this month that Democrats were engaging in “weaponization and lawfare at another level.” He added that “threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat political leaders,” and that he was directing the Justice Department to investigate the letters as “a criminal act.”

A fact sheet released by the White House outlined the new executive order’s goal as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach.” It accused some congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government,” in their efforts to intrude on “executive prerogatives.”

“The executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without concern that confidential information may be released to unauthorized third parties, even by federal contractors from a congressional request,” the fact sheet read.

Government watchdog groups said that the president’s order was an effort to cover up the widespread abuse of the contracting process over the last two years, including lucrative contracts that had been doled out to political allies and unqualified bidders.

“Contractors are paid with Americans’ tax money and must be the best for the job — full stop,” Lisa Gilbert, a co-president of the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said in a statement.

The order, she added, was “dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies,” and was “nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption.”

“It will not succeed,” Ms. Gilbert said.

Erica L. Green is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A. I. Will Bring More Disruptions.

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Cybersecurity has been an afterthought since the early days of the internet. Now A. I. is uncovering dormant problems, making the bill come due for decades of vulnerable code.

By Dustin VolzKate CongerDylan Freedman and Sheera Frenkel

The reporters have been covering how A. I. is transforming cybersecurity, national security and society.

Sometimes, especially lately, it can seem like computer software is built on a house of cards.

That is how the cybersecurity researcher Paulos Yibelo felt when he discovered a vulnerability in document and image processing software that is ubiquitous across the internet. The bug he found, called Upload2Shell, would enable a hacker to break into Google, Zoom and potentially thousands of other companies’ software just by uploading a file.

Mr. Yibelo, who recently founded a company called PWN AI, unearthed the bug by using artificial intelligence to meticulously probe what happens behind the scenes when people upload files to different services. He found that Ghostscript, software initially created 38 years ago to convert images to different formats, could be exploited by uploading files containing a custom font to execute malicious computer code. Mr. Yibelo reported the flaw to Artifex, the Ghostscript developer, and affected companies, which issued patches.

Mr. Yibelo’s finding, which has not been previously reported, is another example of how advanced A. I. has in a matter of months radically transformed cybersecurity and plunged the world into a disorienting new digital chapter in which severe technological disruptions may become far more commonplace than they were in the past, according to current and former U. S. and Western intelligence officials, security engineers and A. I. experts.

Those tremors have now bled into the daily life of Americans, as their email inboxes go dark and their flights are grounded. Viral rumors on social media have stoked confusion and fear about a widespread internet outage that could affect banking systems or critical infrastructure, even if recent events were not all A. I. related. It’s impossible for average people to tell what’s a malicious hack — could, for example, a 401(k) be drained? — and what’s simply antiquated software.

Over the past two weeks, a flood of outages slowed banking transactions, disrupted Microsoft products, interrupted Apple services, shut down a key system at the National Security Agency and temporarily grounded all commercial air traffic in the United States.

Officials have said they had no evidence that those episodes were caused by malicious cyberattacks. Instead, for a number of the outages, aside from the national air grounding, U. S. officials pointed to a more mundane explanation: Companies and government agencies are hardening their digital systems against new vulnerabilities, and these software patches are going awry.

In some of those episodes, including at the National Security Agency, the vulnerabilities at issue were detected with the help of A. I., according to U. S. officials. Individuals and businesses alike are using A. I. models to easily spot overlooked computer bugs and, in some cases, build proof-of-concept hacks in days or even hours that once might have taken scores of elite teams months to assemble.

At the same time, fears that bad actors are also using A. I. to work just as quickly have made defenders feel like they need to sprint to push fixes, which can result in messier updates that lead to disruptions.

Events last month were considered so alarming that some cybersecurity doomsayers (and opportunity-seeking marketing specialists) took to referring to the month as “Black October.” The label conveyed a sense that the world appeared to be suffering through a never-ending cascade of A. I.-powered software vulnerabilities that left defenders outmanned and exhausted.

The gloom has been even worse this month, putting a public already anxious about technology’s rapid pace of acceleration further on edge.

It is unlikely to be a momentary blip.

Estimates vary, but cybersecurity experts have said that the next year or two could be especially perilous, as advanced A. I. models find coding bugs that humans never spotted before — even if many malicious hacks remain more mundane. Some hope that after that painful transition period the internet will reach an equilibrium as A. I. helps overwrite vulnerable computer code. Others hold the more jaundiced view that A. I. represents an interminable threat to the interconnected technology upon which modern life and the global economy operate.

The past week is “the new normal,” retired Gen. Paul M. Nakasone, the former head of the N. S. A. and U. S. Cyber Command, said at a conference held in Washington by Vanderbilt University’s Institute of National Security.

“Industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize and at the same time defend themselves,” Mr. Nakasone said. “A. I. is driving all of this — the opportunities and the challenges.”

Mr. Nakasone, who is an OpenAI board member, described A. I. as “the most disruptive technology” in history, which would have profound consequences not just for the digital world but also the rest of society. “We are in an era where we’ve got to think differently about how we’re going to be more resilient.”

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, is credited with popularizing the Silicon Valley cri de coeur to “move fast and break things.” A more honest assessment of the internet might be that it was broken from the start, and moved too fast to ever be fixed.

The rise of the technology industry has been defined by fierce competition, as companies jockeyed to rush their products to consumers quickly while security, which can create friction and slow progress, often remained an afterthought. Deficiencies in hasty code build over time, a concept known as technical debt. The focus on rapid product development has left many tech products riddled with hidden security holes that, at least historically, only a few determined hackers might find and exploit.

“The amount of technical debt that most companies will allow and live with is unforgivable,” said Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade, a distinguished fellow for security and A. I. research at the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. “Folks have been riding until the wheels fall off when it comes to technology. There’s always money in releasing, and there’s no money in maintaining.”

A. I. has upended the playing field, making it much easier to find the cracks in popular software. New cyber-focused A. I. models that can ferret out vulnerabilities have whipped some bug hunters into a frenzy as they compete to find novel ways to break into systems. Companies have also bought in, using A. I. to blast their own infrastructure and find bugs before hackers can.

“You’re essentially taking these brittle code bases and shaking them,” Mr. Guerrero-Saade said.

Even the N. S. A., which specializes in hacking and cyberdefense, is not immune. It had a days-long classified network outage this week because it installed faulty updates that sought to address flaws in the PHP programming language that were uncovered by A. I.-wielding researchers, officials said.

This week, Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington, the senior Democrat on the commerce committee, and Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota, the Republican chairman of a cybersecurity subcommittee, wrote a letter to the White House warning that A. I.-enabled cyber threats were outmaneuvering America’s defense systems.

“A. I. is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” the senators wrote to Jay Clayton, the national intelligence director, who also leads the White House super intelligence task force. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday’s cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

Recent data shows just how dramatically A. I. is transforming the cybersecurity ecosystem. Microsoft released over 1,400 patches for its various products last month, a rate about 10 times higher than its historic baseline. The tally eclipsed the previous record of nearly 1,000 set just a month earlier, in September.

Experts worry that there are fewer qualified humans available to triage the bug explosion. Major tech companies have made mass layoffs this year, in part because they have sought to replace workers with A. I., leaving them without institutional knowledge about how their old code was written.

New hiring data released this week by LinkedIn and reviewed by The New York Times showed that despite the rise in cybersecurity incidents and more bugs spotted than ever, U. S. cybersecurity hiring has underperformed relative to overall hiring.

Lea Kissner, the chief information security officer at LinkedIn, said that the current cybersecurity challenges meant companies needed humans with expertise more than ever.

“No one knows the best way to do security right now, because everything is changing so quickly,” said Dr. Kissner. “So you desperately need people who understand how things work, and have curiosity, and know how to solve problems.”

Despite the deluge of bugs exposed by A. I., some things haven’t changed. Most recent major cyberattacks have demonstrated hackers don’t need A. I., or only use it on the margins, to achieve their goals.

Iran’s targeting of scores of municipal water systems in the United States this summer largely relied on rudimentary tactics that seized on weak or default passwords on the computers that control operations. A criminal group’s hack of the F. B. I.’s sensitive personnel files relied on unpatched Oracle software that had been available for months. And recent attacks on refrigeration systems in Europe also appear to be relatively unsophisticated.

Of the 1,400 bugs identified last month by Microsoft, only one was something that was already weaponized by hackers, as the security journalist Brian Krebs observed. The gap reflects that for all the fear around A. I. most cyberattacks are still rooted in people not addressing basic, longstanding problems or patching known bugs.

Michael Yeh, Microsoft’s vice president of customer security and trust, said in a recent interview that over the past year, the top five bugs Microsoft was seeing used by hackers were exploits identified with patches three to six years ago.

“None of those are A. I.-driven attacks.” Mr. Yeh said. “These are people exploiting existing legacy vulnerabilities” that can be decades old. The failure to address age-old problems remained a bigger threat today than A. I., Mr. Yeh said. “And so I think they have to be eyes wide open about that.”

Some security experts believe A. I. is ushering in an era of more resilient online systems. They predict a future in which A. I. has eradicated technical debt and systems are far more secure. But others believe that the cycle of bug-finding and patching will continue endlessly, as A. I. systems improve and find more complex flaws.

Rob Joyce, the former top cybersecurity official at the N. S. A., said that A. I. was not “inventing brand new ways to hack” but instead applying more pressure on the need to fix existing problems — while offering a potential way forward.

Speaking Friday at Cyberwarcon, an annual gathering of security experts outside Washington, D. C., Mr. Joyce likened the current situation to a forest fire.

“All that tech that’s on fire and going to burn down, and on the other side of it, all the little things that are down in the forest floor, they’re going to grow,” Mr. Joyce said during a conference keynote. “They’re going to be stronger. They’re going to be more capable. But we’ve got to live through this era where stuff’s on fire.”

Mr. Yibelo, the PWN AI researcher, said he was skeptical that a smoother road was ahead because the newer, stronger models would continue to be capable of finding new flaws, including potentially in code fully written by earlier generations of A. I.

“I don’t know why there would be an end to the bugs,” Mr. Yibelo said. “It’ll always maybe be a cat-and-mouse game.”

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Kate Conger is a technology reporter based in San Francisco. She can be reached at kate. conger@nytimes. com.

Dylan Freedman is the A. I. projects editor for The Times, investigating a range of topics. He has experience as both a reporter and a machine-learning engineer.

Sheera Frenkel is a Times reporter based in the San Francisco Bay Area, covering defense and surveillance technology.

Hakeem Jeffries on Trump, Stephen Miller, AIPAC and the Road Ahead

The New York Times November 21, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Paola Kudacki for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lulu Garcia-Navarro

On Wednesday, House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House, all but ensuring that come January, he will be the nation’s first Black speaker.

Jeffries, who is known for his careful, disciplined messaging and approach, faces a complicated proposition. He has to hold his ideologically diverse party together, navigate a lame duck President Trump, figure out how to quickly deliver on the promises Democrats made to American voters and not ruin the Democrats’ chances to win the 2028 presidential election.

How will he handle this historic nomination and urgent political moment? I sat down with Jeffries on Friday in Washington to find out.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

You had an overwhelming vote for your nomination to be speaker. What was the first thing that went through your mind when it happened? I was just thankful for the support of my colleagues, which came from all across the caucus, every part of the country. The ideological diversity of the caucus is one of our strengths. We have progressives. We have New Dems. We have Blue Dogs. And I was proud to have strong support amongst every group. We have a shared mission and objective, which is to deliver big things for the American people. And I’m humbled.

This is a time, though, when the American electorate is pretty angry. It wants radical change. Democrats have been given a mandate. Can you tell me why you think you’re the man for this moment? House Democrats, over the last several years, have worked incredibly hard to battle Republicans on every single issue, and we’ve done that forcefully and aggressively. Battle them on the One Big Ugly Bill. Battle them on Medicaid cuts. Battle them on the Affordable Care Act tax credits. Battle them on Epstein files and transparency. Battle them on a reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. We’ve battled them on ICE funding — certainly battled them as it relates to the unprecedented corruption that has been unleashed on the American people.

So are you saying that happened because you were leader and you led that effort, and that’s why you’re the man for the moment? No, what I’m saying is that we have a track record of success that I was proud to be a part of in terms of rising to the occasion at a moment where everybody was down on the ability of House Democrats to actually do anything, let alone win a historic election.

But this is a moment for you, and the thing that I would like to understand as we go through this conversation is how you see your leadership. You’ve convinced your caucus, but if you had to tell the American people why Hakeem Jeffries is the man right now, what would you say? Well, when it comes to the pain being felt by the American people — which is extraordinary, because there are far too many people in this country working hard, playing by the rules, but they can’t thrive and they can barely survive — I understand the struggles of working-class individuals, because I grew up in a working-class neighborhood. Both my parents were public servants. My mom worked for the city for 45 years. My dad was a substance abuse social worker who worked in the trenches during some incredibly painful times in the city, both the heroin explosion and the crack cocaine epidemic. I grew up in the Cornerstone Baptist Church and came of age myself in the middle of the crack cocaine epidemic, when most of us weren’t sure we would even be able to survive to the next day, the next week or the next month, because of the violence. So the struggles that the American people are experiencing right now, I’ve lived.

Have you heard from the president since the vote? Not yet.

Are you expecting to? It certainly seems to me that we’re going to have to have a conversation about how we are actually going to respond to the demands of the American people to get things done on their behalf.

Obviously, he is still the president, and he will have a lot of power over your agenda. Do you consider a weaker Trump to be a more dangerous Trump or a more pliable Trump? It remains to be seen how the president is going to respond to the decisive defeat that the American people just dealt to Republicans, to the president and to MAGA extremism. Clearly, the American people want a dramatic change in direction. We’ve indicated a willingness at all times to try to find common ground with the other side of the aisle whenever and wherever possible if it means delivering real results for the American people. That was just done in this Congress on a transformational housing affordability bill, the most meaningful one in a generation. That was done in a Congress where Republicans control the House and the Senate, and the Congress came together to pass this bill. We got it to the president’s desk. He didn’t sign it for whatever the reason, but he didn’t veto it, and it became law. That’s a foundation for the type of things that we should be doing.

We’ve seen Mayor Mamdani find ways to develop a relationship with President Trump. Is that something you’re going to try to do on a personal level? Mayor Mamdani has done a tremendous job. He’s gotten off to a great start in working hard to deliver upon the affordability promises that he made to the people of New York City and has developed the ability to have a working relationship with the president in ways that are designed to serve the City of New York. From our standpoint, we continue to maintain a willingness to work with anyone on the other side of the aisle to get things done. Even if I’m going to strongly disagree with the president, the vice president, members of the administration, on the overwhelming majority of issues, the American people want us to do all we can to deliver for them.

In our brief conversation, I think you’ve said “the American people” like a hundred times, and I know that they are at the center of this, but I do want to understand your particular perspective. You had a controversial meeting with the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner several months ago. You do not get along with Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff. You’ve called him a “stone-cold racist” whom you have “zero interest in working with.” So who is going to be your conduit, practically speaking, to the White House? It could be the vice president. There are cabinet secretaries that we can talk to.

Which one do you like? I wouldn’t say I like any of the cabinet secretaries at this particular point in time. I’ve had conversations probably most frequently with Secretary Marco Rubio. I’ve had a conversation with the secretary of Treasury. Here’s the thing: The Republicans have taken a “my way or the highway” approach over the last two years to jam MAGA extremism down the throats of everyday Americans and the country. That’s what they’ve done. And that approach failed. They broke every promise. This is a group of people who promised to lower costs on Day 1. Costs didn’t go down. Costs have gone up.

Do you imagine sitting down with Stephen Miller? No.

Really? No. I made clear that Stephen Miller’s a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time? This is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine, and there’s cruelty associated with that. There’s chaos. There’s death associated with what’s taking place. Now, to directly answer your question about practical engagement, we understand in prior administrations that it often has been the case that secretaries in the cabinet — Steve Mnuchin, for instance, negotiated a lot with Nancy Pelosi — or that vice presidents, such as then Vice President Joe Biden, was the primary negotiator often with majority leader Mitch McConnell at the time.

Have you heard from JD Vance already? No, I haven’t heard from JD Vance, either. But we have heard from the American people. And by the way, I will consistently use that phrase. You are correct. Because we work for the American people. That shouldn’t be confusing to anybody.

What do you make of your new counterpart on the Republican side, Jim Jordan, who is a very staunch Trump ally? We had a brief conversation yesterday, and we’re going to sit down at some point when the dust settles to see what the opportunities may be to actually get things done.

What signal do you think it sends that the Republicans elected Jordan, who isn’t exactly known as super friendly to Democrats? I mean, listen, I think that’s a question that they’re going to have to answer. The reality is MAGA extremism was completely and totally repudiated by the American people up and down the ballot and all across the country.

Do you see any evidence that Republicans in Congress are willing to break with the president after these elections? It remains to be seen, but here’s what is interesting, and this is one of the things that House Democrats were effectively able to do in this current Congress: We repeatedly forced successful votes on the floor over the objection of both President Trump and Mike Johnson.

So you’re saying you can work around them? Well, what I’m saying is that we’ve repeatedly done it, clearly. We did it on the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We did it on the Epstein files.

Do you think you need them? We have a robust majority. We’re going to have a 260-seat majority. We’re going to move aggressively, as I mentioned, to end the reckless and costly war of choice very early on in the new Congress. We’re going to move aggressively to restore SNAP benefits. We’re going to move aggressively to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We’re going to move aggressively to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We’re going to move aggressively to end these Trump tariffs, which have also increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars per year, and we’re going to move aggressively to ban members of Congress from trading stock. And we’ll see whether a handful of Republicans or more join us.

I want to get to the agenda, but just a few more questions on the situation inside of Congress. Do you have an epitaph of Speaker Johnson’s speakership? How do you view his time there? Not really. I’m sure that Mike Johnson will articulate the story of the Republican accomplishments, such as he believes they are. We’ve tried to have the most communicative relationship possible. At times, certainly very early on when we were in divided government and Joe Biden was president, there was a lot more cooperation, this is what the record shows, in the previous Congress than in the current one. Because Republicans decided to just conduct themselves like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump cartel and serve as nothing more than a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s agenda.

That’s been the criticism of Speaker Johnson’s tenure, that he ceded a lot of power to the executive branch and diminished the role of Congress. Is that the way you see it? Certainly, and the days of the House of Representatives functioning in that fashion are over. We’re going to be a check and balance on an out of control executive branch.

There’s a debate about whether or not Chuck Schumer should be re-elected as Senate majority leader. You’ve had your conflicts with him in the past. I remember one during the shutdown fight of March 2025 in particular. What’s your view? No one has delivered more for the people of New York City and the people of New York State over the last several decades from a legislative standpoint than Chuck Schumer. Those are the facts. I’ve had an opportunity to work with him as the leader in the House over several years. And as you pointed out, there are times that we agree on the course forward, and there have been times that we agree to disagree. That’s just the reality of governing.

But you didn’t answer the question about whether you support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. I’ve said yes, I do. I’ve said that repeatedly.

I think there’s a real concern when you look at Chuck Schumer, not that he hasn’t delivered in the past, but is he the man for the future? Well, listen, the senators are going to have to work that out. I understand the dynamics in terms of the intrigue around the inside parlor game, that these questions are going to be asked.

It’s not the parlor. It’s the American people. I feel like I need to invoke it, too. [Laughs]. I appreciate that. But listen, what I’m saying is that from the House perspective, I can tell you clearly and unequivocally, we don’t like it when the senators start messing around in our stuff, getting involved in our agenda, telling us who our leaders should be, suggesting what bills we should bring to the floor, telling us how they think we should be talking to the American people. We don’t like it. So I think I should hold myself to the same standard in advance of a Senate election. Let them work it out amongst themselves.

Do you think it’s healthy to have the debate, or do you think that it would have been better to just get this majority, a huge victory, and not have the conversation be Chris Van Hollen or Senator Schumer? I think debate is definitively healthy on all things. In fact, that’s the reason why this week, even though my election was uncontested, I called for a recorded vote, a secret ballot recorded vote, to give everybody within the caucus the opportunity to express themselves as to who they thought was best capable of serving in a leadership position of significant consequence.

I’m going to move on, but I guess the question is, can you confidently say that Senator Schumer, who is 75 and about to turn 76, is up for this? Just a yes or a no. What I can confidently say is that I don’t like it when senators get involved in our stuff. And I’m going to answer the question.

Because people are going to hear this and think, “He didn’t answer the question, so that means no.” Of course he’s capable of leading us into the future, but that’s a decision that the Senate Democrats are going to have to make.

OK, I want to talk about the plan, and specifically your first 100 days. As journalists, we always love to have a round number. I’m there with you, by the way. I do think it’s important to contextualize for the American people that we’re going to get off to a fast start.

I want to hear about this fast start. What will be the first bill? Well, we’re going to have that conversation. We just talked about all of us coming together. Here’s what I think we should do very early on in the first week or so of the new Congress: We should aggressively move to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. There’s probably nothing more immediate in terms of being able to provide economic relief to the American people than ending this conflict that should have never started to begin with.

I know Democrats are currently wrestling with whether to demand limits to funding the war in order to vote to fund the government and avoid a shutdown. That’s happening in this Congress. Where is your head on that right now? There are ongoing discussions about what can be done in the appropriations bill in advance of Dec. 11 to make clear that this [war] has to end. It needs to be over. In fact, Donald Trump can end it right now. That doesn’t mean there’s not going to be a lot of work ahead, because Iran is in a stronger position now than they were before this reckless and costly war of choice started.

You’ve been through a few shutdowns. It seems like it’s a hard thing for the country and the Congress to go through. It’s a hard thing for the country and for the Congress. We have made it clear that we’re going to fight for a spending bill that protects the health, the safety, the national security and the economic well-being of the people of this great country.

Are you willing to shut down the government in order to get that? I’m not going to say that one way or the other, because we’ve got to figure out right now what’s possible in terms of the appropriations process. What I will say is that we have made clear repeatedly that taxpayer dollars should be spent to make life more affordable for the American people. And we’ve seen several instances when there was disagreement on the other side of the aisle, including during the 43-day government shutdown, that we were not going to go along simply to get along. That was the longest complete shutdown in American history. And at the end of it, we actually were successful in forcing a vote to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.

A lot of this is psychology, right? You’re just seeing who’s going to blink, where people are at in their relationship with their caucus, etc.? And when you look at President Trump, as you’re going into this, I’m wondering, do you think he cares if there’s a government shutdown that lasts 200 days? Because this is his last term. I think presidents get motivated because they’re worried about the next election. They’re worried about the health of their party. But those don’t seem to be the motivating factors for him anymore. So I’m wondering how you think that this is going to be a tool that he might respond to. It remains to be seen how he’s going to react to what just decisively occurred electorally over the next two years.

I guess what I’m asking is, do you think he cares? I think what I’m saying is that it remains to be seen.

You do have to think about it, because it’s a bit of mental jujitsu here that you’re doing. Well, we certainly think about all these things. It didn’t just come out of thin air that we were able to win a historic majority. It didn’t come out of thin air that we were able to win the narrative around the 43-day government shutdown. And it will not come out of thin air that we will successfully end this reckless and costly war of choice.

But you’re not answering whether you think Trump is actually going to be able to be pressured. I did answer the question.

Do you think he’s going to be able to be pressured? You know what the answer is? It remains to be seen.

That’s not an answer. That’s the answer. Do you think that this is a president who is in any way predictable? This is a president who, in one breath, in a nationally televised interview on “60 Minutes,” said we went too far on immigration and that we need to course correct — on the same weekend that he elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of the violent mass deportation machine.

All right. How are you going to approach investigations and accountability? There’s a danger, which I’m sure you’re aware of, that it can seem like Democrats are looking at vengeance and lawfare, as has been portrayed by the Republican side and by the president himself. How do you get accountability without falling into a trap? The notion that these MAGA extremists are going to lecture anybody around overreach is crazy. These people have weaponized the federal government to go after people they perceive to be enemies of the president, illegitimately and consistently. They have zero standing to talk about overreach. Our perspective has been clear. We are going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may.

You saw when you were an impeachment manager for Trump’s first impeachment trial, it made him more politically powerful. He used that as a messaging device to show that he was the subject of, in his view, unfair prosecution. So there is a danger that the American people might view this as a distraction as opposed to what you are saying it is. I have great trust in the legislative leaders of this effort and every single Democrat who’s on the Oversight Committee. We’ve done accountability in this Congress.

What happened with Pete Hegseth and that impeachment [vote], because there was a real sense that this might be a moment with Thomas Massie’s attempt, and the votes by Democrats fell short. And people blamed you. It was disappointing that a few members were unable to make it to the floor.

Why wasn’t it whipped? It was whipped.

Why didn’t they show up then? Well, we have to talk to them about that.

But do you see that as a failure of your leadership? No, I don’t see it as a failure of our leadership. It’s a collective disappointment. It should never happen again. Now, listen, in the minority, we ran Pam Bondi out of town. She should have never been appointed in the first place, but we successfully, in the minority, ran Pam Bondi out of town. We successfully, in the minority, ran Kristi Noem out of the town, who was a disgrace in terms of what was going on at the Department of Homeland Security. So in the majority, on behalf of everyday Americans and people who believe in accountability in this country, we certainly are going to continue to hold cabinet secretaries who have broken the law accountable.

Are you going to try and impeach Hegseth again in the new Congress? Pete Hegseth should be impeached if Donald Trump fails to remove him. Pete Hegseth abused his power, undermined America’s national security. Of course, he has to go.

In terms of oversight, Elon Musk allegedly throttled Ukraine’s internet connectivity earlier this year. Will you be looking into what happened? Do you think the U. S. government should be in business with Elon Musk? I think we have to look into what happened in Ukraine. We need to look at what has happened with respect to the DOGE assault on hard-working federal employees and civil servants. We need an understanding of what has happened with respect to personal information of the American people.

Do you imagine asking him to come to testify in Congress? That’s going to be in the hands, preliminarily, of soon-to-be chairman [of the House Oversight Committee] Robert Garcia.

Do you think he should? Listen, we have to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and then let the chips fall where they may. And when you conduct investigations — and as you pointed out earlier, I was an impeachment manager — you have to be thorough, and you have to make sure that every step that you take is designed to deliver the outcome that is both comprehensive and consistent with the problems that you are seeking to unearth.

Just this past week, I saw Musk say that he’s suddenly not MAGA. He had said in the past not only was he MAGA but he was “dark MAGA.” Do you think this is political posturing in order to avoid accountability? I don’t know, but —

Because I’ve seen a lot of people now suddenly say that they’re moderates, that they are not MAGA, they’ve found a different political religion. Brutal midterm elections do seem to have a clarifying impact on what people want to say publicly. But we can’t forget what has occurred over the last two years. You had people bending the knee in ways that were inconsistent with their own previously articulated values, pretending as if the era of MAGA extremism was a permanent realignment here in the United States of America. It was not. And the American people clearly and decisively showed that to be the case.

One of the toughest issues in your caucus is the role of AIPAC and what to do about Israel. AIPAC has recently changed the way it’s going to give money to candidates. It’s encouraging individual donations from members because of the blowback it’s gotten. In this most recent cycle, you got money from AIPAC. How much was that, by the way?

You tell me, how much was it? Well, I mean, I get asked the question all the time, and I just want the numbers to be clear. In the last two cycles, I’ve raised — from my own re-election campaign, because there’s been no super PAC involvement in any of my campaign activities related to my own re-election — about $40 million for my own re-election. That’s raised and then spent to help elect Democrats all across the country. The average contribution to my re-election campaign is $29 per donor. I’m proud of that fact. I’m proud to be able to raise money from everyday Americans, not special interests.

The question I have, though, is more about what has become such a very touchy issue, the AIPAC funding in particular. But I presume that the reason why it’s become an issue is because people are suggesting that members of Congress are somehow bought and paid for. When I talk to members of Congress, they’re voting their districts, regardless of who they may be raising money from.

Will you continue to accept support from AIPAC? AIPAC has said they’re no longer contributing the $5,000 per contribution that they can make under the current laws.

But would you accept money from them? They’re not giving money at any point in time in terms of AIPAC as an entity. Now, am I going to continue to raise money in the way that I’ve been raising money? In small dollar increments, $29 per donation? Yes, I will. And I’m going to continue to make the case that I’m going to try to raise money subsequently to help House Democrats now hold the majority. And I’m thankful that we’ve won the majority, but to do it in a principled way and to do it in a way that will hopefully continue to give confidence, all of us, that we’re putting the interests of the people that we represent first. Now, I understand that, from a broader issue perspective, things need to change.

You’ve said about Israel: “The status quo is unacceptable. We need dramatic change.” What do you mean about dramatic change? We have to find a path toward a just and lasting peace between Israel and the Palestinian people. To me, the foundation of that is a safe and secure Israel living side by side in peace and prosperity as a Jewish and democratic state with an independent Palestinian state that provides dignity and self-determination for the Palestinian people. That has to be the North Star. And I think it’s fair to say that the U. S. commitment to the two-state solution has left a lot to be desired for decades. There have been administrations, largely on the Democratic side, that have really worked hard to try to bring that type of just and lasting peace about. It certainly happened under the Clinton administration, and it definitively happened as well under Secretary John Kerry’s leadership within the Obama administration. I think we’ve got to make sure that we revive and renew that commitment with everything we’ve got.

There are bills that are currently sitting in front of Congress, the Block the Bombs bill, which has 82 co-sponsors as we record, and the Stop the Settlements bill, which has 76 co-sponsors. Will you put them up for a vote? What I’ve said is that we have to enact dramatic change in terms of the direction of the way things have been going in both the West Bank and in Gaza. The death, the destruction, the devastation that has been experienced in Gaza by Palestinian civilians is unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American. And the conditions on the ground have to change. That requires a surge in humanitarian assistance, including medical assistance and housing support and ensuring that there’s both clean water and clean air.

Those two bills, do you see them as not addressing that? And do you support them? No, I haven’t articulated a position one way or the other.

I’m asking. With respect to any of these bills, because we’re going to have a conversation about the steps that we need to take together as a caucus, what I have made clear is that within the first 100 days, I think the most decisive step that we can take relative to the situation in the West Bank is to move the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. That is certainly something that I think we’ll have strong support for within the House Democratic Caucus, and I believe we should move on it early in the new Congress as a meaningful step forward to changing the conditions on the ground and hopefully meaningfully improving the relationship between Israel and the Palestinian people in the march toward two states for two people.

Some people see that particular bit of legislation about the West Bank as insufficient. The clarion call in the wake of the Gaza war and the broader conflict in the Middle East is that there needs to be a stop on exporting the weapons from the United States that help enact those wars. What I’ve made clear is that’s a conversation that we are going to have but that the current construct is not sustainable, and it needs to change.

In our last few minutes, I do want to get to your own personal story. We touched on it a bit at the top, but I think people want to get to know you. And I want to ask you about growing up in Crown Heights and how that impacted you. You discussed a little bit about the difficulties that you faced in the community back then. How would you say Crown Heights impacted your sense of justice, political activism and just your own leadership? It’s a wonderful neighborhood to grow up in — a working-class neighborhood, good people, hard-working folks. That’s my parents, but that was our neighbors. That was everybody. I had the opportunity, thanks to my mom, to grow up in a loving environment within the Cornerstone Baptist Church. That certainly has had a big impact on me. What was also interesting to me growing up in Crown Heights is that during the first 12 years of my life, my congresswoman was Shirley Chisholm. I never met her, but it’s an honor to stand on her trailblazing, legendary shoulders and to try to continue the fights that she started in such an unbought and unbossed way, particularly as it relates to the children of the Crown Heights community that she so effectively represented. Black Brooklyn, but all across America. Hip-hop, of course, is also a very important part of my upbringing, because I came up during a golden age where hip-hop artists were telling the story of the streets.

I think you were Kid Fresh at some point? You’ve done some great research. My aspiring hip-hop career turned out to be not too successful. Neither did my desire to be a point guard for the New York Knicks. But playing basketball in the streets of Brooklyn, that was an amazing thing, whether that was in my neighborhood or traveling with my boys from Midwood High School to other neighborhoods to find an outdoor court where we could play ball. It was such an amazing time. It was a dangerous time in New York City. You’re talking about 2,000 plus homicides in the heart of the crack cocaine epidemic. But all of us still grew up in such a loving environment. I think that adversity for everyone who emerged from that time has put us all in a stronger position to deal with the slings and arrows of life.

Can you take me back to a moment, something that you remember that really stuck with you and helped you on your way? Even before the crack cocaine epidemic hit, which was probably around ’84 or ’85, it seemed to me that almost every other week or every month or so, my mother would come home having just been robbed. Now, it can’t have been that frequently, but it happened. She was mugged repeatedly, particularly during the winter months, in my recollection. I’ll never forget: Mom comes home, robbed again, and clearly, my dad, who was a loving man but a tough man, had enough. And I saw him grab a saw and race out of the house, apparently trying to track down the person who had just mugged our mom and his wife. Now, I never found out what happened with the saw or the incident, but it was a searing memory about a dad standing up for his family in the face of all the adversity that was going on. I’m thankful that nothing ever happened from the standpoint of harm being done to Mom.

Is your mom still alive? She is. Dad passed away a couple years ago. He was able to see me transition from being chair of the caucus to this current position that I hold, but passed away at the end of 2023. Mom is still alive. In fact, before the vote, as I often do in connection with any big moment in my life, I’ll call Mom, and I’ll just ask her to pray for me, because she’s a praying woman. And prayer changes things. It doesn’t mean the outcome that I hope for has always been achieved. Everybody faces ups and downs in life. That’s the reality. But the last person I spoke to before I walked into that caucus room on the day of the vote a few days ago was Mom. I just told her I loved her. I thanked her for everything and just asked her to pray for me as she’s always done.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is known to be a cautious speaker and interview subject. But I found our conversation very illuminating. While definitely careful (“It remains to be seen” was a favorite answer of his), he was also willing to be pushed and push back in this wide-ranging conversation about several of the challenges he’s going to face as speaker of the House — which he is all but assured to become in January. He laid out his argument for why he’s the man for this moment. Do you agree?

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Lulu Garcia-Navarro is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a series focused on interviewing the world’s most fascinating people.

The Sisterhood Rocks!

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Washington

I had never called my sister at midnight.

But the minute John Mulaney, the impish host of last week’s “Saturday Night Live,” uttered the word “sister,” I picked up the phone.

“Are you watching this?” I asked Peggy.

“Yeah, it’s not funny,” she replied. “It’s hitting too close to home.”

We hung up to experience a flashback to a decade engulfed by caring for our mother. In the sketch, Mulaney plays a man mulling how to care for his aging dad without a nursing home or a costly private health aide.

“That’s when I heard about ‘Sister,’” Mulaney says brightly. “‘Sister’ is a live-in 24-7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister. Now I don’t have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

“I love my mom more than anything,” another man says. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t, either, but she will, whereas I won’t.”

A third man says “Sister” won’t affect your inheritance: “You’ll still get 50 percent of the house she’s currently deep cleaning.”

It’s also a good bonding opportunity for father and son, Mulaney’s character says. He agrees with Dad that Sister’s a “bitch” after she tries to curb Dad’s salt intake to help with his high blood pressure.

When I tried to curb my mom’s salt intake, she gave me a withering look and said, “I’m 97,” before shaking the saltshaker so hard the top flew off. She kept eating because she liked a little food with her salt.

The “S. N. L.” sketch sparked a million palavers about the fact that America’s strategy for elder care often defaults to the kindness of daughters. As we’ve been startled to learn lately, a lot of our infrastructure systems are shaky and stitched together haphazardly. (Fixing one router in Arkansas should not shut down America’s whole airspace.)

The viral hit surprised me because I thought things would have changed by now, 20 years after my mom died, with a couple of generations of men raised by working women less prone to live by outdated gender roles. But, as I always say, men are evolving a lot slower than women.

“We give little girls baby dolls to play with, to train them to be caregivers, where we don’t do that for little boys,” said Jessica Calarco, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin and the author of “Holding It Together: How Women Became America’s Safety Net.”

“Women are making less than men in most fields and so it becomes sort of easy to assume that it’s not only natural but also logical for women to be the ones doing this kind of work when care becomes this hot potato.”

I was a bad nurse. I focused on making Mom look stylish and pretty, with eyebrow tints and pedicures and silk and velvet jackets, working on the premise that if you look good, you feel good.

“You treat her like she’s a doll,” my brother Kevin said with an accusatory look. But my mom was beautiful, with porcelain skin and snowy hair, and she loved looking good. She was blind the last seven years of her life, so she asked me to put on her red lipstick.

“You’re not doing it right,” she complained. “You’re not doing it like Max Factor.” It turned out that she had actually once had her lipstick applied by Max Factor, himself, when he was just starting out and exhibiting his new makeup line in a Washington drugstore.

Just as my three brothers had fewer household tasks growing up, they knew my sister and I would take care of Mom.

My brothers were great, but they focused on the less onerous, less “maternal” jobs. Michael brought dinner every week. Martin often came over to take Mom out to lunch, gossip about the family or read fun newspaper clippings to her. Kevin watched “Seinfeld” with her.

Peggy and I didn’t resent their doing less. Mom adored her sons, and they adored her back. But it’s often harder for men to see their parents get frail — and people are living a lot longer now. My mother’s growing helplessness — blind and in a wheelchair — made my brothers feel helpless.

“It’s also expediency with a lot of guys,” Kevin told me. “They have a life and they can’t interrupt a good part of it to alter their schedules. But I was always inclined to tell myself, ‘This happened on your watch and it’s your problem.’”

While more of my mom’s friends who had only sons ended up in nursing homes, some men are amazing caretakers. Kevin and his sons, especially his youngest, Brian, have spent years tenderly caring for Kevin’s lovely wife, Ellen, who has M. S.

When my mom’s health problems grew more severe — she once broke her neck trying to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night — we got round-the-clock help. We lied and told her it was paid for by Medicare so she wouldn’t feel sad about draining her bank account. She was living, after all, on a police widow’s pension.

Peggy and I continued to spend an enormous amount of time with her. We both had demanding jobs that required a lot of travel, and I remember feeling guilty that I couldn’t travel as much as I needed to.

It was stressful and I sometimes gave up on my own grooming; I spent way too much time in black yoga pants. But the way you exit relationships shows character. And my mom was not a whiner. She managed her pain — and sadness about losing her sight — with two bourbon and sodas in the late afternoon. (When I gave her a bottle of Maker’s Mark, she hid it in her underwear drawer; it was too fancy to drink.)

If you read her a book or a newspaper or even just ads about sales on food and fashion, she was content.

One day, I told her there was a sale at Saks on control top panties.

She looked intrigued. “Who do they control?” she asked.

She was so warm and funny, it felt like a gift to spend her last years with her. I was glad I was on hand when she fell or fainted. The Bethesda-Chevy Chase Rescue Squad was there in a flash; she never missed its annual oyster roast. I still shudder, though, when I hear a siren from an ambulance speeding through her old neighborhood.

I was happy to be there when her fading memory scared her.

One night, watching “Gone With the Wind,” she began crying because she couldn’t remember the plot of her favorite movie. I hugged her, knowing that I wouldn’t remember the plot, either, on the off chance I made it to 97.

I was happy to be on hand to straighten her out if she got confused and thought she wasn’t in her own home, or thought, because my dad wasn’t there, that he had left her for another woman.

“No,” I reassured her, “he’s waiting for you in heaven.”

There was one particular moment that made it all worth it. Late at night, when she couldn’t sleep, I held her hand.

“I love you,” she softly said. “Very much.”

At the end, as she had her last dose of morphine, with a bourbon chaser, her three sons huddled around her bed, crying. Then they left and my sister and I curled up with her.

Even though it was July, I played Christmas music because she loved it. When “Sisters,” the Rosemary Clooney-Vera-Ellen classic from “White Christmas,” came on, Peggy and I sang along. “Caring, sharing. … All kinds of weather, we stick together.” We knew all the words by heart.

Wow. Thanks for the reminder that, while I was the “sister” in my family, and often resented it, I was there for the honor of witnessing final moments with both my parents. My dad, at 93, told me toward the end, “don’t worry, it is ok, it is my time and they are calling my name.” That was a surprise connection that my other siblings (who lived far away) never experienced. Tucking in my mother’s always cold feet, on her last night, and being the only one in the room, holding his hand, as my father passed, are somehow treasures in their own right. I resent that us “sisters” are the default caregivers, but you remind me of the honor we receive in witnessing.

Some say you can't experience true love until you have a child, but helping someone in the last phase of life is equally a gift and privilege that is hard to grasp until you do it.
