Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

“Stranger Things” vaulted him to stardom. With his Broadway debut in “Other Desert Cities,” he wants to get back to “why I started doing this in the first place.”

Credit...

Supported by

By Alexis Soloski

Visuals by OK McCausland

Joe Keery reached high to grab a package of nori for a woman standing nearby.

“Should I get one of these?” he asked her sweetly. “Are they good?” He took another package for himself.

On the first Tuesday in November, Keery, 34, a star of the Netflix fantasia “Stranger Things” and a chart-topping solo musical artist, had blocked out the afternoon for errands. On the agenda: a frame shop, a florist’s for soil and a tiny houseplant, a Japanese grocery for mochi rice, part of a resolution to cook more. (A bandage covered a recent zucchini-related burn.) Then he would walk the 30-odd blocks to the Hudson Theater, where he is starring in a revival of the Jon Robin Baitz play “Other Desert Cities.”

That afternoon, Keery, who has an apartment nearby, had dressed casually in dark jeans, a denim jacket and a red-and-blue baseball cap, matching the “I Voted” sticker pasted to his shirt. It wasn’t the most camera-ready look. That didn’t deter the half-dozen fans who stopped Keery for selfies or several paparazzi. The woman in the grocery was the rare person who seemed not to recognize him.

Keery was gracious throughout, effortlessly decent. If there were Geiger counters to measure kindness, they would go crazy around him. He posed when asked and made time for a couple of student journalists outside a polling site. Asked about voting, he told them, “It’s invigorating and exciting to do and it makes you feel like you’re taking an actively participating role as a citizen.” At the frame shop, where he is a regular, he gave the owners his personal phone number, so that he could arrange discount Broadway tickets for them. I followed the man into traffic and didn’t think twice.

“Everyone who meets him falls in love with him,” Matt Duffer, a co-creator of “Stranger Things,” said.

Keery is ambivalent about this adulation. On his most recent album, “The Crux,” a song includes the lyrics: “I don’t want your money / I don’t care for fame / I don’t want to live a life where that’s my big exchange.”

So it’s a paradox that just about everyone thinks they know and love Keery, just at the moment when he is trying to complicate how people perceive him as an artist. That complication is why he put himself on Broadway, despite not having done a play since college.

“I really wanted to do something that felt like getting back to why I started doing this in the first place,” he said.

Keery has the problem and the gift of being associated with a single role, one he played for about a decade. He was 23 when he was cast in “Stranger Things” as Steve Harrington, a high school bully with unusually good hair. Matt and Ross Duffer, the creators of the series, watched plenty of audition tapes. Only Keery’s lofted Steve beyond stereotype. “He brought a humanity to him, a charisma,” Ross Duffer said in a recent interview.

Steve was meant to die at the end of the first season. Instead he survived, becoming a hero. He also became a lot more like Keery. “Joe’s charm was undeniable,” Matt Duffer said. “We just started to really lean into that.”

In between the show’s five seasons, many of his co-stars took on other jobs, diversifying their résumés. Keery didn’t do much. “Truly not for lack of trying,” he said. He wasn’t interested in roles that too closely resembled Steve, and casting directors turned him down for others. “Just because you have this thing on a silver platter doesn’t mean you get everything else,” he said.

Still, he kept making music, psychedelic synth pop that unpacked personal experience. A musician since his college days in Chicago, he’d had to part from an early band, Post Animal, when “Stranger Things” first aired. (Filming interfered with touring and fans started showing up to gigs in “Stranger Things” merch, which messed with the vibes.) But as a solo artist, who performs and records under the name Djo, he could make his own schedule. One bittersweet song, “End of Beginning,” which seems to reference his life before and after fame, has reached the top of several global charts.

As we sat, post-errands, in Union Square Park, a man stopped to tell Keery that he had his latest album on vinyl. “Oh, thank you, man,” Keery said. “Thank you. Thank you so much. Enjoy the day.”

As “Stranger Things” neared its final season, Keery made moves. He reunited with Post Animal. He starred in a season of “Fargo” and made a couple of movies. And he began looking for a play to appear in, as a way to reconnect with the actor and the person he had been before he was famous. He struggles to remember how people treated him back then, how he felt in his own skin. “Which is a little scary for me,” he said. “But I try not to get negative about it. Otherwise, I feel like it could be easy to spiral or feel trapped.”

He hadn’t heard of “Other Desert Cities,” a 2010 drama, set in 2004, that drops in on a prominent California family as they celebrate a fraught Christmas in Palm Springs. But he was invited to participate in a workshop of it last winter, opposite Allison Janney and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and he found that he loved it. John Benjamin Hickey, the play’s director, loved him, too. “Joe was just so remarkably self-possessed and took such ownership of the part that it was sort of a no-brainer,” he said.

Rehearsing the play this summer and fall was daunting, especially as tour dates necessitated that he start a week late, but he enjoyed the luxury of working a scene again and again, going deeper each time. And thinking about what makes and breaks a family — he remains close to his parents and four sisters — was a pleasure, too.

Keery plays Trip, the family’s youngest child. Helen Shaw, in The New York Times, wrote that Keery, “a real discovery, manages to be droll with a heart.” For most of the play, Trip serves as a joker, a peacemaker. But in the second act, he delivers a monologue that concludes with the lines, “I am California! And California is not happy!” It’s a big, emotive speech. He delivers it with the naturalness and grace of someone who has been onstage all his life.

“Joe brings such ease,” said Lily Rabe, who plays his older sister in the play. She noted that Keery, who has the dressing room next to hers, was easy offstage, too: “He just does not carry himself at all like someone whose first job rocketed him to lightning-strike superstardom or someone who has women waiting in droves for him at the stage door.” (Several of Keery’s “Stranger Things” co-stars, including Charlie Heaton and Maya Hawke, have also come to see the show.)

Keery has never chased superstardom. He doesn’t want to seem ungrateful, and he isn’t. But he would live less publicly if he could. He seemed most joyful at the Japanese grocery, sincerely congratulating a new cashier on his first day on the job. “And on voting day, too!” he said. His face lit up when he talked about his family, about making music, about finding roles that show he is more than his charisma and wavy hair.

“I can surprise people a little bit,” he said. “Attractive to me in any piece of art is something that is shocking or subverts my expectation. I’m looking for ways to be able to do that.”

Alexis Soloski has written for The Times since 2006. As a culture reporter, she covers television, theater, movies, podcasts and new media.

A New Trump Tactic to Restrict Transit Funding: Rewrite the Rules

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The changes could make it harder for dozens of projects across the country to get funding they have pursued for years.

By Emily Badger

The first Trump administration tried, unsuccessfully, to eliminate a major grant program that funds public transit infrastructure around the country. Nearly two years into a second term, transit officials and advocates fear the administration is squeezing the program instead.

Since returning to office, the administration has awarded just one grant from the multibillion-dollar program, called Capital Investment Grants, which helps local communities build costly rail and bus projects that expand transit service. The White House budget office has pushed more than $5 billion in funds appropriated by Congress for the program into fiscal year 2028, locking away money that could be spent today.

And in a proposal released this fall, the administration wants to significantly overhaul the program’s rules in ways that could make it harder for communities to secure grants and, ultimately, to take on complex construction projects they can’t afford on their own.

The Federal Transit Administration says it wants to streamline the program and improve accountability for communities that sometimes seek hundreds of millions in taxpayer funds. The Department of Transportation, which includes the transit administration, said in a statement it was moving to deliver transit improvements on time and on budget.

“That means setting strict deadlines and demanding real local accountability up front so we can finally build these systems faster, better and safer,” the agency said Friday. “Moving forward, the federal government is focusing on smart, affordable projects with high ridership. If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing.”

Transit infrastructure costs in the United States have soared, raising questions about how to build projects more efficiently. But transit advocates note that by delaying grants to ready projects, the administration is driving up their costs amid inflation, not reducing them.

Transit agencies and local governments, who have filled the public comment docket in opposition to the new rules, say the changes would make the grants unattainable for many and pull the rug out from under communities that have spent years pursuing funds.

“Because of the large number of disruptive and unsound elements of the proposed policy guidance, we must consider if F. T. A.’s intent is to undermine the C. I. G. program and discourage future applicants,” wrote the top Democrats on committees overseeing the program and its funding, the senators Elizabeth Warren and Patty Murray and Representative Rick Larsen, in a letter to the F. T. A. and White House budget director this week.

Their letter noted that major rail projects in Boston and Los Angeles have been waiting a year to advance into the final stage of the program. In response to questions from The New York Times, the administration said Friday evening that it had approved the Boston project to advance closer to an award, with a maximum potential grant of more than $2 billion.

Over decades, this federal program has helped fund rail networks in Seattle, Los Angeles and Phoenix, as well as modern bus service in midsize cities like Albuquerque, Raleigh, N. C., and Grand Rapids, Mich. Transit agencies and local governments typically spend years in the program’s pipeline developing plans and trying to prove their value. The grants then cover a portion of any project, with communities also piecing together local taxes, bonds or state funds.

The Federal Transit Administration wants the changes to apply immediately to dozens of projects in the program’s pipeline. Some began the process a decade ago.

Note: Entry dates reflect when projects entered the first project development stage. Projects with “TBD” funding requests have not submitted that information or are revising it. Source: Federal Transit Administration The New York Times

The new proposed rules would adjust in numerous ways how the program scores projects and then determines their funding.

“It’s just systematically designed to make it so projects look substantially worse, and then are judged on that worse score,” said Yonah Freemark, a researcher at the Urban Institute.

The rules would make cost effectiveness more important, while tightening what counts as a good cost effectiveness score. The outside funding that large projects must secure midway through the process would go up. A measure of the strength of an agency’s financial plans would be rounded down (defying “generally accepted mathematical standards,” as one agency put it).

The agency would “weaponize” the new ratings to drive down funding, Sound Transit in metropolitan Seattle wrote in its public comment. The system would effectively “dismantle the current project pipeline,” transit advocates in Virginia wrote. Other industry officials warned the changes would particularly penalize rail projects, which are inherently more expensive.

Another change in the rules that has perplexed transit officials would give a funding boost to projects in communities with higher-than-average birth and marriage rates, a priority of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. That proposal is unrelated to the goals of public transit and unworkable in practice, local officials say. Census data measuring marriage and birthrates in corridors within a mile of transit infrastructure, they said, could be prone to error.

Dozens of people wrote to the agency mocking the idea or labeling it social engineering. One said: “‘Honey, let’s get married and have two kids! Because our town’s transit agency depends on married couples having babies for its capital budget!’ Said no one ever.”

Put it all together, and advocates fear the administration has delayed awarding grants for nearly two years while it wrote new rules that would render many waiting projects ineligible.

“You reach a pretty logical conclusion that this administration is trying to eliminate funding provided by Congress for transit projects,” said Steve Davis, director of the advocacy group Transportation for America. “And who’s going to suffer? Americans in cities of all sizes just trying to catch the bus to work.”

The Federal Transit Administration has not publicly released its own preliminary analysis of how the changes would affect the projects now in the program’s pipeline.

The American Public Transportation Association warns that many of them would no longer qualify for funding. And those that do could receive smaller grants, potentially forcing them to abandon projects where they can’t replace that funding. Either outcome would waste millions of dollars and years of time, local agencies said.

“APTA has met with dozens of project sponsors who believe the proposed guidance will threaten” their plans, said Ward McCarragher, the association’s vice president for government affairs and advocacy. The group supports simplifying the program, and it welcomed changes in the guidance that would give agencies more flexibility to tap other federal funds while they pursue these grants. But those benefits were swamped by the changes transit agencies have opposed. And some changes, Mr. McCarragher said, would violate the law authorizing the program.

Republican appropriators in Congress have signaled their unease, too. In releasing a draft transportation appropriations bill this week, Senate Republicans proposed language urging the F. T. A. not to delay grants and directing it not to apply the new guidance to projects that have already been rated under the current rules.

As Congress debates the spending bill and as the new guidance moves forward, transit projects stalled in the pipeline continue to wait. That includes smaller bus rapid transit projects in Chapel Hill, N. C., and Montgomery County, Md., which had been expected to receive grants this summer.

“Changing the rules in the middle of the game is not the action of a trusted partner in advancing the development of vital public transit investments,” wrote Dow Constantine, the C. E. O. of Sound Transit.

The federal program at issue here, which funds big-ticket new public transit infrastructure, has extensive rules requiring local agencies to document their ridership, their engineering plans, their financial health and the cost effectiveness of the projects they want to build. It’s totally unlike how highway and road projects are generally funded, with far fewer questions asked. And now the Trump administration wants to tighten those rules further. Their efforts illustrate one way the administration has sought to restrict spending it dislikes. But this story also points to the reality in Washington that transit is treated with a greater degree of scrutiny.

Rachel Buigas-Lopez contributed graphics and production.

Emily Badger writes about cities and urban policy for The Times from Washington. She’s particularly interested in housing, transportation and inequality — and how they’re all connected.

Anthropic’s Debut Shows the Disconnect Between Wall Street and Silicon Valley

The New York Times November 21, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The A. I. giant broke records with its initial public offering this week before a rocky first full day of trading, as the markets plunged on worries about artificial intelligence spending.

By Cory Weinberg

Cory Weinberg reports on Anthropic and artificial intelligence.

Anthropic on Thursday celebrated its first day of trading as stock prices surged and the company touched a valuation of $2 trillion. On Friday, its stock deflated, sinking 9 percent.

In the aftermath of its record-breaking initial public offering, Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, has vacuumed up more than $120 billion in investor funds. It also consumed the good will of investors, many of whom were already becoming spooked at the artificial intelligence industry’s trillions of dollars of spending on data centers and other infrastructure to power the technology.

Following the huge investments in Anthropic, rival OpenAI and other A. I start-ups may face new hurdles going public, analysts and investors said. And even more established A. I. companies which need to raise debt or equity to pay for their expansion projects may encounter an uphill battle as the sector loses its glow.

That new hesitation was on full display this week, reflecting the widening disconnect between Silicon Valley optimism over A. I.’s potential and Wall Street’s growing doubts about whether the businesses are financially viable.

“The old-school way of looking at this is: This is the largest I. P. O. in history, late in the A. I. cycle. Psychologically, that could be a topping event,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, which brokers stock sales for hedge funds.

The market was shaken on Friday by some of those fears, ending the week with the worst stock slide in more than a year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 5.3 percent, wiping away the gains it had made this year. And the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent, reaching correction territory, or a drop of 10 percent from its recent high.

Stocks of bellwether A. I. companies including Nvidia, CoreWeave and Advanced Micro Devices fell by double-digit percentages on Friday.

Contributing to the sell-off was last week’s resignation of Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, and worries about what that means for the chip maker’s important role financing other A. I. companies. Interest rates are also rising, making it more expensive for some companies to build data centers and buy chips. And Democrats swept into power during the midterm elections, many promising A. I. regulation.

Those developments put the enormous amount of money needed to finance the chips, data centers and electricity underpinning the technology at risk. Companies are planning to spend about $5 trillion between now and 2030 on the infrastructure, said Michael Arougheti, chief executive of Ares Management, a large investment manager, on an earnings call last month.

SpaceX, Meta and others tapped the markets last month for tens of billions of dollars to fuel their A. I. spending. Executives at most tech giants have told investors they are increasing their spending on the technology each quarter. And Anthropic’s initial public offering piled on top, causing fatigue, analysts and investors said.

Many concerns about A. I. spending are easily dismissed in Silicon Valley, which, by nature, lives in a different world. Venture capitalists this year have minted nearly 200 new unicorns, or start-ups worth more than $1 billion, more than in any other year since the private market frenzy in 2021, according to PitchBook, which tracks start-ups.

But a market for the kinds of initial public offerings or mergers to justify the velocity of investments hasn't yet emerged.

Even in Anthropic’s case, the company allowed early employees to sell more than $25 billion of combined stock at the start of trading, an unusually large sum that some investors and analysts viewed as aggressive. Companies and their investment bankers usually limit employees and other shareholders from selling their stock for weeks or months after I. P. O. s to help stabilize the price.

Many hedge fund managers failed to get stock in Anthropic’s offering at the initial price of $83 per share, said Raphaëlle D’Ornano, an A. I. industry analyst who also invests in public stocks. The hedge funds instead paid a significantly higher price for shares when trading opened on Thursday at $111.50.

Those hedge funds would have lost money as the stock quickly sank, closing at $88.91 on Friday. At the same time, funds have been trying to limit how much stock they own in A. I. companies overall, she added.

Friday “was pure panic,” Ms. D’Ornano said.

Wall Street and Silicon Valley largely agree that A. I. tools are certain to upend how people work, use the internet, and maybe even make discoveries in medicine. But no one is confident on how quickly the technology will produce those benefits.

And as the tech companies invest heavily, it isn’t clear how many will bring in enough revenue to become profitable. Anthropic’s rapid revenue growth has depended on businesses that use Claude for automating software engineering work, and the company will need to broaden that customer base in the coming years, analysts said.

OpenAI, which has filed for an initial public offering expected as soon as next year, is hoping for a similar shift into a broader customer base. The company also wants to get more free users of its popular chatbot, ChatGPT, to start paying.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Those business realities have led to some criticism from Wall Street fund managers, who feel that many in Silicon Valley are overly optimistic about potential returns. For example, Dylan Patel, a closely followed A. I. industry analyst, has predicted unrelenting growth, saying Anthropic and OpenAI would together surpass a half-trillion dollars in revenue by the end of next year, despite shaky markets.

As Mr. Patel walked onstage at a private San Francisco conference for venture capitalists and start-up founders this month to an upbeat electronic song, “Levels” by Avicii, tech stocks were tanking. “Do you have more depressing music, given what’s going on in the market?” he joked.

Mr. Patel, who runs the San Francisco-based market research company SemiAnalysis, said at the conference that investors’ skepticism about the continued pace of revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic was one big reason for market turmoil. He predicted those companies would generate more revenue from new business lines, like offering cybersecurity tools and designing chips.

“I myself am a little cuckoo, and I think they actually will hit this, just to be clear,” he said. “But I think many people are a bit skeptical.”

Some A. I. start-up executives said they have noticed a pullback from investors as they consider jumping into their next rounds of funding. Those company leaders are starting to openly acknowledge one awkward reality of the A. I. boom: The technology’s growth has been largely powered by a relatively small number of voracious business customers and consumers who pay for it.

“Eighty percent of the revenue is probably coming from 20 percent of the users. It might even be 90 percent,” said Aravind Srinivas, the chief executive of the Nvidia-backed A. I. start-up Perplexity, at a conference last week hosted by the tech publication, Newcomer.

(The Times has sued Perplexity, accusing it of copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The company has denied the claims.)

Even as Silicon Valley venture capitalists watched Anthropic’s rocky entry into the public markets, they remained upbeat about the future.

Hemant Taneja, the chief executive of tech investment firm General Catalyst, said he felt relief that Anthropic’s stock price held above the offering price amid “turbulent” markets. Anthropic, he added, was not a one-off example of a venture-funded company that would capitalize on A. I. advances.

“I’m walking away saying: Who’s the next set of founders with the same opportunity?” he said.

Erin Griffith contributed reporting.

Sarah McBride, Barred From Capitol Bathrooms, Wins Top Post

The New York Times November 21, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Republicans have targeted the Delaware Democrat, the first openly transgender member of Congress, since she came to Washington. Her party just elevated her to a key job.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from the Capitol

Two years ago, Representative Sarah McBride arrived on Capitol Hill as the first openly transgender member of Congress and was immediately targeted by majority Republicans who moved to ban her from using women’s bathrooms.

On Thursday, on the second anniversary of that day, Democrats elected Ms. McBride, of Delaware, to serve as one of their top leaders, in charge of helping to oversee messaging for a large new majority that has promised major changes.

Her election as a one of a trio of co-chairs of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, the No. 8 position in leadership, reflected a swift rise for a first-term lawmaker, and a notable shift in the culture of the Capitol that is underway as Democrats prepare to take power next year. (To wit: the bathroom ban will simply expire next year.)

Some of the Republicans who most frequently badgered Ms. McBride, misgendering her in committee hearings and on the House floor, will be gone from Congress next year. Ms. McBride, 36, on the other hand, will assume a seat at the leadership table for weekly strategy meetings in the speaker’s office.

For two years, Ms. McBride rarely engaged with the personal attacks against her, preferring to focus on policy and not be drawn into a partisan culture war. But in an interview in her office this week, she spoke in more personal terms about what the experience had been like and the significance of her ascent to a leadership position.

“Two years ago, I came into this place and was thrust into the middle of the conversation in a way that I wasn’t eager to be,” Ms. McBride said. “I’m really grateful that after two years of relentless attacks on a community I’m a part of, after two years of some in this building using me as a pawn in their efforts to get attention, after hundreds of millions of dollars spent to demonize people like me, my colleagues demonstrated their values.”

She added: “They didn’t elect me because of my identity; they elected me because of my ideas.”

Ms. McBride, a former Delaware state senator, has always presented an unflappable exterior as some Republicans tried to get a rise out of her, walking to votes and meetings with a Mona Lisa smile on her face.

“Sarah McBride doesn’t get a say,” Representative Nancy Mace, Republican of South Carolina, said in 2024 as she prepared to introduce a resolution barring Ms. McBride from using the women’s bathrooms in the Capitol complex. “I mean, this is a biological man.”

Ms. McBride’s response was to say as little as possible and focus on the kitchen table issues that got her elected.

“Good to see you all,” she greeted reporters as she made her way through freshman orientation, dodging questions about whether she anticipated needing security. Over the next year, she went out of her way to work with Republicans who wanted to collaborate on bipartisan bills.

But beneath that serene exterior, she said that being in the middle of a national news story about her identity was one of the most jarring experiences of her life.

“I remember walking into the Capitol that morning feeling like I had been hit by a truck,” she said of her first day of freshman orientation in 2024, when the Republican effort to bar her from bathrooms had made national news. She had anticipated being a target, but “I didn’t realize how much attention it would get.”

At one point, she recalled walking into a Republican lawmaker’s office for a meeting and hearing an intern taking a call from a constituent apparently complaining that the bathroom fracas was a waste of energy.

“I heard him say, ‘OK, you’re more concerned with Republican congressmen in bathrooms than you are with Sarah McBride,’” she recalled. “It was absolutely an out of body experience.”

Her goal was to be seen as a serious person, whatever amount of heat she took from professional provocateurs.

“Anyone who is ever a first,” she said, “you understand very clearly that if you respond in the way that they want you to respond, it deprives the public of the very clear visual contrast of who the aggressor is and who the person just trying to show up and do their job is.”

The flip side of it all was the well of support from Democratic colleagues. As she walked into her first caucus meeting, she smiled for the cameras because she knew that “if I have a picture where I look sad, they’re all going to use the picture of me looking sad.”

Inside the room, she was greeted with hugs, support and outrage on her behalf.

“I genuinely fell in love with this caucus then,” she said. “It’s a big reason why I wanted to pursue this position.”

In the new job, Ms. McBride has specific ideas about how Democrats can reach more voters and promote what they are doing to make life more affordable, including booking members on general interest podcasts that can penetrate communities that have no interest in politics.

“We’ve got a diversity of talents and backgrounds and interests as a caucus,” she said. “I want to make sure we’re getting that background and interest pitched in front of largely nonpolitical audiences that we often struggle to reach.”

Ms. McBride also said that given the size and ideological diversity of the Democratic caucus, she planned to provide a “bifurcated” approach to getting their message out beyond Washington — one tailored to members from competitive, conservative-leaning districts, and another for progressives who hold seats in solidly Democratic territory.

Ms. McBride’s own experience tuning out personal attacks has also shaped her view of how her party should try to govern.

“What instantly plays well with your own chorus online isn’t always the most fruitful strategy in making progress,” she said. In a world of digital noise, she added, “the algorithms can impact real life, but they are not representative of it.”

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Powerful Health Panel Has Tumultuous First Meeting With Kennedy Appointees

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Since March 2025, the work of the U. S. Preventive Services Task Force has been at a standstill.

By Maggie Astor

After a year and a half of paralysis, the United States Preventive Services Task Force reconvened on Thursday and Friday for the first time with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s newly appointed members.

It quickly became apparent that a bumpy road lies ahead for the task force, which plays a critical role in Americans’ health care by informing what screenings clinicians recommend and what preventive services insurers are required to cover. It considers topics including mammograms, colonoscopies, H. I. V. prevention medications and much more.

The 16 task force members — eight appointed by Mr. Kennedy in September, and eight predating the current administration — aired significant disagreements on whether they should continue to evaluate evidence through the task force’s traditional processes.

At various points, some new members made comments that suggested they were unfamiliar with those procedures, and with the types of questions the task force seeks to answer.

One, Dr. Louis Wilson, asked what the task force normally did in the virtual meetings its internal work groups hold between its three annual in-person gatherings. And in discussing whether to make a recommendation about screening adolescents for unhealthy alcohol use, two — Dr. Ronald Karlsberg and the new chair, Dr. Seth Corey — made comments that suggested they believed the question at issue was whether teen drinking was healthy, rather than whether there was enough evidence to support the benefits of screening.

In a significant departure from past practice, the task force spent Friday morning listening to presentations from outside experts with financial conflicts of interest.

Conflicts of interest also required three new members to recuse themselves from discussion of a long-delayed cervical cancer screening recommendation. All three were among those who received waivers to serve despite owning stocks in large pharmaceutical and biotech companies, whose products are affected by numerous task force recommendations.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

In the past, people with such conflicts were not appointed to the panel to begin with. Very occasionally, someone had to recuse because of a narrow conflict on a single topic, said Dr. Michael Silverstein, the chair of the task force until March. But he could recall that happening only twice in roughly a decade. Three recusals on one topic suggest a body of members “for whom conflicts of interest are going to be a very big problem,” he said.

This was the first in-person meeting since March 2025, after the health department canceled four in a row. While members continued to meet virtually in the intervening time, political appointees prevented them from posting drafts for public comment, voting and publishing final recommendations. Guidelines on at least 18 topics stalled.

On Thursday, Carrie Patnode, a behavioral epidemiologist at Kaiser Permanente, presented the findings of a systematic evidence review her team completed last year for a pending recommendation on lifestyle changes and cardiovascular disease. But she noted that it didn’t incorporate more recent evidence published since the review was completed. Evidence reviews on many topics that stalled over the past year and a half are likely to be similarly out of date.

Perhaps the tensest part of the meeting came when the members discussed edits that Dr. Roger D. Klein, a political appointee leading the federal agency that oversees the task force, had requested to the cervical cancer screening recommendation. These included objections from Dr. Klein to mentioning racial disparities in cervical cancer.

During that conversation, Dr. Sei Lee, a member whose tenure predates Mr. Kennedy, said he wanted to “call out the elephant in the room.”

“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the top line may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Dr. Lee said.

Ultimately, the task force went into a private session to discuss whether to ratify the recommendation, along with the one on alcohol abuse screening and a third on screening for perinatal depression. The task force’s press office said the vote tallies would be made public, but didn’t say when.

A person who was in the room, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that after arguments in which Dr. Klein heatedly defended his removal of the mentions of racial disparities, the task force approved the recommendation with its original language. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Under a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling, Mr. Kennedy has the authority to overrule the task force’s decisions.

Maggie Astor covers women’s health and the health effects of government policies for The Times.

OpinionGuest Essay

By Zachary D. Carter

Mr. Carter is the author of “The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy and the Life of John Maynard Keynes.”

It wasn’t too long ago that Silicon Valley was celebrating the greatest invention in economic history. A dazzling new medium called cryptocurrency had arrived — at once an extraordinary investment, a government-proof digital money and perhaps a way to bring world peace. It would end global poverty and cure inflation. The possibilities were endless — until the public face of the crypto revolution landed in federal prison and the American president began winning his family millions through Trump-branded crypto schemes.

Cryptocurrency still exists, though few take seriously the grandiose promises of yesteryear. As the public’s enthusiasm for digital currency faded, some of its most prominent boosters began showering praise on another shiny object: The artificial intelligence universe is just lousy with crypto players. A. I. “is our alchemy, our Philosopher’s Stone — we are literally making sand think,” trumpeted Marc Andreessen, whose firm has been one of the most influential crypto and A. I. players over the past decade.

Of course, the extreme prognostications about artificial intelligence aren’t exactly like the woo-woo crypto hype of 2020. A. I. already has some genuinely useful applications in software development. It might even blow up the world! Maybe that’s why Silicon Valley’s hype machine has been so successful at turning the economy into a huge one-way bet on delivering a still undefined type of “superintelligence” to the globe. Last year, according to the St. Louis Fed, nearly 40 percent of American economic growth came from the A. I. build-out.

These days, however, excitement is mutating into anxiety. A major A. I.-themed hedge fund collapsed over the summer. Days ago, shares of the A. I. chip giant Nvidia plummeted upon the abrupt resignation of its megawatt chief executive amid allegations of extramarital affairs with a Chinese spy and two women who reported to him. Whatever technological changes may lie in store, the bigger picture is starting to look a lot like a movie we’ve seen before — wild promises and warnings, unusual financing arrangements and the collapse of highflying adventurers. One of our newest industries is following a highly familiar script: The A. I. build-out has become so dependent on the riskiest lending practices of Wall Street that Silicon Valley itself might now be better understood as a wild, unregulated division of the banking sector.

If you haven’t seen this movie, it usually ends in a mess: the 2008 financial crisis, or the collapse of railway mania in 1840s Britain that spurred an industrial depression, or the Panic of 1873 that caused a global catastrophe so bad they called it the Great Depression until that other one came along.

When financial history repeats, fatalism can be hard to resist. It is genuinely disheartening to see people pitch and fall for farcical nonsense, time after time. But our present is not simply repeating the recent past — in important ways, the cycle is getting worse.

Since the 1980s, the United States government has been subjecting more and more of the national economy to the risks of runaway finance. When any financial mania ends, the public shoulders the costs. Crushed stock markets erase savings and ravage job prospects. And when the government has to deploy taxpayer dollars to bail out, say, a major bank that got in over its skis, there’s less money around to fill the potholes, pay for the bus drivers or fund struggling schools. Almost everything working families rely on in daily life gets worse after a financial crisis, and the effects linger for decades in the form of lost earnings and family lives turned upside down by unemployment.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Or at least, it doesn’t have to be this bad. About 90 years ago, the economist John Maynard Keynes observed that monetary markets are inherently preoccupied with stories about the future. We save money to spend it later; we spend now to build and attain the things our future selves will appreciate. Keynes realized that attempts to calculate the future value of an investment accurately would require a level of certainty about the future that human beings do not possess. Sometimes things just happen — strange wars, senile presidents — you never know. Financial judgments are thus inevitably susceptible to the “animal spirits” of human psychology, Keynes wrote, carrying “only a little more” scientific precision than predictions about “an expedition to the South Pole.”

But Keynes insisted that while there may be no perfect economic system, there are degrees of dysfunction. The more a nation’s economy — be it based on manufacturing home appliances or on developing software — is absorbed by the vagaries of its financial functions, the more prone it will be to financial calamity.

At a time when valuations for A. I. firms like Anthropic are rising into the trillions, the American government is pouring gas on the fire. President Trump has been heralding enormous A. I. spending as the economic future, before championing the coming of a “Supreme Intelligence” (since modified to “Super Intelligence,” his preferred term of art). Mr. Trump loves a soaring stock market and understands that the stock market is currently running on A. I. spirits — more than a third of the entire value of all U. S. equities is now subsumed under A. I. stocks. By late summer, tech stocks accounted for more than half the value of the S&P 500.

Not every stock market crash ends in a Great Depression, but the 1929 crash did. That experience persuaded the American government to institute a strict legal separation between financial activities and the rest of the economy — you couldn’t run a manufacturing operation that was also a bank. You couldn’t even run a bank that was also speculating in the stock market; these businesses had to be independently operated and regulated in order to isolate financial contagions, and to protect other economic sectors from the risks inherent to finance. And between the 1930s and the 1970s, this program basically worked. The catastrophic cycle of boom and bust that had plagued the American banking sector since the Civil War came to an end.

In the 1980s, however, President Ronald Reagan ushered in a fundamental redesign of the American economy. There hadn’t been a serious bank crash for decades, and Reagan was convinced that post-Depression regulations and other government red tape were to blame for the rampant inflation and grim productivity that dogged the 1970s. The marching orders were clear: Decentralize government oversight, and unleash the power of American profit.

These changes were not merely legal — they transformed the culture of the economy. For decades, bank executives had been the helpmates of heavy industry, living by the “3-6-3” mantra: borrow at 3 percent, lend at 6 percent, and hit the golf course by 3 p. m. Now they were to be masters of the universe, commanding the American economy from the skyscraper on down, disciplining bloated industry and complacent labor with the relentless drive for lower costs and higher profits. The earth-toned images of crime families and crooked cops that had dominated the late 1970s sharpened into the slicked-back icons of best sellers such as “The Bonfire of the Vanities” and “Liar’s Poker” and the director Oliver Stone’s “Wall Street.”

By the end of the 1990s, it seemed that nobody could imagine an economy pushed onward by anything other than the wolves of Wall Street. When Bill Clinton reviewed his presidential achievements in his 2004 memoir, he didn’t even mention two major financial deregulation bills he had signed into law with overwhelming bipartisan support. Finance was fundamental; financialization was just how the world worked.

The dismantling of Depression-era firewalls has predictably been accompanied by banking crises. As the 1980s turned to the 1990s, over a thousand ordinary savings and loans failed — roughly a third of the entire sector. Private equity firms had seized on new Reagan-era rules to turn these local lenders into dumping grounds for ultra-high-risk debt.

A decade later, executives at previously staid banks like Wells Fargo, Citigroup and Bank of America were enjoying new abilities to cross state lines and storm into the insurance and securities businesses. Once regional operations exploded into multisector international behemoths whose byzantine exposures were all but impossible to track, let alone manage. Even General Motors, the nation’s largest auto company, began exploiting various legal avenues to transform itself into one of the nation’s largest mortgage lenders, a move facilitated by a 1997 Utah state law allowing the company to operate its own full-fledged bank. It was an open mockery of the wall between finance and commerce that had been built after the Depression. Federal regulators looked the other way — until the financial crisis. By 2010, the U. S. Treasury had devoted $17.2 billion to rescuing G. M.’s bank, and $49.5 billion to save General Motors. Congress authorized hundreds of billions of dollars to help save the rest of the nation’s financial system, with trillions more in emergency lending from the Federal Reserve.

All of these debacles resulted in privileged insiders’ reaping enormous rewards while ordinary Americans were called in to clean up the mess. Banks dependent on public support paid out billions of dollars in bonuses to their top executives. The national unemployment rate hit 10 percent.

Financialization changed American institutions and altered the national culture of work and reward. Today, roughly one in four young men in America trades stocks on a daily basis; a similar percentage of young men gamble on a daily basis. Most of them, according to a conservative think tank, “feel like failures.” The, ahem, traditional sports betting industry in the United States scored record revenues of nearly $17 billion last year — never mind the growth of the indistinguishable activity at new sites called prediction markets, which are moving $24 billion a month globally.

Dudes have more time to trade these days: Between 1980 and 2000, the United States lost about two million manufacturing jobs. Mr. Clinton didn’t just deregulate finance; he attacked domestic industry by signing the North American Free Trade Agreement into law and welcoming China into the World Trade Organization. As a share of the U. S. economy, today’s financial sector is roughly triple the size of its post-World War II nadir — but even this figure is difficult to estimate, because so much financial activity has been subsumed into the tech world itself, with trillions of dollars in investment now hanging in the balance.

Everywhere you look in 2026, multitrillion-dollar tech companies are storming into the financial world. Meta and Apple now move funds for digital shoppers around the world, while Amazon and Apple pitch credit cards. Nvidia, the country’s largest computer chip manufacturer, is also a major lender to the A. I. industry and its insatiable hunger for cash, approving $500 billion worth of partnerships with big banks and private equity firms. Nvidia doesn’t just make and sell the chips that power the A. I. revolution. It also invests in the data centers that power the technology, and is partnering with OpenAI and other A. I. developers to provide hundreds of billions of dollars in additional financing for still more A. I.-related projects.

Nvidia is even in talks with insurance companies to insure these loans against default. This should sound familiar: In the early 2000s, big banks turned to the insurer A. I. G. to protect themselves against losses on risky mortgage bonds. But when home prices crashed, A. I. G. collapsed, risking the viability of Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and others. Insurance did not alleviate financial risk — it loaded an extra layer of financial risk atop the market, amplifying dangers rather than reducing them.

Whether Nvidia can, in fact, secure an insurer remains to be seen. But the impulse is revealing. By operating as a lender, Nvidia is already injecting the instability of Wall Street directly into what has become the most economically critical manufacturing operation in the country — as a matter of standard corporate policy. How fitting that the executor of many of Nvidia’s aggressive financial moves, the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has just been named its interim chief executive; the company’s financial maneuvers may be as critical to its future as its physical products.

Nvidia isn’t propping up the sector alone. A multitrillion-dollar sub-industry of “private credit” — a term of art for loans made beyond the purview of traditional financial regulations — has ballooned at the nation’s largest banks and private equity firms. And this shadow market just happens to specialize in hard-to-value projects related to A. I. and data centers.

The candle is burning from both ends. Wealthy individuals are increasingly relying on tech stocks as collateral for loans that are propping up our economy — loans to buy real estate, or cars, or even more tech stocks. A tech blowup could thus easily disrupt lending to other sectors of the economy: Mess with either the A. I. build-out or its increasingly fragile financial underpinnings, and both will be in trouble. They are already in many respects the same entity.

In other countries, innovation isn’t so heavily focused on A. I. China is investing in A. I. too, but it is accompanying its computer push with $2.2 trillion a year in green tech investment that is about strengthening manufacturing prowess rather than pure processing power. China has been developing better solar panels, more powerful wind farms, more efficient batteries and a new generation of electric vehicles. These innovations have their own stories to tell about the future, but there is an important difference between promising to improve something that already exists — say, a car, an effort that adds jobs — and vowing to change the technological foundation of all work without a plan. In the United States, the bulk of A. I. spending goes into building data centers with temporary local benefits; once they’re built, the construction jobs are gone, while the tax incentives deployed to get them constructed drain resources from state and local governments.

It is folly to hope the Trump administration will do anything to avert an A. I.-driven financial crisis. The administration is not only encouraging the tech industry’s leap into the turbulent waves of finance; it is helping car manufacturers get back into banking, too. In January, about 17 years after our government was forced to bail out G. M.’s bank, the Trump administration approved applications from Ford and G. M. to open new banks, headquartered in Salt Lake City.

This is probably going to hurt all of us, and managing the fallout from a crash is as much art as science. How we ought to structure the economy going forward, however, has been clear since the Great Depression: Don’t let big business merge with big finance. Our government needs to hold big tech and big finance accountable for operating deeply uncertain businesses with vast public consequences. We need smaller, simpler tech companies that support American industry rather than dominating it.

A. I. optimists tend to spend a lot of time talking about how the technology will cure cancer or end poverty — an acknowledgment that A. I. is a means to other advances that actually matter to people. If you follow the money, however, Silicon Valley is far more focused on generating more computing power, in the belief, held by some, that it will give A. I. superhuman abilities that will fix all of our problems. Not everyone agrees with that belief. Major A. I. executives can’t even agree on what A. I. is. (Most do seem to agree that they should not be liable for crimes committed with their new tools.)

Better computers can help with all kinds of things, but you can’t cure cancer with data centers alone. As with the pandemic-era crypto boom, A. I. has let its stories about the future run so far ahead of economic reality, the ultimate project starts to look like sweeping economic change for the sake of sweeping economic change. There are better futures to bet on.

Living in a state that surprised everyone on Election Day, I think you are expressing exactly what people voted for. We want America back. The country that once stepped away from royal centralization in favor of the People. That may sound naive but it is exactly where we are.

I wish I thought the recent election indicated a realization that our values were off track. I'm afraid for many people it just reflected their unhappiness with gas prices. Some people have (somehow) been surprised at the ugliness of this administration's "immigration control" efforts, and reckless use of war as distraction, but we have a disappointingly large number of people who would overlook any stupidity, until it affects the price of gas.

Zachary D. Carter is the author of “The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy and the Life of John Maynard Keynes.”

The Outages Are Just Getting Started

Wired November 21, 2026

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”

Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at kernelpanic@wired. com. And stay safe out there.

A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

The chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:

Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

How We Test Power Banks

I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

Wired November 21, 2026

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

But questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

Hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

According to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.
